TO SINGLE LADIES. To be let at a very desirable rate, . A. snug little house, in a fine healthy state: 'lts a bacheior s Leart, and the agent is Chance, Affectt in the rent—to be paid in advance. The owner, as yet, has possessed it alone, So the figures are not of much' value; but coon 'Twill be furnished by Cupid himself, it a wife Take a lease for the term of a natural life The tenant will have a few taxes to pay— Love, honour, and—heaviest item—obey! As for the goodwill, the owner's inclined To have that—if agreeable, settled in kind— Provided true title, by proof can bershown To a heart encumbered and free as his own. So ladies, dear ladies, pray do not forget, Here's an excellent bachelor's heart to be let. CALEDONIA: Written aboard the ' thansmaa ' during a cruise among the Hebrides, in the heart of some of the finest scenery in Scotland. '0 Caledonia, stern and wild!' I here, , Amid thine awful rocks and wondrous isles And flowing stretch of land and sea and sky, Where Nature garbs her in her grandest robe. Would sing thy prates I EaChanting are thy lochs, Stupendous are thy memorable bens. Thy wave-beat shores are vastly beautiful. And every valley has Its magic charm. Thy teal sons are noble as the hills Enviroeing thtir treasured northern homes! We, sows of Albion, would hall ye, brothers! . And vow with you to cherish more and more The b rids of love and mutual sympathy. Which long have held ekessession of oar souls. And if, as would-be prophets grimly say. Terrib e storm o'erhangs our sacred coasts. Or should opposing forces rush to wrest The dear eld laud from out its chitdren's grasp, They'll find them one beyond what thy had deemed In nearest surmise to the spleuelld truth; And we and ye united. flinchlei sly The tempest's utmost wrath will gladly dare; Or, blazing with a quenclolers patriot-fire. Shall hurl the shivering enemy away. Cursing the day he saw the light, as back These rugged mountains hurl the foaming Waves. Would that our Sister, Edn, sorely bruised— Red with explriug eras of kean woe— %Yount cease to brood over her dying wrongs And join the alliance grand three neighbouring realms— Thou. whom I chiefly sing, and Cambria The :air and white-cliffed Albion—have sworn To keep inviolate till doom shall strike. Erin, we trust thou wilt! We three are one! Come, join the group! Together we'll mainta:n Our empire's glory and our world-wide fame Uninjured, spite of ereakerei doleful tales. And madly misanthropic fear of fall, 'Until the giant world grows hoar with years. And Time himself begins to think of death. Come, lay thy weary head upon our breast! Old Albion loves thee. Erin, as she loves Cambria and Caledonia, and as they Love her with fondness most reciprocal. Why wilt thou linger in the bitter cold, And gnaw, Ir:flexible. thy lo3alt away With futile pining; for a lore career, Which could but end ia huger woe To-day. Surrounded by warm, loyal ecottish hearts. I dream of future gloties that awalt A tour-fold nation and I breathe the hope— Greeting mere strong in this fee atmosphere That as the sunshine from these ancient peaks Bids the thick mists begone, so speedily Our triple love for thee shall all disperse The lowering clouds that long have girt thy shores ; That thou, whose generous sons are IN ave as these 'Hong whose delightful glens I glide entranced. In this 'the land of mountain and of fl sod,' May 'at' leave the tracks that lead down to the dark, And with thy els, ers three espouse the right,— quadruply walking in the stainless path Of liberty; a pattern to the world, Redressing wrong, alding the good and true, And heralds of a time when humankind Shall be a mighty brotherhood. Warrington. ARTIt cc BIUMETT.

A wise man orders what is necessary to that which serves •only for curiosity, ornament, or pleasure. A man would never be too confident of anything if he always remembered how often he had been mistaken. "When I was a boy," said Thackeray, "I wanted some toffy. It was a shilling; I hadn't one. When I was a man I had a shilling; but I did% want any toffy..." English nobleman to Highland ghillie somewhat deficient in English, and whose father had been a weaver: "What occupation did your father follow, Mac ?" Ghillie: "My father wass a spider, my tort, he wass." "No, sir," said the men, "you needn't tell me a woman over had her dress pocket picked. I don't believe a thie4 could discover it. I know I've tried for two hours to find the pocket of one of nay wife's dresses, and then had to gice! it tip." Alexander Dumas was one day the guest of Dr. Gistal, a leading practitioner in Marseilles. After dinner, while the coffee was being handed round, the host requested the great novelist to enrich his album. with one of his witty itnprovi- nations. "Certainly," replied Damao, with a smile; and drawing out a pencil he wrote, under the eyes of his enterl tamer, the fell° wing lines : Since Dr. Distal name to our town. Ta care diseases cesual and hereditary. The hospital has been pulled down— " You falterer 1" here exclaimed the doctor, mightily pleased; but the poet went on— And we have made a larger cemetery. HARRIET MARTINEAU'S LAST yEaus.—Throughout the invalid existence which she was doomed henceforth to lead, she was resigned and cheerful; not a word of complaint, though she suffered mach pain, fell from her lips or from her pen; bat she never recovered her old spirits. Our simple junketings and merriment were over. Year after year I used to come and see her, and every time there was a dis- tinct decay of strength. Her intelligence remained as keen as ever, and her interest in the affairs of the world from -which she was cut off; but to me, with the remembrance of other days in my mind, those visits were very sad. At first I was admitted at the same familiar door, on the same terms as usual; then only an hour's interview was allowed by the doctor's orders; then only half an hoar. She wrote to me, however, though even letter-writing had become toilsome to her, pretty frequently. Her own increasing ailments were dismissed with a word or two; but all that pertained to those she loved was interesting to her, even to quite trivial details. "I was rejoiced to hear from Mr. W., she says in her last letter," of your dear wife looking so well. My love to her. So you are getting bald? Never mind so long as it is you, not she. If men cal shave all their liven, instead of wearing their proper beards, they must not complain of growing bald. A mile and a half (isn't it?) of hair shaved off in a man's lifetime may well make him bald. . . Oh, yes, I am worse—much. It has been a terrible summer for pain. Seven weeks without one minute's intermission! That is over now; a great increase of opiates, and now the cold (the letter is dated November), have caused a consider- able rally for the present. . . . Love to Tiny [the worker of the book-marker so many years ago], and all of you, from your affectionate old friend." Those were the last words I had from Harriet Martineau.--Cornha Maya.

eat. WeePoer Tun ClontraMT.—" I never passed a more agreeable day than yesterday. The day was delightful, the scene transporting; the trees, lawns, concaves, all in the perfection ie which the ghost of Bent would joy to see them. At twelve we made the tour of the farm in eight chaises and calashee, horsemen and footmen, setting out like a picture of Wcaverman's. . . . We had a mag- nificent dinner, cloaked in the modesty of earthenware; French horns and hautboys on the lawn. We walked to the Belvidere on the summit of the hill, where a theatrical storm only served to heighten the beauty of the landscape, a rainbow on a dark cloud falling precisely behind the tower of a aeighboaring church between another tower and the building at Claremont. . . . Thence we passed into the wood, and the ladies formed a circle on chairs before height ethhet month of the cave, which was overhung oa as with woodbines, lilacs, and labernums, and dignified by tall, shapely cypresses. On the descent of the hill were placed the French horns; the abigails, servants, and neighbours wandering below by the river; in short, it was Parnassus as Watteau would have painted it. Here we had a rural syllabub, and part of the company returned to town; but were replaced by Giardini and Onofrio, who with Nivernois on the violin and Lord Pembroke on the bass, accompanied Miss Pelham, Lady Rockingham, and the Duchess of Grafton who sang. This little concert lasted till past ten; •then there were minuets, and as we had several couples left, .it =eluded with a country dance. A quarter after twelve they sat down to support, and I came home by a charming moonlight." This was Landon in the country; but of true 4011ntry society as he found it at Houghton, cr in the com- pany of the neighbouring Aldermen from Lynn, Walpole was by no means so fond. 'Were I a physician," he says, "I would prescribe nothing but, recipe, CCCLXV. drachm Londin." His neighbours in Norfolk struck him as illustra- tions of "the atupifying effect of beef, ale, and wine," and his description of them gives a horrible idea that Hogarth's pictures really must have represented the human beings of , hiS day :—" Hvery day I see men who are mountains of roast beef, and only seem just roughly hewn out into the outlines of human form like the giant rock at Prabolino ! I shudder when I see them brandish their knives in act to carve, and look on them as savages that devour one another. I should not stare at all more than I do if yonder Alderman at the lower end of the table was to stick his fork into his neighbour's jolly cheek, and out a brave %ilea of brawn and fat. Why, swear I see no difference between a country gentleman and a sirloin ; . . . indeed, the sirloin does not ask so many questions." After this it is a comfort to learn that even after his experience of an election, Walpole thought the Aldermen of Lynn had improved, for he tells us 20 years after, in 1763, that-" To do the folks justice, they. are sensible reasonable, and civitlhis eemd .; tpaetirtrivbeurtye language is polishedsince I lived among this to their more frequAlt intercourse with the world and the capital, by the help of good roads and postchaises, which, if they have abridged the King's dominions have at le.at tamed his subjects. The story comes from Paris that a lady, who visited four churches in one day; missel her umbrella on returning horns. She immediately revisited all four churches, and found her umbrella in the last one. When the umbrella was handed to her she thankfully said to the sexton, "The people at this church are much more honest than those at the others." WHY He FELT MEAL—If ever Igo into a new locality again I will study up my geography better than I did this time, for my ignorance got me into a most uncomfortable position. As the boat neared Sanford I was standing with others on the deck, when a very pretty young lady came up I to me, and, with a sweet smile on her face, up into mine with a pair of lovely eyes and asked, "Are you going to kiss me, sir?' If someone had offered to lend me 510 I could not have been more surprised, and hardly knowing what to say and in order to gain a little time I gasped oat, "Pardon, Miss, what did you ask ?" I felt that she knew I heard her, but she said sweetly, "Are you going to kiss me , to-night ?I' There was no misunderstanding her this time.: heard her, and so did others, and I felt the blood rushing into my face, and I stammered out, "I would like to accoat- modate you, miss, I would truly, but I have a wife and 13 small children on board with me, and if my wife should see me kissing you —" " Kissing you, you hateful old thing! who asked you to kiss me?" "You did," I yelled "you asked me twice!" "You old fool, I asked you if you were going to Biasime—Kissime City—to-night (don't you know anything ?" and off she went. But if ever anybody felt meaner than I did, I would like to exchange photo- graphs with him.—Florida Letter. Nov g SaYLOCE.—A day or two ago a man who was at the Central depot to take a train suddenly cried out that some one had stolen his valise, and he began such a hulla- baloo that everybody had to be interested. "I sot that 'ere satchel right down that' and stepped, to the (loci," he ex- plained to Officer Barton, "and when I returned it was gone." "Well, you should have been careful. We are not: responsible for such losses." "You ain't, eh? Whar's the president ?" "Out of the city, sir." Whar's the general manager?" "He's sick abed." "Whar's the superintendent ?" "Won't be here till four o'clock." "Wall, now, somebody's got to make good that loss, or about a dozen men will go to iVhessalt„ s What t a the hospital for six months d nitnatnhs apiece a iece N value?" "Fifty dollars, were the contents?" "I had 12 shirts, a new Suit of clothes, an overcoat, and lots of other things." "Was it a carpet sack?"Sh' "She was. one as2' handle handle cone and the lock broken ?" "Yes, was gone, and I had her tied with a string." "Is this it?" asked the officer, as he took the baggage off a bench not six feet away. "Great snaken I , That's herr' chuckled the owner. In handing it to him the I string broke, the bag flew open, and out rolled two old shirts, a pair of socks, and five or six paper cellars—all ' S ' I there was in it. "Then these were the dads you wanted 50 , dollars for?" queried the officer. " o, sir, was the in- dignant reply. "I should have taken the money for loss of time and damage to my feelings. I'm no Shylock, sir!" PARTIAL TO FOLICEMEN.—A. few years ago a policemae was killed near Dublin, and a sharp, active little spaniel would go in and out of the chamber where the body was some , nnd one ly- ing, and seemed to take a personal interest in the inquest. The conduct of the dog occasioned surprise of the magistrates questioned the inspector as to whom the dog belonged. And this was the story he heard about "Peeler," the policeman's pet. Some years ago poor little Peeler had tempted the appetite of an enormous dog of the Mount St. Bernard breed, the giatt--I may say the orgre of his race. The unhappy spaniel ran great risk of Wing served up and devoured at the breakfast of his canine majesty, when a policeman interfered, and with a blow of his staff laid low the strong and released the weak. From that moment Peeler entertained unlimited respect and grati- tude towards policemen. Pnesicar, EFFECTS OF MANURES.—It too frequently happens that in considering the effect of a manure, its chemical action on the soil is alone thought of; besides this, however, its mechanical action should also be taken into account. It is, as we have previously maintained in these columns, very much to its influence on the physical proper- ties of the Boil that the universally good results following the application of farmyard manure are to be attributed. Wollny has made some experiments with artificial fertilisers which are worth notice. He mixed clay thoroughly with water, so that the liquid was crowded with innumerable fine particles of the earth. On adding small quantities of ammonia, or of alkaline phosphates or carbonates, to the water, the clay is at once precipitated in a dense form. On the other hand, mineral acids and their salts, such as nitrate of soda, act in the opposite way, precipitating the clay, it is true, but in a light and spongy form, occupying much space. Henceahe concludes that the addition of alkaline substances to soils has an unfavourable effect upon their porosity and lightness, and consequently on their fertility; an he he quotes, as cases in point, the alkali plains of Ne- v a and California, the soil of which is hard, dense, non- ttorous, and sterile. On the other hand, such salts as nitrate of soda,salphate of potash, saltpetre, and kainit produce at once a benedcial effect on the porous character of arable soil; but the salts mentioned are so quickly washed out in , case of rain that the effect is not lasting. Of all artificial 1" fertilisers it is found that ,tole exercises the most favour- able influence on the physical properties of the soil, causing it to aggregate into flocculent particle which persist for , years, thus making it light, and therefore more fertile. , Eirtre ssatim IN DEREYSHIRE.—Th be e members of the Derby- eh .Agricultural Society and others to the number of over a hundred on Monday respondedo an i ; Mr. J. OATMEAL FOR Maar Cows.—There exists in Germany a decided preference for oatmeal as a milk-producing food for cows; but until Dr. Scam& lately conducted a series of experiments no exact information had been obtained. He has given the results of each experiments with five cows for four 30-day experiment periods. In each period the cows had the same coarse fodder, which was straw and roots, hay, and the same quantity of cottonseed meal, about 11b, per day per head. The grain only was varied. In the first period it was 6 51b. of wheat bran; in the second, 8 81b. of a mixture of equal parts of rye, barley, and oatmeal; in the third period the same total quantity of grain was given, of which one-half was oatmeal instead of one-third; and in Oc flurth period the cows had the same ration as at first.

Max's DIGNITY AND DESTINY.—As a rain-drop falling into the ocean leaves no noticeable change in the atmosphere I from which it fell, so a man dropping out of life into the mysterious depths of death leaves no very perceptible and durable vacuum in the social sphere wherein he wrought , out his destiny. How humiliating to human pride is this fact! But looking again at the lost rain-drop we see it raised in the arms of the sun to its former place in the heavens, while it swells the cloud which gives moisture, verdure, and beauty to the productive earth. In this too, it is emblematic of the good man, whose influence is not buried in his grave, but lives on in the souls he helped while living, and will through them be distilled on still other human hearts. How grand a creature, therefore, is man, who can transmit an endless benediction to the world! HBART MDSIC 'OF SOEIROW.—Very many of the sweetest joys of Christian hearts are songs which have been learned in the bitterness of trial. It is said of a little bird that he will never learn to sing the song his master will hare him sing whilst it is light in his cage. lie learns a snatch of every song he hears, but will not learn a fall, separate melody of his own. And the master covers the cage and , makes it dark all about the bird, and then he listens and learns the one song that is taught te him, until his heart is frill of it. Then, ever after, he sings the song in the light. , With many of us it is as with the bird. The Master has a . song Be wants to teach to us, but we learn only a strain of it, a note here and there, while we catch up snatches of the , world's song and sing them with it. Then He comes Be makes it dark about us •till we learn the sweetest melodyand would teach us. Many of the loveliest songs of peace and trust sang by God's children in this world have been taught In the darkened chamber of sorrow.—lllustrated Christian WeddS4 THE " DARvEsT" OF LAXYLAND.—At that time tastes were simple, and persons who like Dr. Syntax came in search of the picturesque, were content with cleanliness and home- liness. Nevertheless, the whole district even then laid itself out for "the visitors." The irruption of the cheap trippers which Wordsworth feared (though he did write "The Ex- ; cursion") had not yet come, but in summer and autumn the district was thronged with strangers, who generally made a considerable stay in it. When any of these were clergy- ' men, the local divines got them to preach for them, and I remember at Bownesa Church a curious incident arising from *, this circumstance. There had been a good deal of dry weather in the south, and an Oxford man who occupied the pulpit began to read the prayer for rain, when the clerk pulled at the skirts of his surplice. "You musn't read that sir,” he whispered; "we don't want it." "But it's aprwaayne: • for a good harvest, my man," reasoned the minister, "That's just it; the visitors are our harvest, and we none of your rain." I need not say that this occurrence amused Miss Martineau (who had her own views about the rainfall) not a little.—Cornhill Magazine.. : KEPT HIS BOOTS Os. —Dr. Muller, the head physician of the Prussian general staff, was allowed to go.to Japan in order to assist in the arrangement of the Japanese Military Academy. When the hour came for his presentation to the Mikado, he naturally clothed himself in full uniform. The Court officials informed him that he could not be permitted to enter the awful presence unless he complied with Japanese usage., and pulled off his boots. Dr. Muller re- fused to comply. There was much debate over the diffi- culty, the Court .Chamberlain insisting that the physician must nnboot himself, and he declaring that he would not enter without his boots. At last Dr. Muller hit upon the ingenious notion of casting all the responsibility of the situation upon the Emperor Wilhelm. "My master, the German Kaiser," said he. " commanded me to present my- self before the august Emperor of Japan in fall Prussian uniform. Now, the boots constitute an important part of the Prussian uniform, and I dare not appear as his repre- sentative without these important accessories." The Cham- berlain went to the Mikado with this explanation, and the result was that Mr. Muller marched into the audience• chamber in his boots. His was the first shoe-leather which had ever desecrated the floor of the Mikado Palace in Tokio. CURIUM Trtams.-;;Few fruits are more appreciated tiles well-ripened sweet Cherries, and we only wish the birds were not so fond of them. The sight of a ripe Black Heart or a Bigarrean is so irresistible to a blackbird that he will venture inside the net that is used to protect the fruit if there is an inlet sufficiently large to admit him. The Kentish Cherries and the Morello's are similarly fascinating, but from their acidity Mr. Blackbird spends much of his time in simply tasting one Cherry after another, and he will serve the whole so before he will be convinced that they are

not the same kind as he feasted on earlier in the season when he left us nothing but the bare stones dangling on the trees like so many pendants destitute of utility. The sweet Cherries require a wall to protect them, the end or that part of the dwelling which faces south is the most suitable. • We know of one in such a position that has not failed to bear a good crop of fine Black Bigarreans for years, and all the labour bestowed upon it is very trifling, about an hour in the whole year, which is devoted to securing some of the thick branches. Strong tar !string, fastened to nails driven In the well, should be used for the purpose of tying. The Cherry is, such a resolute flowerer that it is rarely seen at the proper time destitute of thousands of clusters; but its early flowering habit and tender nature subjects it to frosts and other adverse circumstances, so that comparatively few come to perfection, and they are frequently flowers that have developed last. What little pruning the trees require should be done now. We shorten the long shoots to three or four eyes or buds of the base, similar to the spurring of Red Currants, and occasionally we deem it necessary to cut some of the very long spurs clean off, more especially if they have the appearance of being crowded. The Morello is much hardier than the sweet Cherries, and is highly esteemed for tarts and for making Cherry Brandy, and consequently realises high prices. The beat position for these is against a wall facing north, and they will also do well as dwarf standards or dwarfs like the Apple and Pear, in which case they need no pruning, but when against a wall the case is different. When once the wall is covered it is obvious that as much old wood must be removed as it is necessary to lay in this year. There is no shortening of shoots of the past year's growth, but they must be laid in full length, and in- ferior ones removed to make space for them. It must not be understood that the whole of last year's growth must be nailed to a wall, but a selection of the strongest and straightest shoots. Tint FRONT GARDEN.—The Dahlia roots that were taken up and stored away in the autumn should be examined. When placed out of sight they are liable to be forgotten, and when actually required are, in a season like this, found shrivelled, and in one more severe in a semi-rotten state— the result of having been frozen at some time or other. If the roots are not found plump, place them in pots or boxes, and cover them over with moderately moist soil, but 'with- hold water for the present. Anemones, or the Windflower, may be sown at the end of the month. Select a warm sunny spot, and if the soil is inclined to be stiff mix with a foot of the top soil some sand and light rich manure. Drills 2in. deep should be drawn, in which the seeds should be thinly sown. The cottony substance which surrounds the seeds makes it a difficult matter to distribute them evenly. We therefore pull them apart, and mix some sand, so that they may not re-adhere. Many of the seeds sown during the next three weeks or month will flower well before the close of the year. Taz WINDOW.—WATERING.—The best time for watering is in the morning at this season of the year, and the best water is rain water; and whether it is procured from the pond, the ditch, or the tub, it is of the utmost importance that it should be at all times of the same temperature as the room the plants are in, and it will be all the better if it Is two Or three degrees higher. When the roots of plants have applied to them a quantity of water colder than the soil they are in, they receive a check from each application. Roots of many indoor plants are now being formed or in a state of activity, and the white-looking spongieles are far more susceptible of injury than the matured roots. Luke- warm water will stimulate them by increasing the tempera- ture of the soil for a time, whilst cold water cools it and temporarily paralyses the plant. Primulas, hardy and half- hardy, are very beautiful, and many may be cultivated in tke window or with the protection of a frame. Primula loarniosa, or the "Dusty Miller," will soon be throwing up its flowering spike as white as if it had been dipped in a flour bag, but the expanded flowers are pale lilac. From this time forth they must not be allowed to get anything like dry. Prirnala Cortusoides, of which there are several varietieS, varying in colour from deep dark pink to a very pale shade, as well as a white variety. They are all decidu- ous, and at this time show indications of growth, when we re-pot them by shaking all loose soil away from the root and introduce in its place such as we use for Pelagoniums and, if the plant demands it, we give a larger pot or divide the plant and make two or more from it, and place them in pots according to their size.

It is announced from Nagasaki that Professor Milne, of seismic fame, has arrived there from Yokohama, and will institute an underground observatory in the Takashinoa mines. The objects sought to be determined are variou., and amongst other paraphernalia instruments will be placed 1 to discover if the seismic phenomena observed "at grass" are coincident with and of similar intensity to those at various levels in the mine. This observatory will be unique, no other similar establishment being in existence in any

country. The Royal Astronomical Society has awarded Mr. T. Ainslie Common its gold medal for his photographs of celestial bodies. This high reward has, it is believed, been mainly bestowed on account of the magnificent photograph he has succeeded in taking of the great nebula in Orion. It is not often that a non-professional astronomer has gained the honour of gold medalist. Since the award to Mr. De la Rae,in 1862,f0r his photographs of the solar eclipse, Messrs. Huggins and Miller received a joint medal for their re- searches in astronomical physics in 1867, and Baron Dena- brouski one for double star work in 1878; the 14 other medals going to professional astronomers. THE WESTINGHOUSE SAFETY APPARATUS FOR CROSS- INGS.—The croesing of the Philadelphia and Reading and Lehigh Valley Railroads, two miles west of Bound Brook, New Jersey, has been fitted with interlocking signals and derailing switches upon the Westinghouse electro-hydro- pneumatic system, the movements of the switches and sig- nals being effected by compressed air coht,rolled by electri- city from the signal cabin. This arrangement allows a train having the right of way to pass the crossing at fall speed, daring which passage it automatically locks open the derailing switches on the intersecting track, thereby preventing all possibility of collision. The apparatus has been erected by the Union Switch and Signal Company, of Pittsburgh, and came into operation on January 6. This is stated to be the first apparatus of the kind ever erected, and has excited much interest among American railway men.— Iron. INSTINCT—At a meeting of the Royal Institution recently, Mr. George J. Romanes delivered a lecture on "Darwinian Theory of Instinct." Instinctive actions he defined as ac- tions of consciously adaptive character prior to individual experience, performed without necsssary knowledge of the I relation between means employed and ends attained, and similarly performed under similar appropriate circumstances by all individuals of the same species. Instinct, however, when fully formed, is not invariably fixed as generally sup- posed; bat, on the contrary, is highly plastic under the guiding hand of intelligence. As an experiment, after a hen has laid dummy eggs, Mr. Romanes introduced four young ferrets to her nest. The growl of the ferrets, instead of the chirp to which she had been accustomed, apparently puzzled the old hen; but slut clung to them, and after the manner of her kind sought to make them follow her—unsuccessfully, I of coarse. She tried to keep the tender animals, but would often fly from them screaming when they gave the nip that evidenced their search " for the traditional source of main- Malian nutriment." ASIERECAN INVENTIONS IN PatN4rlNG.—k very ingenious invention for the simplification of letterpress printing is about to-be introduced into this country from America. Its object is to supersede the movable types now in use. A kind of manual is employed, turning a cylinder upon which the various letters of the alphabet are arranged. From this cylinder, whtch revolves very rapidly, impressions are con- veyed to damp papier mache slips, which are subsequently arranged in frames for the purpose of being stereotyped. The services of compositors are therefore, when this ma- chine is employed, dispensed with entirely. The great diffi- culty which will occur to practical men is as to the possi- bility of making corrections when there are no movable types to be dealt with, but the inventors claim that they have managed to solve that problem. The. machine has been submitted to several eminent firms of printers in Lon- don, and has been received by them with considerable ap- proval.—The discovery of a new process which enables any I number of copies to be taken of the oldest book without set- ting a line of type is also reported. A compound has been discovered which may be spread upon a page without in the slightest way injuring the paper, and which refuses to rest upon ink. It can be easily removed to a stone, and there , 'oecomes the matrix for stereotype, or can be used for print- log from at once. You hand your best beloved Aldine to the inventor of this new process, and he will return it to you without a stain or a mark, uninjured and only cleaned, and he will give you along with it an exact fac-simile, let- .3;hae ter for letter and broken stop for broken stop, of the volume great which he has had in his possession for only a few days.

ANNUAL MEETING. The annual general meeting of the shareholders in the above company' was held at the Public Hall, on Monday last, at noon, for the transaction of the ordinary business. In the absence of Dr. Smith (chairman of the company), Mr. John Ryland (deputy-chalet:can) presided; , there, being also present Alderman Joseph Davies, Covpcillors John Pier- point, Dr. Mackie, Whittle, Messrs. John White, Robert Garnett, T. B, Carter, .Blackhurst, and William Johnson (secretary.)

div.p: The total Income for the past year (including piano and organ receipts) has been £484 9a 34, and the total expenditure £3BO 193 eld. This latter stun includes £4O brought front the pre- vious year, being the balance paid for permanent imorove- meats during 1881. As will be seen from the annexed balance sheet, the amount available for dividend is £l4l Is Oid, out of which 'r I. proposed to pay a dividen-d of £3 per cent, carrying forware a balance of £lO is Oid. Two of the director, Mr. &be Armitage and Mr. T. B. Carter, retire by rotati m. 1 hey are eligible, and are recommended for re-election. The auditor, Mr. Holmes, is also eligible for re-election. The CHAIRMAN expressed his regret at the absence of Dr. Smith, the chairman of the Company, who was seriously and prevented from attendise that meeting. He then moved the adoption of the report, which he remarked cnn- tamed nothing calling for special mention except that he had to congratulate the shareholders upon the past year having been a tolerably successful one. Councillor PIREPOINT oeconded the adoption of the re- port. A conversation ensued as to whether it was necessary for the directors to appeal against the assessment of the build- ing, £l4O gross, which was considered too high, and which the Secretary stated represented a dividend of over 3 per cent.—The Crietnatax pointed out that they were not as- , sensed upon the amount of capital but on what the building would reasonably be let at to a tenant who would make such a profit as the Company was making, and certain allowances would be made.—Councillor FIERPOINT thought that inas- much as the institution was not paying 4 per cent that they were over-assessed seeing the amount now charged.— Dr. MACKIE asked,what portion of the year the Hall was now used? Was it a third?—The SECRETARY said it *as more than a third—about one-half.—Dr. MACKIE drew at- tention to the fact that the city of Perth, although already possessing a large hall belonging to the Corporation and seVeral small ones, whilst the town was only two-thirds of the size of Warrington, they had lately built is public Wall at a cost of upwards of £9,000. They were endeavour- ing to create a profit by getting-travelling parties to take the building on share.—The Cmainstax interrupting, observed that that was rather a matter for the consideration of the directors than the annual meeting. He thought also that the question of the assessment of the Hall might be left in the hands of the dlrectors, and that the latter should decide whether it was necessary to appeal against the amassment. or not,—Dr. MACKIE believed that anything coming from the present meeting woutd strengthen the hands of the I directors.—The CHAIRMAN said if the directors prepared a matured scheme they might bring it before the shareholders at a special meeting convened for the purpose.—The re- port was then adopted. Mr. Glanwurr moved—" That a dividend be declared for the past year at the rate of 3 per cent, free of income tax, payable on and after Ist March, 1584."—This was seconded by Mr. JOHN WHITz, who remarked that although he wished they had been in a position to declare a larger divi- dend, yet he considered they had reason to be Bedell with what they had done during the past year. During the twenty years the Hall had been in existence they had never once met without being enabled to give a dividend to the shareholders, and that was a great deal more than the proprietors of many of the public halls throughout the king- dom could say. (Hear, hear).—The resolution was carried.

RE-ELECTIONS.—VOTES OF THANKS. Mr. BLACKHURET moved and Mr. WHITTLE secon led, and it was agreed, "Thkt Mr. Ziba Armitage and Mr. B. Carter be re-elected directors of the company." On the motion of Mr. GARNETT, seconded by Mir. BLACK- HURST, it was resolved "That the thanks of the meeting be given to Mr. C. J. Holmes for his services as auditor, and that he be requested to continue the same for the ensu- ing year. Also that 215 be paid him for his services dur- ing the past year." Mr. WHITTLE moved and Mr. BLACKIMR,T seconded, "That the thanks of the meeting be given to the chairman and directors for the services rendered by them during the past year, and that an honorarium of one olinea be paid them." The CHAIRMAN replied to this compliment on behalf of Dr. Smith, who, he said, had been a most zealous president of the company ever since its establishmenf, A Vote of thanks to the Chairman for Ptesidin r. on the proposition of Alderman DAWES, seconded by C. ncilior Ptut,YvidT, concluded the business of the meeting.

WARRINGTON LIBERAL ASSOCIA- TION. LIBERALISM AND THE WORKING CLASSES. This WAS the subject of the sixth of the series of lectures in connection with the Warrington Liberal Assocciation, which was delivered at the Co-operative Hall, Sankey- street, on Tuesday evening last, by the Rev. R. Nicholls, of

div.head: Darw.en, lecturer (or the N'ation'al 'Reform Union
div.p: Darw.en, lecturer (or the N'ation'al 'Reform Union
William

Long, E:q., JP., of Grappenhall, occupied the chair, sup- ported by the Rev. R. Filcher, Councillor Greenin4, Mr. F. A. Roberts, Mr. P. Hall, and Mr. Henry Roberts (secre- tary.) Toere was a very good attendance. The CHAIRMAN was cordially greeted, and in the course of a few opening remarks observed that he had heard a

great deal of the very interesting series of lectures which they had been having in Warrington. and he regretted that owing to other engagements he had been prevented from at- tending some of them, but from what he had read was suffi- cient to have shown him that those who had attended them

regularly, or had taken advantage oT reading them at home, must have gained information or instruction in the forma- tion or maintenance of their political opinions. (lieu, hear.) It was a plank in their political platform as Liberals that they were very anxious that all should show that they were able to give a reason for the faith that was in them.. (Applause.) They _

wanted the people to be convinced for themselves that the Liberal party was a party of progress, and the party which would in the long run be to their best interests to join with and uphold by all ineans in their power. (Elear, hear.) That was his candid opinion after some vears'ex- . .

perieUce. (Hear, hear.) 'He felt sure all present that evening would give an attentive ear to the address which was about to be delivered, because the subject was one which must beoof especial interest to the working classes as electors. (Applause.) The LECTURER in commencing his address observed that ,he could very heartily endorse all the Chairman had said I with regard to the object of meeting there. They had not come with the idea that they would be able to persuade everybody to assent to all that they might advance, much less had they any notion to attempt in any way to over- ride the judgment of persons in that assembly; but they would be doing their best to try to show the meeting that it was to the advantage of those who belonged to what was called the wage-earning class to support the doctrines and principles of Liberalism, and whilst they would be doing this as effectually and as thoroughly as they could, at the same time they would be quite prepared to admit that there was room for differences of opinion on the question, and if there should be any at the close of that meeting who thought that after all it was more to their interest to support the Conservatives and the Conservative policy then they would not by any means attempt to interfere with their right and their liberty. (hear, hear.) Proceeding with the subject of his lecture, he said that there were a great many people whose political opinions were not of a definite charac or, and which were as liable to be swayed in one direction as another, whilst all needed a little stimulus in the right dii ection, and therefore it would not do them much harm, but on the contrary a great deal of good to review the grounds on which people, eTecially those engaged in busi- ness, should give their hearty support to the doctrines and principles of Liberalism. There were some people, and he believed the number were increasing in the country, who were trying to persuade the working classes to b3lieva that it was not to their interest to identify themselves, with either of the two great political parties now existing, and the notion seemed to prevail in Some Tiarters that Party [ Government was a very great evil, and the sooner they. did array with Party Government the better. Well, vrhatevef ' ankght be said on that side of the argument it must, after all, lit 9 admitted that. it was not just now a practical question. For instance, they considered that with Mr. Gladstone, Prima Minister of this country— (applause)—he represented not merely the opinion or con- viction of a few of the classes, but that he represented by far the majority of clasees, and the working class above all others, and, therefore, they could hot think that the work- ing of his party was an evil. He hoped they would not re- fuse to give their support to one or the other, or the end would be that their policy would be a do-nothing policy. Haring spoken of the unfriendly attitude which the Conservatives had always displayed towards the woFk- ing man, he said they could appeal confidently to the prin- ciples of the Liberal party—to what Liberalism had dons in the past and what it promised to do in the future. (Hear, hear.) The principles of Liberalism might be seen to be such as working men above all others should have perfect sympathy with, because Liberalism recognised this fact, namely, that the altered conditions of society did necessi- tate certain changes or certain reforms in the law. Now that there were changes taking place in thie country, and that there had been very great changes during the past 20, 30, or 40 years was a matter about which there could be no doubt or question whatever. It was not simply what they read in the newspapers or elsewhere, but they had only to go back in their own memory to see the changes that had taken place around them as regarded the condition of the people and the state of the whole nation. They had increased in population, and, on the whole, had, vastly increased in wealth; they had in- creased also in their educational establishments, and in their endeavours to raise the social standard of the people. The doctrine of Liberalism was, seeing the changes that had, taken place, that the law should be brought into harmony with the altered conditions. It was often said by Conservatives that they never knew what was going to hap- pen if a Liberal Government was in power, and especially if the Liberal party was presided over by such a dangerous man as Mr. Gladstone. (Laughter.) Well, they did not think it was necessary for them to defend Mr. Gladstone, whose career spoke for itself, whilst such meek and mild gentlemen as Lord Salisbury and Lord Randolph Churchill —(laughter)—would have to undergo a considerable change in their character and purpose before the country would be prepared to put very much confidence in them. (Hear, hear.) Liberals did not believe in changes just for the sake of changes; they did not believe in abolishing what was worth preserving; but what was effete, what was out of har- mony with the present state of civilisation, ought to be removed out of the way. (Applauee.) The franchise question as it now stood waS an ualaii State of things, .and ought to be altered as soon as possible. They believed taXation and representation ehould go together, That was was one ef the grand doctrines of Liberalism as professed in the past and one which they resolved to cling to as long as they lived. Another dcctrine was that there should be perfect equality displayed independent of social position or religions creed, and to illustrate this they as a Party said that the electors of Northampton ought net to be debarred of their rights because they had selected as their representative a gentleman whose opinions upon religious questions he sup- posed very few of them agreed with. It was a question for the Northampton people and if Mr. Bradlaugh or any gentle- man proclaimed his right as a citizen than he ought to take his seat in the House of Commons without being put to the trouble, inconvenience, and expense which were now laid upon him by the Tory Party. (Applause.) They con- sidered also that the holding of land which had so much to do with the progress of civilisation and the development of the country that it should not be governed by the dead man that old formulas and arrangemente en- tered into centuries ago should not stand in the way of their progress to-day. (Hear, hear.) Another doctrine of theirs was that what was morally wrong could never be politically rigat. The appli- cation of that doctrine might refer to certain matters con- nected with their social life; in this country, and so it could apply as it had often done to their foreign policy. In the Government of Lord Beaconsfield there was a constant vio- lation of that principle—the matter of being morally right was not thought cf. The interests of British advancement and so forth were constantly presented to them, but not the question of what was morally right or what was morally wrong. Under the leadership of Mr. Gladstone they felt confi- dent of being guided by the ?principle that what was • morally wrong could never be politically right, and the question of moral justice ought to be carried into their poli- tical life as well as into their daily and religious life. Further, they believed that there should be government by the people, and not simply a government for the people. They did not want to have dictators—men taking upon themselves responsibilities which the electors had not in the first instance placed upon their shoulders. They be- lieved pre-eminently in the doctrine that there should be in this:country a government by the people, and not as the Tories often represented, and as they tried to carry out, a government simply for the people. Those were the salient doctrines of Liberalism, and whilst they fully admitted that they had not always been carried out as clearly and as thoroughly as they should have been, yet they said that for the extension of Liberal principles in this country the working classes should give their hearty support to them, and their leaders would then have greater confidence in abiding by the doctrines just laid down. They, as Liberals, believed their ground was firm, because the principles they held were firm, and they could point to what the members of the Liberal party had done in times past. (Hear, hear.) When they spoke of the past they were always apt to come in collision with their Tory friends (laughter)—who seemed to detest the name of history. They said the Liberals in speak- ing of the past were always going over the same ground and showing the great changes that were brought about by Liberalism and Liberal movements, but they sa(d, why not deal with the present? It was true that they did not un- duly parade themselves or their works, but it might occur to some of them that the reason the Tories did not like to speak of the past was because they had cut such a very poor figure in the past—(laughter)—and they could not re- fer to any great movements that they had helped on which had brought about progress, or iv better condition of people in this land. (Hear, hear.) It was because of their reac- tionary policy in opposing that which was for the welfare of ' the country that they were reluctant to speak of the past. Whenever Mr. John Bright had rose to speak, the Tories had said " Of course, its the old tale over again, the glorifi- cation of Mi. John Bright." They (the Liberals), however, did not think Mr. Bright spoke to glorify himself, but he did very proudly glorify those interests established by Literal work and Liberal legislation. (Applause.) As to the work of Liberalism in the past, what had been done? , The lecturer pointed first to the abolition of the corn laws brought about by that man whom they delighted honouring—Richard Cobden—(applause)—who . was aidedi n what he did by the support of Liberals at that time, and who associated himself with Mr. Mi.ler Gibson (one who had jest passed away) Mr. John' Bright, and other noblemen of the tinae. Cobden' was rc. ,ilved on procuring a cheap lotf for the people, and that bron'tht about ens of the most unportant refullus ever in-
augnrated in this country. There existed, too, at that time excessive tariffs on imported goods, and other matters which were for the benefit of certain vested interests. Their re:

moval was fur the benefit of the masses of the people, and that was brought about by Liberal legislation. (Hear, bear.) A great work of reform which moved the indigna. lion of the House of Lords to a great extent was the re- moval of the stamp duty, which gave a free press to Eng- , land, and on which their liberty so much depended to-day. (Hear, hear.) But there had been no Government which had more thoroughly deserved the name of Liberal than tho Government conducted by Mr. Gladston3 from 18e18 to 1874, when a number of great measures were carried out. Mr. Gladstone did, as far as he possibly could, justice to Ireland in disestablishing and disendowing the episcopal church in that country, and giving the right of religion.f liberty to the inhabitants, and he also gave them the pri- vilege of the Lmd Act. As regarded the measures brought in at the time in reference to the whole of the United Kingdom, he referred to the Ballot Act, by which it was possible for working men and others to go to the polling booth without having the fear of landlord, of employer, or anyone elso before their eyes. Then they .had

, ene of the greatest measures passed in the present century. the Education Bill of 1970, by means of which the blessing% of elementary education were brougat to the door of the poorest man in tha land. Then the ancient National Universities which had been used up to that time almost entirely in the interests of one sect or party in this country, were made from what they had merely been in name to aaality—national universities. (Applause.) The lecturer alluded to the reforms in the army and the reduction of the National Debt, And then went on to say that notwithstand- ing all this, when Mr. Gladstone appealed to the country in 1874. after having a surplus ef .f.'3,000,090 in the Ex- chequer, they had become so rich that they thought they . .

should like to be Tory for a time. Sums of their isoncon- formist friends and others with them appeared dissatisfied with the Education Act of 1870, ani in 1874 they went away from Mr. Gladstone,and the reforms which he proposed to carry out. Mr. Gladstone would have re-adjusted the whole question of tuition, and yet although he was prepared to do that and told them plainly he woall do so, they went over to the " mystery " man to see the tricks Benjamin Disraeli would play in the name of that country. (Laugh- ter.) Then they knew the loss of national hono:‘: and fame . . . . . . . . . .

they sustained met how domestic legislation was hindered. Disraeli, or Lord Beaconsfield as he then became, because he had made the Queen Empress of India, aad it was only right that she should make him an earl—(laughter)—Lord Beaconsfield. sustained by Royalty and the high personages of the realm, thought he could lead the people of the country net as he considered proper. He appealed to the country in 18$0, hat by that time they had got out of their sulky mood and knew the true state of affairs, and, therefore, they resolved to have no more of Lord Beaconsfield at any price. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) The Liberal Cabinet was formed at the request of the majority of electors of this country. What had been done? On the whole he thought R had placed the 4iesidn af. national finance in a more healthy condition than it was in • the time the Con- as vatives were in office. They had abolished :126 raal,t tat in the interests of the farmers, and which he suppose,: vfa! not a blessing to be despised by those enereged in agricule .1 tural pursuits. The Gevernment, too, had done something for them as working people. They had passed the Erna ployera' Liability Act, the Ground Game Bill, and a mea- sure which Nonconformists and ministers had asked felt many years—the Burials Bill—by the passing of which a grave scandal was removed from their religious life. (Ape, plause.) Haying spoken of other Bills brought in by the pre. seat Administration, he asked how they had nerforraed etei: work. The Gutiermaent had not patroeised them as workt lug men, but she had done her work honestly and fear- lessly. As to the action of the Conservatives it reminded him of the old lady who travelled in the train for the first time in her life and when she arrived at leer destination she was asked what she had seen on the way. "Oh, nothing," she replied, "except a haystack, and that was going another way." (Laughter.) So the Conservatives had always gone in the opposite direction, and as the Liberals had been travelling on in the car of progress they had never seen the Tories except when, they bad been going the other way. (Hear, hear, add laughter.) But they could not live on mere abstract prin- ciples, and the question was not only what had the Liberals done in the past, but what the Liberals would do for theist as a class in the future. Ile had had as much to do with workingmen as a class as anyone, and he believed that workingmen as a whole did not cote for a special previlege to be accorded them, but what they asked for was a fair field and no favour. With regard te future legislation the first thing they would undoubtedly ask for and what they in' tended to obtain was for a reform.bill giving the franchile to those occupying ar)113,35 in the rural districts upon some- what the same principle, if not entirely the same princip-e, as the franchise new granted to those in boroughs. They were told that with regard to this measure that the Tories would be prepared to give them all that they asked for, but he had a little doubt in his own mind as to whether that was accurately true. They must remember the words of Lord Randolph Churchill, who was one of the many leaders of the Conservative party. (Laughter.) Whether he (Lord Randy) was at the bead or tail of that very respectable body it was difficult to say, but he was a man of whom the Conservatives made a great deal of. Lerd R. Churchill Was not satisfied in his own mind that the franchise ought to be granted to the agricultural labourer. The poor agri- cultural labourer! He had been kept out in the cold a long time, and if he was not tired of his lot he (Nlr. Nicholls) did not know where his manliness had gone. The agricultural labourer had to bear his share in the taxation of the coun- try, but he was deprived of all civil rights at the time of election. However, it was not only the agricultural labourer, but operatives or workingmen who lived outside the borough were inferior to those who lived inside the borough. As far as his own judgment went, they would find the best specimens of the working class in what were termed the rural districts, and he had put it in that light be Mr. Gladstone. In his concluding remarks he said that they expected great things from the Liberal party in the future, and after comparing the two parties in relation to financial nutters in the last 25 years, remarked that the net turplus in the sixteen years the Liberals were in office amounted to 29 millions, while the net deficit of the Tories during a period of nine years was nearly 9i millions. The fidelity of the people of this country to Mr. Gladstone and those associated with him was as true and firm ae it was in, March, 1880—(applause)—and they were resolved to ghee hira in the evening of his life and these associated with him as loyal and as constant support as they could possible" render. (Applause.) The CRAIRAIAN having stated that the Lecturer would. be pleased to answer any questions put him, Mr. WALLINGTON said that he saw Lord R. Churchill the other week said that it was quite possible to save tett millions in our national expenditure. He quite believed the Gladstone Government—the Liberal chancellors—had been more economical on the whole than the Tories, but be should like to have a little more economy still. John Bright had said that the country should be carried on for 50 millions, but it was costing 70 or 80 at least. If Lord R. Churchill was correct, their members were a little bit remiss in their duty, and ought to watch that point a great deal more that it Was being done. The LECTURER said there was room for improvement, and there could be no better plan than that suggested, that week to bring pressure to bear on the representatives of the Heease' of Commons. They would he diepo:ecl to watch Lord Churchill when when Mr. Peter Rylende and others beought for- ward some proposal to lessen expenditure, '.nd see whether his creed and practices were in harmany with each other- (Laughter.) Rev. R. PILCIIER moved a vote eaf thanks to the Lecturer for his admirable speech on the pie history of the Liberal party, and also on the princiailes which they as Liberals had always relied, and upon achich he took it they intended to rely in future. (Hear, hear.) He did so with peculiar pleasure, because it, was a good thing, especially for the younger men, to be reminded of past. achievements, and it was pleasing to the elder people to recall those matters, concerning which some of them had taken their litte part- Paradoxical as it might seem to the Lecturer, there were Conservative workingmen. He did not used to believe in Conservative workingmen, but he was converted through the perusal of a placard in the town where he was staying a week or two announcing " A great Conservative gathering of working men," and that it was intended for workingmen was shown by a note at the bottom of the placard "that carriages were to be ordered for 10." (Loud laughter.) He had always believed in Conservative workingmen since. (Whew I) Councillor GREENING seconded the motion, and compli- mented the lecturer on the exhaustive address he had given. The LECTURER replied, and moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman, remarking that be was glad to meet with a gentlemao who was 80 pronounced in his political opinions. Mr. HENRY ROBERTS seconded the motion, and said Mr. Long, although not a Warrington Biberal, was a prominent Liaeral in his own district, and he hoped it would not be the last time they had hint in Warriogton; and perhaps the time might come when they would congratulate him ae one of the members for Mid-Cheshire. (Applause.) Mr. Roberts said the next lecture would be on the pension list, by a working man. The Cum/MAN having briefly replied, the meeting ter- minated.

div.p: 3fISCELLANEWS. Over 1,000 children are now affected with measles at 'Macclesfield. All the schools are closed. Sir Robert Peel will be the second Conservative candi- -date for Blackburn at the next election, having accepted an invitation to contest the borough as the colleague of Mr. W. Coddington. The Tunbridge mail cart was found lying on the road near Seven Oaks, on Monday morning. The cart was shattered and the horse Much injured. The driver and the bags were missing. ' In the Queen's Bench, on Tuesday, in the case of Major- General Bereton versus the Great Easterri Railway Corn- Deny, for compensation for injuries, the jury found for the plaintiff, and awarded £6,500 damages. In the Queen's Bench division, on Monday, a special illrY gave a verdict for Canon Brereton, with £4,000 damages, against the Great Eastern Railway Company, as compensation for injuries by' an accident on the defen- dants' line ',between Ely and Cambridge, in August,l 1882. A parliamentary paper issued on Monday gives the number of lives lost by drowning and other accident in British merchant ships registered in the United Kingdom in the several years from 1871 to 1882 inclusive. In the twelve years the total loss of life was 38,722, of which 35,660 were crew' and 3,062 passengers. The largest num- bers were in 1873 and 1874, this being mainly due to the great number of passengers drowned in those years, 1,167 in the former, and 572 in the latter. Another step towards placing the North Wales University College in practical working order was tak n on saturday, When a full meeting of the Court of Governors was held to elect the Council of the College. It was decided that the Council should consist of seventeen members, and a double ballot was taken, the result being the election of a council Of a very representative character. The Earl of Powis haa been elected president of the institution' Mr. 0. Morgan and Mr. R. Davies, M.P., vice-presidents, and Mr. John Roberts, M.P., honorary treasurer. BRUTAL 141unnert OF A POLICE SERGEANT.—Sergeant William Smith, of the Durham county constabulary, stationed •at Woodlands, near Staindrop, had visited a Public-house on Saturday night to ascertain if all Was right, and he was subserviently passing a colliery heap when he was assailed by a shower of stones and felled to the ground. When assistance arrived Sergeant Smith was dead, one side of his skull being smashed in. Dr. Middleton, of Wood- lands, who proceeded to the scene, was also knoceed down by a brick. Three miners named Joseph Lawson. William Liddle, and Joseph Hodgson were arrested. THE BLASPHEMY PROSECUTIONS:Mr. Foote, late editor of the Freethinker, was released on Monday morning from Holloway Jail, London. An immense concourse assembled outside the prison, and there were about 20 crowded breaks from various Secularist Halls in London. Mr. Bradlaugh, M.P., Mrs. Foote, the Misses Bradlaugh, Mr. Angell, Mr. Foote's father-in-law, and Dr. Aveling were admitted in their carriages into the jail conetyard, and Mr. Bradlaugh received Mr. Foote. The ex-convict was welcomed with immense enthusiasm, the people pressing upon the carriages. A long procession of conveyances was formed and proceeded to the Hall of Science to breakfast. Mr. Foote complained of the stringent regula, ions of the prison, but warmly acknowledged the kindness of the governor. THE NEW SPEAKER.—The new Speaker was born August 6th, 1829, was educated at Eton and at Balliol College, Oxford, and was subsequently entered at the Inner Temple, but was not called to the Bar. Mr. Peel unsuccessfully contested Coventry in 1863, and two years later was returned for Warwick. He was Parliamentary Secretary to the Poor-law Board from December, 1868, till January, 1871, when he became Secretary to the Board of Trade, Which office he held until August 1873, when he was ap- pointed Patron tge Secretary to the Treasury. On Mr. Glad- stone's return to power after the general election of 1880, Yeel was appointed Under-Secretary for the Home De- Partment, but he retired from the office at the close of the session, and until his election as Speaker on Tuesday re- teamed an unattached Liberal. T. Joe's, MILES PLATTING.—The new rector of St. John's, Miles Platting, was inducted to the living, on Saturday. There was a large assemblage of people to wit- ness the ceremony, but very few were present of those who attended the church in former days. The -Bishop, in his remarks to the congregation, said they could easily under- stand the very mingled feelings with which he found him- self amongst them. He wished to draw a veil ever, and, if he could, to blot out from his memory the painful incl- lents—to him exc sedingly painful—which had happened With regard to the parish during tha last five years. He asked for a loyal and hearty co-operation with the rector, in the work of the church, adding that he was bold enough to hope that the future of the parish might not be has uaPley than its past had been, and that the church might yet be as well attended as ever it had been. LORD R. CHURCHILL AND THE KHEDIVE.—The papers relating to Lord R. 0-urchin's charges of complicity in the Alexandria massacre egamst the Khedive were published on Monday morning, and precede a letter from Lord Granville to Sir E. Malet, to whom the papers were forwarded. Lord Granville remarks that the whole case rests upon surmise, suspicion, and hearsay, on unsupported statements by un- named persons, and on these whose hatred of the Khedive has been created or embittered by measures taken against them during the rebellion. He adds that no prima fade evidence exists in support of the charges. The inferences attempted to be drawn from the passages quoted from the Blue Books must be received with great caution, for it is to be regretted that Lord Randolph Churchill should not have taken more care correctly to extract the quotations on Which he bases the serious charges he has preferred. THE ACTION AGAINST LOLD CrARMOYI.E.—In the action for breach ef promise of marriage brought by Miss Finney, known in theatrical circles as Miss Fortescue, against Lord Garmoyle, the solicitors for the defendant applied on Satur- day.m morning to Master Gordon, in Chambers, for an exten- on of time wherein to prepare a statement of defence in answer to the statement of claim already delivered, in Which the damages sustained are laid at £30.000. Mr. Mote, solicitor for the plaintiff, opposed the application, On the ground that Miss Finney was anxious to have the action tried as soon as possible, being desirous of securing an early opportunity to publicly explain in court the circumstances Of the case as far as she was concerned.—The Master, how- ever, thought that as this Was the first application which , had been made in the matter it should be granted, and allowed a fortnight for the delivery of the statement of defence, the ordinary period of ten days permitted for this Purpose having expired. THE UNEMPLOYED OF MANCHESTER AND BALFORD.—A Second meeting of the unemployed workpeople of Manches- ter and Salford was held on Monday. Since the last meet- ing, various authorities have denied that there is any unusual distress at the present time, and Monday's demon- stration was held to disprove this, and about 1,000 people assembled in the city and walked in precession to Pomona Gardens, where it was estimated by the promoters there Were 5,300 people present, but other independent estimates F"5 the number as between 3,000 and 4,000. All of them declared by a show of hands that they were out of work; and in the same way a unanimous declaration was made that they were not in receipt of relief from boards of guardians. The Bishop of Manchester and the Bishop of Salford wrote stating that if the distress alleged to exist could be proved, l'nete would be a ready response to the appeal for help.- It Was decided to canvass the merchants and employers of the district for funds to relieve the unemployed. TERRIBLE MURDER IN A LIVERPOOL HOSP:TAL.-+Oa Sundayb morning, about three o'clock, the attendants at the ill-road Hospital, Liverpool, where infectious cases from the West Derby Union are treated, were aroused by hearing loud, screams proceeding from one of the nurse's rooms. On going the apartment the attendants found a nurse named Ann Groves, about 50 years of age, lying in a pool of blood With her throat cut. She was unable to speak, but pointed t,2 a corner of the room, where was found a man named Thomas Rutherford, lying on the floor, also with his throat nut, and an open razor lying by his side. The woman died shcrtly afterwards, but the man still survived last Sunday night,though he was in a very precarious condition. It seems that Rutherford was formerly an inmate of the hos- pital, but had been discharged cured. He had no business in the establishment, and must have effected an entrance surreptitiously during the early morning, gone right to the nurse's room, and attacked her. So far no motive can be ascertained for the crime. Rutherford remains at the hos- pital in charge of the police. MR. HARTLEY.—BooiIe, Liverpool. THE IMPECUNIOUS CONDITION OF THE MANCHESTER uoNsEuvanvits.—At a meeting of-Irishmen held in Man- - .ehester on Sunday, a circular letter purporting to have been' jlned by Mr. Henry Samson, treasurer of the Manchester onservative Association, was read. In this document Mr. _ :ftrotton claims credit for the Conservatives for having -Purified" the list of voters, and reduced it in three years to the extent of above 8000. The Association confidently ex- .l;Oct to regain two seats at the next general election, but l'ueT must be provided with the means to keep the perma- tent staff in its present state of efficiency, and to defray the An outlay which the next registration work will entail. ;111 appeal is made for an annual subscription to the general land of the Association, or a “more substantial amount" as a donation to the ele7ctien fund. A resolution was passed rparessing "condolence" with the Conservative party in nchester on its "present impecunious position," and Pledging the meeting to do all in its power to reinstate the thousands of Irishmen who "have been deprived of their lust rights qt hide eiship." It was further suggested that ,Irge aqmsuf, mousy are no longer required if the spirit of Corrupt PraWlCes Act is to be op.:wive in electidne. Of fifty-two questions upon the paper of the House of Commons on Monday night, just over half (twenty.seven) stood in the names of Irish members. Mr. Biggar contri- buted over one.minth. . _

The nomination for Brighton took place on Tuesday, Mr. Romer,Q.C., Liberal, and Mr. Marriott, Q.C., who is a Con- eervative with Liberal principles, were respectively pro- posed. The polling takes place (to-day) Saturday. A Congregation of Oxford University on Tuesday, ap- proved by 100 votes to 46 the preamble ot a statute having as its object the admission of women to the same University examinations as men in mathematics, modern history, natural science, and moderations. The supplementary estimate for Civil Services and Revenue Departments was issued on Thursday morning amounting to £365,429. Of the additional sums required by the Civil Service Department beyond the original estimates, £120,000 is for the Post. Office. Joseph Jones, the head fireman at the Rosehill Colliery, Bolton, belonging to Messrs. Scowcroft and Sons, was killed on Monday by a tub of coaLdescending a jig brow. He had finished his inspection of the mine, and was turning towards the pit eye when he met with the accident. A goods train drawn ap near Brighouse Station on the Blanchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway„ early on Tuesday morning, was run into by anothergoods train from Manchester. Considerable damage was caused to rolling stock, and a guard named Shivers was badly bruised. From the supplementary Army and Navy Estimates, issued on Tuesday, it appears that the additional charges for the Navy on account of operations in Egypt:amount to £147,200, and for the Army to £2o9,oso—making a total of £358,250; and there is for other purposes an additional charge for the Army of £161,850. ACCIDENT AT • FOOTBALL MATCH.—A Man named' kl'Cullock had his -leg broken while watching a football match at Carlisle on Saturday. He was standing in a crowd of spectators upon the touch line when two of the players, rushing after the ball, ran against him, and the ground beiug very slippery he fell and broke his leg. Great amusement was caused at a meeting of the Maccles- field guardians, on Tuesday, by the opening of a parcel ad- dressed to the chairman, which was found to contain a quantity of Coffee and a couple of pistols which the chair- man was instructed to present to a couple of antawonistic guardians, who recently challenged each other to a duel. A DECEASED WIFE'S &mg.—At Bolton, on Thursday, a case of interest to marriage law reformers was heard. A painter named Gosling, who had married his deceased wife's i sister, summoned her for a breach of the peace. He turned her out of his house, but she came back and created a dis- turbance, whereupon he took out the summqns. The woman is now destitute in the workhouse. She wal bound over to keep the peace. LORD Jona Blawszns.—The leaders of the Opposition and many distinguished members of the party were present at the Mansion House on Saturday evening at a presenta- tion to Lady John Manners of a bust of her husband, executed by Signor Riggi. Subsequently there was a ban- quet in the Egyptian Hall, the Lord Mayor presiding. Lord JolataManners, the Marquis of Salisbury, Sir Stafford North-1 cote, and Viscount Cranbrook were amongst the speakers. Form MEN KILLED ix A WELSH QuAuitY.—Bya dyne- I mite explosion which occurred on Wednedeay night at South Dorothea Slate Quarries, near Carnarvon, four men were killed and 16 others severely injured. The men were at tea in a but in the lower part of the quarry during blast- ing operations, and a stone weighing about a ton, was hurled amongst them. Three of the men killed are William Owen, Robert Jones, and Thomas Williams. The name of the fourth has not yet been asCertained. The Rev. George Lewis Campbell, minister of the Argyll Free Church, Glasgow, was on Wednesday convicted of im- proper behaviour in the public street on the night of the 16th instant, and was fined two guineas, or 21 days' im- prisenment. He pleaded that he was giving charity to the Woman in connection with whom the charge was laid. Two members of the Glasgow Free Presbyterian Church watched the case. The accused declined the aid of counsel. The case has been taken up by the Glasgow Presbytery. Richard Constantine has the satisfaction of knowing that he is the first milk dealer who has managed to contract himself out of the operation of the Adulteration Act. He has a contract to supply Mill-road Hospital with milk, and was charged before Mr. Raffles, at Liverpool, on Wednesday, with sending an article containing twelve to fifteen parts of water added to one hundred parts of the poorest milk from which a portion of the cream had been removed. It was denied that water had been added to the milk, but it was admitted that some of the cream had been taken off. As, however, there was a clause in the costract providing that if the milk upon being tested was found to be not "up to the mark "it should be returned, Mr. Raffles held that this clause freed Constantine from liability. I ATROCIOUS CRUELTY TO A Wouset —Early on Tuesday morning a brutal attack was made upon a young woman ' named Mary Jane M‘Namara,in Manx-street, Toxteth Park, , Liverpool, by a man named Robert Black, who is also known as "Major.' On Monday night the taco quarrelled, and Black kicked the woman in a savage manner, and at one o'clock on Tuesday morning he threw a lighted lamp at het head, saying "he would bang for her." The lamp broke, the oil ignited, and the woman's clothing was soon in a flame. Then Black locked the door, and coolly walked away, leaving lai`Namara to her fate. A constable shortly afterwards entered the room through the window, and he woman was removed to the Royal Southern Hospital, where she now lies in a very precarious condition. Black has been apprehended. HEAVY DAIIAGES AGAINST A RAILWAY COMPANY.— General Brereton, who was travelling with his brother, Pre- bendary Brereton, is the train which met with an accident on the Great Eastern line, and who also received serious in- juries, has obtained a verdict for £8,500 damages. The General sustained injuries more severe than those of his brother. Both his legs were broken below the knee, and one leg is now an inch and a quarter shorter than the other. He Is 55 years of age, with a family of six children. He re- tired from the Indian army in 1859, with the rank of Major. General and a pension of nearly £6OO a year. It was his hope to have secured employment as an estate agent, and he had gone to considerable expense in educating himself for this position, but any prospect of that sort Noas now at an end.

Examsu PATENTS. The following patents, amongst ' others, published in the Official Journal of the Patent Office, were sealed during the week ending February 23rd, 1884 Thomas Briggs, Darwen, improvements in the construction of carts, carriages, and other vehicles ; Carl Albert Week- becker and Lawrence Schwabe, Manchester, improvements in apparatus for marking and measuring lengths, chiefly applicable to textile fabrics, but applicable else to other goods; Thomas Wrench, Waterloo, Lancashire, improve- ments in or appertaining to the manufacture of umbrellas; Henry Leeming, Manchester, improvements in sewing machines; John James Kenyon, Manchester, improments, in fusible plugs; Thom & Humber, Beeston, Notts, improve- , ments in tricycles; Joseph T. Jones and Joseph H. Wild,l Leeds, improvements in rock-boring apparatus; John Makant Cryer and William Ord Matteson, both of Bolton, improvements in machinery for wringing, mangling, and calendering or finishing lace, calicos, and other like fabrics, which are also applicable to machines for calendering paper; Daniel Smith, Wolverhampton, improvement in the manu- facture of hoes, spades, adzes. &c.—List supplied by Mr. George Davies, C.E., Fel. Inst., P.A., Patent Solicitor, 4, St. Ann's-square, Manchester. DYNAMITE EXPLOSION IN LONDON.—A die nitrous explo- sion occurred on Tuesday morning at Victoria Railway Station, London. About one o'clock two loud reports Were heard, and it speedily appeared that a strong explosion had destroyed the hooking office of the main line, the cloak room and waiting room, shattering the glass roof and blowing out the windows on the platform Many windows in the neighbourhood were also shattered. The explosion was heard three miles off. Three men were injured, but not dangerously, and conveyed to St. George's Hospital. The police and Government inspectors were actively engaged during Tuesday in searching—the one for a clue to the perpetrators of the outrage, the other for facts which would show the nature of the exploslys agent that had been em- ployed. The theory that there had been an explosion or gas was refuted by the appearance of the premises, and it was also clear that the damage had not been caused by gun- powder. Some compound of the nature of nitro-glycerine must have been used. The theory at present adopted is that the substance was introduced into the room late on Monday night, and was exploded by means of a " clock- work " arrangement such as lima and other members of him party are known to have had in their possession. The damage done to the station is estimated at £4,000. Two persons were also severely injured by the stone and wood work which was projected in all directions by the force of the explosion. In clearing away the damaged luggage and 'other abris from the cloakroom at the station on Wednes- day morning the police found what are believed to be the remains of the "infernal machine" which was used by the perpetrators of the outrage.
