man said there were still in.justices to be remedied in con- - - • -

nection with the burial grounds. He condemned Mr. Lea- tham's proposal to transfer Church patronage from private hands to the bishops, and spoke deprecatingly of the con- stitution of the Ecclesiastical Commission and their report. While warmly supporting Mr. Gladstone they must tell hint that the constitutional principles must be regarded, and personal predilections must not lead him nor other ministers into devious ways in dealing with Church questions. He warmly advocated disestablishment. Mr. Lee, M.P., and the Rev. Dr. Allon spoke in favour of the disestablishment of the Church of England. Mr. Richard, M.P.; said the Governments engaged in foreign wars to divert attention from domestic reforms. If they wanted disestablishment or any measure of reform they must join the Peace Society, for whenever there was foreign war the country was in such a state of excitement that no reforms could be accomplished. Mr. Rees, Swansea, and Mr. Dillwyn M.P., spoke in favour of the motion to be sub- mitted to Parliament for the disestablishment of the Church in Wales. Mr. Dillwyn did not appeal for disestablishment in Wales simply on Liberation principles, but as a matter of justice to Nonconformists, who were more numerous in Wales than Churchmen. The three murderers of Count Mallath were hanged at Pesth on Saturday: ' . Frequent shocks of earthquake are being felt at,Various places in Asia Minor, particularly at Mosel], but no damage has been sensed. e Tue Dominion House of Commons on Saturday adopted a resolution in favour of a loan of 822,500,0e0 to the Cana- dian Pacidc Railway. The Lower House of the Hungarian Diet on Saturday unanimously approved the Austro-French commereial treaty concluded on the l&h inst. Tin masked " Anarchists " entered an inn at Argentieres in Franca, on Monday, and ransacked the place. In the Bonita which ensued with the friends of the proprietor one person was killed and seven wounded. Seventy years ago the present Emperor of Germany, who .was then with the Allied forces in Franceereceived the Cross of the Russian Order of St. George in the ranks of the Kaluga Regiment. A memorial of the event was presented to His Majesty, on Thursday, by a special mission from the Russian Court. FRANCS AND TONQUIN.—A. telegram from Hong Kong states that it is believed there are 20,000 Chinese at Becninh. The whole of the French reinforcements have arrived in Tonquin, and a telegram from Haiphong reports that the troops are completing their preparations prior to taking the field. FIGHTING IN AFGHANISTAN.—The Daily News corres- pondent at Calcutta telegraphs that the Ameer of Afghani- stan is engaged in a war with the Mangal tribe, who re- cently defeated his troops and captured four guns. Reinforcements have been sent against the tribe, and the fighting has been renewed. Disturbances are expected among the Knrram tribes. It is reported from Teheran, unofficially, that Ayoub Khan is to be detained as a prisoner of State in the frontier town of Meshed. The Shah will in that case resume the payment of the annuity to Ayoub, concerning which there has been much correspondence between the Teheran Go- vernment and our Foreign Office. It is argued that Lord Ripon might find it advisable to charge this annuity on the revenues of India, as a supplement to the twelve lees which are now paid to the Ameer of Afghanistan. RUSSIA IN CENTRAL ASIA. •-••• According to a Russian newspaper, a number of tribes in the neutral territory be- tween Russia and Afghanistan have solicited Russian pro- tection, and it is also stated that the creation is contempla- ted of n governor-generalship In the Amur territory, and rthat Oroneral Tobernayeff is to be appointed a member of 1 the Council of War, and "will take part in the deliberations I of the commission for the re-organisation of Turkestan. iThese rumours are evidence of the interest taken in Russia In the extension:of the empire in the direction of Afghani- stan and Persia. A NAPOLEONIC Mesuragro.—Prinee Napoleon has put forth what is described as a manifesto. Addressing a ;number of "delegates" on Saturday, the Prince felicitated ' the country on the circumstance that whenever a national crisis occurred a Napoleon was always on the spot to save 'society. Id the present instance the crisis- has been brought lOn by the Constitution of 1875, and the Prince is ready I with his nostrum. He advises all "loyal" mew to unite in ' demanding a revision of the Constitution, and Offers them his patronage and support. Prince Victor was present at the interview with the "delegates," many of whem we are justified from Prince Napoleon's antecedents in suspecting were merely hill posters in disguise. FRANCE AND Enarnem.—The Ripublique Francaise• has published an article on foreign affairs which is regarded by some persons as a "palpable overture for a rapprochement." with this country. The French journal, after noticing the progress of Russia in Central Asia, remarks that European politics "in which it is well known France has no concan," have the following objective :--0 Austria, to command the Eastern Mediterranean by the possession of Salonica ;Aussie, to subject Babul to her influence, if not to her absolute dominion. What will England do to escape the clutch of the two monstrous claws stretching towards India and the letbmus? What has she done up to this time ? It would strike one that she might find it useful to have allies in the Mediterranean, and what does she do? She drives Italy into the arms of Germany, and she drives France out of Egypt." The Republique, with an eye to the restoration of the Dual Control, advises England to change its foreign minister. lieersear, Tcnenxeyere's Doweienee.—Considering the well-known opinion of General Tchernayeff that a succeso- ful invasion of India from Turkestan was impossible, it is surprising to be told on the authority of the Times corres- pondent at St. Petersburg that one of the principal reasons for the General's downfall was.that he had "drawn up- an original plan for the conquest of India." The General, we are told, attempted to force hi a plan upon the Imperial Go- vernment. Before starting from Tashkend for St. Peters- burg he sent his plan to the Minister of War General Vannovsky, to be presented to. the Emperor; but the Minister angrily refused to give it to His Majesty. When he arrived in the capital the Minister of War asked him whether he could not let India alone and be quiet. as there was nq desire to bring up that subject again just now. General Tclaer- nayeff persisted, however, in his wish that the Emperor should see the plen, and he accordingly sent two fair copies of it to two other influential functionaries at Court. Both of these plans appear to have reached the ears if not actually the eyes of the Czar without the knowledge at first of. the Minister of War. The matter caused His Majesty to be dis- pleased with the General. The story is a very curious one.
IMPERIAL PARLIAMMT.

_ HOUSE OF LORDS.—Mot:DAT. The House sat for twenty minutes. Several notices of questioas affecting the British operations in the Soudan were given; the bill for amending the law of evidence passed through committee; the report of amendments to the Contagions Diseases (Animals) Act was agreed to; and their Lordships separated after a soothing assurance from Lord CarlingfOrd in respect of the arrival ef infected cattle and sheep from Canada at Liverpool. HOUBB OF COMMONS.—Pricervar. EZINERDALS RA/WAY BILL.-Mr. BRIO/ moved that It I

be an instruction to the Committee en the Ennerdale Rail- way Bill to Inquire and report to the House whether the proposed railway would interfere with the enjoyment of those who visit the Lake District—The motion was, after a discussion, carried by 121 to 101. GORDOWS PEOCIAMAT3ON.-..The PREMIER, replYing to Baron de Wor.rns, said the authentic text of Georg! Cor- don's proclamation had been laid upon the table date eren-, ing. Ile reiterated his declaration of the Government's' unabated confidence in General Gordon.

THE SPDAYERSRIP.—At the close of questions Mr. Ofet, STONE proposed that the thanks of the. House should be voted to the Speaker (Sir H. On the motion of Mr. WHITBREAD, seconded by Mr. RATEDONE, it was unani- mously resolved that Mr. Arthur Peel do take the Chair. Having taken his seat amidst loud cheers, the new Speaker was congratulated by Mr. GLADSTONE on the high honour he bad attained.—Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE having as- sured Mr. Peel that so long as he occupied the Chair he would receive on the part of all members of the House full and undivided confidence, Mr. O'Dorucam. added a few words of congratulation; and on the motion of Mr. GLAD- STONE the House adjourned until Wednesday in order that the new Speaker might receive Her Majesty's approval of his appointment. OPERATIONS Its/ THE SOU,DAN. BRITISH ADVANCE. ! It will be learned with satisfaction by those who have been fretting for news df active operations on the Red. Sea littoral that General Graham has made an advance, and driven the Arabs out of the fort erected by Baker Pasha's troops beyond it,, morass that forms the inland boundary of Trinkitat. The British force to the number of about 5,000 is thus fairly ashore, and General Oraham is ready for what- ever movement he may contemplate. From Suakim we have serious news that the black troops have mutinied and made theis way, with arms in their hands, into the town, where they defy the British, force and threaten to join Osman Digma'n army. In consequence of this defection, Sir W. Hewett .aas been obliged to keep the ma,ines a: Suakim, and send to General Graham only the native contingent and six machine grins. The Admiral feels complete confidence in the ability of the marines, assisted by the warships, to defend the town against any danger that may threaten it, and though the condition of the place is anything but satisfactory, Sir Wil- liam has no doubt sitisfied himself as to his power to main- tain order an& public safety. General Gordon has sent from Khartoum an interesting defence and explanation of his proclamation with regard to slavery. He points out how helpless he would have been in the face of a hostile population, whom his proclamation has conciliated, and says that although he permits domestic slavery—as he has always done in the Soudan—he will, "God willing," take such steps as will put a stop to the terrible practice of "slave hunting." The General has issued another proclamation, which informs the insurgents of the Soudan that they had better II accept General Gordon's offers of peace and so avoid a Turkish invasion, as the commander of the Faithful intends to despitch a great army to conquer the country. This is a declaration as to Turkish policy which will excite the keenest curiosity of the critics. No serious engagement his yet taken place between General Graham's force and Osman Digma's followers. On Tuesday the advanced parties of both armies remained " looking at each other," without coming to blows. Strong complaints are made of the ill consequences of Lord Wolseley's order that no field gnus should be taken with General Graham's force. The enemy might have been severely punished if a battery of artillery had been at the front on Tuesday. As it is, the orders from London leave the force practically without artillery. The usual com- plaints of deficient transport are made; and a military writer in the Times vehemently denounces the "maddening concentration" of indispensable stores at Woolwich. From Khartoum General Gordon continues to send cheering tele- grams. Accounts have been received in this city to the effect that three Englishmen, who were with Hicks Pasha, and were taken prisoners at Kashgil, are in the hands of the Mandi, who has ordered them to be well treated.

Owing to the additional work imposed en Sir Evelyn Baring, the Government has despatched Mr. Egerton from the British Embassy at Constantinople to assist him. An interesting item of news is that Baker Pasha, on leaving Suakim with Major-General Graham, wore a British uniform. It has been thought that he would never be al- lowed to don the Queen's colours again.

The main change of the bill eras that it would 'import into the counties the samehousehold franchise as was given to the boroughs. Then the bill proposed to equalise the franchises of the three kingdomss and make them one and the same. As to Scotland, very little change would be necessary, but as to Ireland there would be a . .

, - - greater change. The lodger franchise would remain the same. As to the property franchises in all the three kingdoms, they would in substance remain, and they would not be made subject to residences, but measures would be taken to guard against these property franchises being abused, as they had teen abused in some parts of the coun- try. The bill would disqualify those incorporal heredita- meats Which were employed for the creation of votes. It would abolish franchises created by rent charges, feus, head rents,. and the like, excepting only tithe rent charges held in single ownership. And it would prevent the sub- division of hereditaments, and that operation by which the manufacture of votes had beet' carried on, One principle which it went upon was that of giving the frairchiee to persons belonging to, or residing-in, the tow-see the county, and keeping it tram those who came into the constituency by the process of foreign importation. The object of the .whole scheme was co put the franchise into the poesession of the heads of families and householders. These were the .objecte which the Lill proposed to accomplish. He wair prepared for the complaint that it was not a complete bill. .No bill dealing with reform ever was-a complete bill, and there never would he wear:replete bill dealing with the sub- t, and in his opinion Parliament would be out of its senses-if it attempted to make a complete bill. There were three-divisions into which-refer= was dirkled by the nature of the case and by the nezessities of Parliamentary goYern- menie- The first question wa3 to fix the franchise e the second wee that of providing macLeaery for the exerete of the franchise by, means of registration ; aid the third was to gather the nersoos exercising the franchhee into local communities—that was, the distribietion of seats. The present measure only desk with one division. The Government had, he hoped, too e much of English sense to de more than look at what was attainable and prom 'cable, or to be drawn away by what might be done in a Utopia from a path that-they were coavinced would lead to great practi- cal good for the people of England'. The right hon. gentle- men then dealt with the arguments-la favour of keeping the franchise separate from the queethen of redistribution and maintained that even if this Parliament should not he able to deal with the latter part of the questien after dealing with the former no great harm would result. To attempt both ob- jects in one bill WAS in the opinion of, the Government to deck-load their vessel and greatly' increase the risk of disa.ster. So laras-thie franchise waa' concerned, he -held that the bill was as-complete as it cCuld well be made, because it dealt with-the whole of the kingdom. Ile for one would be to party to passing a Franchise Bill for England and Scotland and leaving Ireland to take its chance. In his opinion the demand Ler a Franchise till for Ireland was-stronger than that :or England aead Scotland. Referring- to the history of previous Re- form Bills he pointed out that it hatl never been the renestion of the franchise but always that of redistribution that had caused the series crisis and the destruction of Governments. But on-general principles he- maintained that the two questions aught to be kept separate and apart. The 4sestion of the franchise Was one that shonid be dealt with only on broad and national principles, while- that of redis- tribution raised points-of local interest and prejudice. He admitted that legislation on redistribution ought to follow legiolation on the franchise at the earliest moment. That earliest moment wan-the next session, and the Franchise Bill was introduced Ine/.884; in order that in the ordinary life of the present Parliament the question of redistribution might also be dealt with. lie did not intend to be lei into any trap; but be did not mind giving the Hduser the benefit of his-own views on the subject. In order that it might have some approach to finality a measure of redistribution should be a large one. If not so large as that of 1832', at any rate nearer to that than to the one of 1861. He was not in favour of-the system of equal districts so far as population was concerned, and he thought that the dis- tinction-between town and country should be maintained, notwithstanding that the franchise would be almost identi- cal. Again, he could not-reduce the proportional share of representation accorded to • Iteland. Some consideratioe ougl.t t7.be had in fixing the numerical share of representa- •tion to the comparative nearness and remotepess of the districts. The small boroughs in the south of England would have to give way to the claims of London, Scotland, and the north of England, and in any measure of redistribu- tion the whole question of -the representation of minorities would ha7e to be considered. He saw no reason to change the views-be had always held on the subject, but he ad- mitted that the matter waedeserving of consideration. The bill was in, no danger from direct opposition. There might be some danger from indirect opposition, but of this he was not afraid unless it was-aggravated by the danger that reight ensne from friendship. It would be easier for friends to destroy the measure by additions that it would not bear than by opposition. lie asked if the mea- sure was worth having 1' What would it accomplish as compared with what previous measures had accomplished? It would add to the English constituencies, according to the best calculation that could be made, 1,300,000 voters, to the Scotch 200,000, and Irish 400,000, or nearly 2,000,000 altogether. Was not that worth some effort and some sacrifice? Yete called on the Liberal party to do as the Liberal party did with regard to the measure of 1832—t0 waive the examination of minute details and all personal predelections, and to deal with it as a broad measure of reform. What was wanted to carry the measure was union, and union only.. What would defeat it would be disunion.and disunion only. The right hon. gentleman resu:ned his seat amid applause, haying spoken an hour and forty-five minutes. Sir JOHN HAY moved as an amendment that no Bill to , amend the representation of the people of the United King- dom would be satisfactory which did not provide an in- creased number of representatives for Scotland up to tho full measure which justice demands in accordance with its population. The debate was continued by Mr. Salt, Mr. Gibson, Mr. H. Fowler, Lord R. Churchill, and subsequently, on the motion of Mr. BLENNERHASSWYT, adjourned.

Whitworth) read the Tofhe town's meeting ter Manchester Waterworks Committee correspondence which had taken place with respect to the apnr odp co leddi she uepadp y originally asked that a guaranteed annual income of £550 ehould be forthcoming to meet the interest odthe expendi- ture of laying the water mains, but this earn they after- wards reduced to £487. The property owners in the district offered a yearly guarantee of £2lO, in addition to the water rentals, which would be received for property supplied with town's water, and they asked the Rural Sanitary Authority to contribute £lOO yearly out of the rates. The Authority instructed their surveyor to prepare a report moon the sub- ject, and his estimate of the cost of laying the mains was less than that of the Corporation. Considering that a portion of the mains will pass through another Sani- tary Authority's district, and that the Corporation itself has property in the district, they (the Rural Sanitary• Authority) decided to offer a guarantee of £5O yearly for five years. The Clerk read a letter yesterday from Mr. Berry, super- intendent, stating that the Waterworks Committee, having carefully considered all the circumstances of the case and the nature of the country through which the water mains I would have to pass, declined to alter their terms of the 29th December last. The Clerk also read a letter from Mr. Sum- merfield, on behalf of the property owners of Cadishead, asking the reasons why the Authority now proposed only to contribute £5O yearly instead of £lOO as previously agreed to, and he (the Clerk) had forwarded to Mr: Sum- merfield a copy of the surveyor's report. The Clerk also read a letter from the secretary of a meeting held at Dim in favour of a supply of town's water to Irlam and Cadis- head, enclosing copies of resolutions passed at that meeting. The whole subject was raerrel to a committee.

div.head: TIE WARRINGTON £lOO CLAIM FOR SLANDER.
div.p: TIE WARRINGTON £lOO CLAIM FOR SLANDER.

On Thursday afternoon the case of Mrs. Charlotte Pet- ford, keeper of the Red Lion Inn, Hollins Green, Flixton, against Joseph Shaw, of the Eagle and Child Inn, in the same village, for slander, came before Mr. Nicholson, regis- trar, at the Warrington County Court. The defendant at the last court agreed to a verdict for the plaintiff, who claimed £lOO damages, and the settlement of the question of damages WAS referred to the registrar. Plaintiff was re- presented by Mr. Moore, and defendant by Mr. Jenkins. The plaintiff's statement of claim charged defendant with having committed the following acts :—Wantonly and maliciously spoken and published of the plaintiff, in her business as a licensed victualler, that she was not a fit person to hold a license ; that she was a bad character—which assertion he could. prove. On another occasion falsely and maliciously spoken and pub- i lished the statement that plaintiff had obtained her license under an assumed name, her real name being Harriett That she used to keep a brothel in Manchester, was one of the worst characters in that city, and had been convicted many times. That the defendant, after the pub- lication of the slander last mentioned, and meaning to impute to the plaintiff that she was not a fit and proper person to hold a publican'a license, maliciously caused to be written, sent, and published by his solicitor (Messrs. Brett and Craven, of Manchester), to Superietemlent Jackson, of the county pollee, the following false and malicious words, in the form of a letter :—" Dear Sir,—We are instructed to request you to ascertain the name and character of the holder of the license of the Red Lion alehouse, Flixton, before the Licensing Committee meet at War- rington on Saturday. We are informed that Superintendent Piggett,ef the Police Department, Fairfield. Street, Manchester, can give yen important information on the subject." That defendant, on the 6th June 1883, went Into a public-home in Buttermarket-street, Warrington, and Mid plaintiff was formerly a woman of the town on the streets of Manchester, and could not possibly make the ale-. house at Hollins Green pay if she conducted it properly. That defendant by the said slanders and libels had been guilty of an indictable offience ; that she was not a fit per- son to carry on the business of a publican, and carried it on Immorally and illegally, so that she had been cruelly pained and injured in her business, and suffered disgrace, anxiety, -annoyance, and ill-health.—Mr. Moore, in opening the ease; said the writ in the case was issued on the 20th November, 'last year, and, the order for remissior High Court of Justice to the Warringt o_k from mounty , Court #as made on the 4th December, 1883. The solicitot ! read the statement of claim, which had been t n the' plaintiff. admitted, as the defendant bad consented to a verdict —The Registrar was of opinion that by admitting ;o dmittiag the state,- ment of claim defendant admitted that there was a Cause r action, but did not necessarily admit all the assertions in the claim- Defendant agreed that he had Bald or done what he Was not authorised to do, and he had left it to him (Mr. Nicholson) to say to what extent he had iajored her. replyin' g to tbe interrogatories put by plaintiff's solicitor, defendant admitted having made the remaskareferred to in the Warrington public-house, but he was at !the time under the impression that she was the same woman. as a certain Eliza Mitchell, who formerly kept an ienmoral house in Shepley-street, Manchester. Another. query ptlk to plaintiff elicited the reply that she was formerly at Ow dispensar# in Radnor-street, Manchester. Plalntiff was examined, and Mid she kept the public-house for Mr. Parker, Wine ar.d 'spirit merchant, King street, Manchester. ' Mr. Moore, in Addressing the registrar, saii the aranciseNiii, as cruel as could be uttered. The Registrar intidarated that it the case had been pressed by the plaintiff it was questionable whether she would not have obtained the full arnen it claimed. The defendant might be thankful for this, and he should give r damages SAO, and tax,e 'it t tetween party and party,

GOOD TEMPLAR! AT EARLESTOWN.—The usual weekly meeting of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Tem- piers was held in the Good Templars' Hall, Bridge-street, on Monday evening, when there was a good attendance of members. Bro. John Taylor, W.C.T. presided. Two new mem- bers were initiated, and others proposed. One or two items of business having been transacted the members spent the evening in singing, reciting dm. MASONIC BALL AT NEWTON.—A gay and festive scene was presented at Newton Town Hall on Tuesday evening last, when a Masonic ball, under the banner of the Lodge of Faith (No. 484), Ashton•ln-Makerfield, was held for the benefit of the Royal Masonic Benevolentlnstitution, London. Messrs. Evans and M'Clure of Earlestown, most elaborately bedecked the ball, under the superintendence of Brothers Stone (St. Helens), Harwood, W. Hibbert, and J. Devereux. The windows were draped with long, handsome lace cur- tains, choice plants being placed in the recesses between the windows. Beautiful silk banners, bearing representations of the insignias peculiar to the Masonic Order, were sus- pended on the walls, while the orchestra presented a splendid sight, a number of choice plants and exotics being placed on a raised dais. The floor was covered with specially prepared canvas. Dancing commenced shortly before nine o'clock, and was indulged in until about four o'clock on the follow- ing morning. The members of the Order appeared in their regalia, and presented a charming contrast to the fine dresses of the ladies. The band was Messrs. Greme's string band from Wigan, who gave every satisfaction. Brothers W. Hibbert and J. Devereux,..P.M., were the masters of cere- monies, and Brother E. C. Cooper, P.P.G.5.8., P.M., offi- ciated as director of ceremonies. The refreshment and supper were provided by Brother H. Hibbert, under the superintendence of Mrs. Perev4l.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, MARCH 1, 1884.

THE great measure of the present Session, if not of the present Parliament—the Bill whereby the franchise in the counties is to be extended and assimilated to that in the boroughs—was introduced into the House of Commons, on Thursday, by the PRIME MINISTER, who, in a speech of considerable length and showing a marvellous command of details, unfolded the Government propoglS with remarkable perspicuity. The scope of the Bill, on which there has naturally been much speculation, is now, therefore, fully dis- closed, and its provisions are of so liberal and comprehensive a character that the measure ought to command the undivided and ungrudging support of the Liberal party both within and without the walls of St. Stephen's. We submit that it ought, also, to secure the, sympathy, if nothing more substantial, of many Tories, who would not have been in Parliament but for their promise to vote for such a measure, and who must recognise in the Government scheme an honest effort to remove a crying grievance. Politicians who thought the provisions of the Bill would be few and brief will be disappointed. It is not so long since the Marquis of HARTINGTON, in one of those sagacious speeches for which he is noted, pointed out that the assimilation of the borough and county franchise involved complex difficulties little dreamt of by people who had not studied the question deeply; and the speech of the PRIME MusirsTEß, in introducing the measure, further reveals the extent and nature Of those difficulties. What is rather surprising is this, that the Bill affects the boroughs as well as the counties If we except freemen, liverymen, and others whose ancient right to vote for members of Parliament are not affected by the Bill, the franchise in the boroughs is of three distinct characters—the householder, the lodger, and the o occu- pier. The first two qualifications are to be left untouched; but as regards the third, it is to be extended so as to include occupiers of land on which there are no buildings. To these three qualifications is to be addod a fourth, christened by Mr. GLADSTONE the " service franchise," which will give a vote to persons who are neither owners nor tenants, but who occupy premises. This qualification will, perhaps, be best explained in the PRIME MINISTER'S own language— The service franchise is a far-reaching one. It goes to men of high class who inhabit valuable houses as the officers of Government institu- tions, and it descends to the humble classes who are the servants of tIL gentry, the ser- vants of the farmer, or the servants of some other employer of labour, who are neither owners nor tenants, and who in many cases cannot be held as tenants in consequence of the essential condition intended to be realised through their labour, and who yet duly fulfil the position of responsible inhabitant house- holders." These are the alterations so far as regards the boroughs, and we how come to the counties, where we find the qualifica- tions are also of a three-fold character, viz., the £5O occupier, the tz rated occupier, and the freeholder. The Bill proposes td abolish the Lso qualifications, since there is no one possessing that qualification who will not otherwise obtain the franchise. The rating franchise is to be reduced from LiZ rateable value to £ o clear yearly value, and all the borough franchises household, lodger, and service—are to be imported into the county, thus securing assimilation. The property franchise is to be retained, but we are glad to find it is to be surrounded with securities to prevent its abuse hi the manufacture of faggot votes. These, in brief, are the chief features of the Bill so far as they affect England and Wales, and the changes introduced are to be made directly applicable to Scotland and Ireland, leaving intact the peculiarities local to the several countries. It will be noted that the leading qualification is the occupation franchise ; the property franchise will, we take it, be comparatively few. The prin; ciple on which the Government have acte is that every head of a household should be enfranchised, and their scheme they have evidently worked out with much shill' It will not, or should not, we think, awakerl any surprise that the Bill is made applicable to Ireland, it would have been an injusti_ce had it been otherwise, and therefore I\l,rj GLADSTONE'S avowal that nothing view compel him to deviate from the path el duty in this regard may be taken asl o: hint that any attempt on the part ni the Opposition to exclude Ireland fro the. scope of the measure will be rev)*

lutely resisted. The fundamental principle of the Bill is equal treatment, and the com- plete assimilation of the franchise through- out Great Britain and Ireland. This is as it should be; and it is only by treating Ireland as we do other parts Of the United Kingdom that we can secure the contentment of the country. The comprehensive character of the Bill Will be gathered from the figures quoted by the PRIME MINISTER. Careful calculations show that if passed the mea- sure will add to the English and Welsh con- stituencies something like 1,300,000 persons, to the Scotch constituencies zoo,ooo, and to the Irish 400,000. To the present aggregate constituency of the United Kingdom, taken at 3,000,000 voters, the Bill will add 2,000,000 more, nearly twice as much as was added in 1867, and more than four times as Much as in 1832. In his opening remarks, Mr. GLADSTONE said he introduced the Bill not only in redemption of a pledge and be- cause it was desired by the people, but also because it was calculated to add strength to the State, There are, happily, few who now contend that the admission of two million People to the rights of citizenship is not a source of strength to the Constitution; but the wonder is not that so many people should nOW be admitted, rather that they should have submitted to exclusion so long. Now that this great measure is before the country we may be allowed to express the hope that it will speedily become law. It will be assailed, of course, by the Tories who, though Projessing to be anxia.us to extend the fran- chise, are not slow to adopt every means to thwart any step in that direction. But Mr.l GLADSTONE has not so much fear of direct as indirect opposition, which, of course, means , °Pposition from Liberal crotcheteers. We ! trust these gentlemen will see it to be their duty not to play into the hands of the Op- Position, but to sink their minor differences and concentrate their energies on making the Measure the success which it will assuredly Prove to be. If Liberal members will only be true to their principles and to the traditions of their party we feel sure that this the greatest measure of reform which has yet Qeen submitted will pass the Commons with a large majority of the people's representa- tives declaring in its favour, and the Lords Will then hesitate before they attempt to im Pair its efficacy in any shape.

vernment, only show the immense importance ' which has always been attached to Merv, and indicate that the event which has now taken place was not unexpected, though it may be only a corrollary of what has gone before. It is to be hoped that the Parliamentary papers when they are iubmizted will show that there is no settled purpose on the part of Russia to invade Afghanistan, as some alarmists imagine; and that on the other hand, finding I she has advanced in Central Asia as, far as she safely can, she will be content to remain where she is. Under any circumstances, however, it seems to us that our responsibili- ties towards Afghanistan are increased. These we would no doubt willingly relinquish, but we shall be unable to do so if Russia is to re- main so close to the Afghan frontier; and, therefore, it is gratifying to find that the ! Government are fully alive to the gravity of the situation, that our position in Afghanistan at the present time is stronger than ever it was before, and that no effort will be want- i ing on the part of the Ministry to protect ! our Indian Empire against the aggression of Russia or any other Power. At the same time the Government will not allow themselves to be hounded on in a course of hostility to- wards Russia which would necessarily pro- voke difficulties and dangers the end of which it is impossible to foretell. The present, above all others, is, in the words of the foreign under-secretary, a time for moderation alike in speech and action.

Tun Russian occupation of Mery was briefly, and on the whole temperately dis- cussed in the House of Commons the Other evening. This Was Only as it should be con- sidering the very limited information with Which we have so far been supplied; but we May be sure that on an early date—after Papers relating to this important event have been submitted by the Government—the i Whole question of the advance of Russia n Central Asia will form the subject of a I spirited and interesting debate in both 1 11.0 uses of Parliament. Though we fail to discover any sufficient ground for the alarm and irritation which , Russia's action has provoked in certain quarters, we are bound to admit that, having regard to the safety of our Indian possessions and our position in Afghanistan, we cannot afford to treat the matter lightly; and consequently it is necessary that in future Russia's forward movement should be eagerly Watched if not promptly checked. We doubt not, however, that at the close of the diplo- matic negotiations now proceeding between the Governments of this country and of Russia it will be found the annexation of Mery is only a necessary consequence of the advance of a civilising power, and that Eng- land would have done exactly what Russia has done had she been placed in a precisely similar position. We do not believe, as some excellent Tories would have us believe, that there is any settled desire on the part of Russia to invade India, nor do we think there Is any reason to fear her intriguing in Afghan- istan. Her game there has been played out. We could, however, have understood her adopting such a policy had the late Govern- ment remained in power and continued their °Perations in pursuit of scientific frontiers; But the policy of the Beaconsfield Adminis- tration has been reve,s3d, and between our Indian possessions and the Russian frontier there is now a strong and friendly Afghanis- -1.41n, in which our influence is paramount. It Is well known to be our intention to sustain Inn' influence with the Ameer of Afghanistan, and so long as that ruler finds we have no 'desire to annex his territory, and that 'he can • .rely f Upon us for support in case of aggression •'r°rll without, we feel sure that Russia will see it to be policy on her part to keep her ,eutposts at a respectful distance from what I,llnY justly be regarded as our preserves. C-AMELINt4 IN A WIDNES PUBLIC-llOUSE.—Before Mr. F. li.ierossage, Mr. J. Brock, and Mr. F. W. Earle, at Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday, John Gill, landlord of a beerhouse in Wellington-street, was summoned for unlaw- fully suffering gaming to be carried on in his licensed premises —Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared for the defendant.— P.C. Thompson said at ten minutes past midnight, on Satur- day, the 16th February, he was on duty in Waterloe-road. slle saw a light in the defendant's beerhouse, and looking .over the wall, he•saw several persons playing cards in the .kitchen. He then obtained the assistance of P.C. Towneley, and they went into the back yard. The landlord was in the room, and three men named Patrick Garraty, Patrick O'Brien, and Joseph Curley were playing a game at cards called " banker," for money. There was money on the table near O'Brien, and money was placed on the cards when they were dealt out. O'Brien was the banker. He watched them play for ten minutes to twenty minutes past twelve, and he saw money pass , several times. Ile then went into the house and took pos- session of the cards. The defendant eaid, "My back yard was fastened when you came here, and you had no right to break in." The back yard door was only fastened with the latch.—ln cross-examination by Mr Swift, the witness said the men were lodgers.—P.C. Townley gave corroborative, evidence.—Mr. Swift said the defendant admitted the facts of the case. but contended that as the three men were actors, lodging at the house, they were at liberty to use thehoose as though it were a private residence. If the defenndant had broken the law it was unwittingly, and an order for the payment of vests would amply meet the case.—Superintendent Barker said the defendant was fined lOs and costs in December, 1881, for permitting drunkenness.—The Bench now sen- tenced him to pay a fine of 303 and costs 12s, or go to gaol a month.--Superintendent Barker requested their worships to endorse the license, but they declined to do so. -

Mr. Oscar Wilda has now entirely dropped out of the arms of society where he was once dandled with a kind of amused affection. He will, however, come to be talked of again by and bye when his marriage takes place. Miss Lloyd, the happy object of 51119thetic love, is passably pretty, very sprightly, and comfortably endowed with money. As for Oscar, he has not advocated any new style a dress of late, standing faithfully to the cut away coat with the high collar, the tight trousers, the opulent shirt front, with the small linen collar turned down over a broad black band. He is, however, getting a little flabby in the face, and begins to look more than ever like the fat boy in Pickwick, grown in stature, and admitted to the drawing-room. Mr. Bright has during the recent political crisis observed an attitude distinct either from that of Mr. Forster or Mr. Goschen. He has neither attacked his old colleagues with venomous vigour, nor has he supported them whilst dexterously showing that their policy is not perfect. But Mr. Bright's views en affairs in Egypt are well known, and are sometimes indicated in private conversation. A capital story, illustrating this condition of mind, is just now de- lighting the House of Commons, though, I believe, Mr. Gladstone did not smile when it was retailed in his hearing. The position of the Ministry in respect of Egypt was under discussion over a friendly cigar. " There's something in it," said Mr. Bright, "that reminds me of a case that hap- pened at the quarter sessions in Somersetehire. A man was charged with stealing a pair of ducks." The evidence was undeniable: The jury found him guilty. "Have you anything to say, prisoner 2" the Chairman asked. " Yes, sir," said the man, "I have to say I wish to God I'd never seen those damned ducks."

An amusing result of the present aspect of the Garmoyle case is the innocent fraud which the retail photographers have practised on the public. It did not do that Miss Fortescue —a future countess—should have her portraits exhibited and sold in every stationer's for a florin. So the supply was stopped;and of course the demand increased. These cabinets went as high as 3s. 6d. No more were to be issued. But now that the match is broken off the market is flooded at the normal price. The disconsolate fairy is to be had in every attitude, and she has now gone down to tire level of Mrs. Langtry and the other professionals. In the meantime, one hears all sorts of rumours about the breach of promise case. I think I may say this on authority, that all Lord Grarmoyls has is £50,000. He has, of course, "great expec- tations," but that is all his actual money. There are no entailed estates. This £50,000 was left him by a relative, a Mr. Al acCalmont. I think, too, it will be found, when the trial comes on, that it is, in a way, non-contentious litiga- tion, that Miss Fortescue went down to Bournemouth in order that the question might be adjusted, if possible, amicably; I mean that a compromise might be arranged, and that the amount of the cheque Should be settled by consent. The parties themselves could not agree. The Pen i asked too much, or the Peer would give too little. And N a jury must settle the matter. Ready money and not acrimony is the difficulty, and both confidently appeal to what Mrs. Gamp calls a "A British Judy."
THE BRIDGEWATER FLATMEN.
THE STRIKE CONCLUDED.

The inevitable result of the strike of the fiatmen employed by the Bridgewater Navigation Company, Limited, which was foreseen from the commencement, took place on Thurs- day, when the men returned to work. Without organisa- tion, or a common fund, it was impossible for the flatmen to remain inactive for any ,lengthened period; and rememberng their iformer disastrous and unsuccessful struggles against the will of their masters, their action was, to say the least, injudi- cious. Certainly the men had the sympathy of the public. The injustice of reducing their wages when the firm was in a position to pay a dividend equivalent to 91 per cent, was strongly commented upon in many quarters,and a fund which was opened in Runcorn for the relief of the "strikers" was supported from a variety of sources. The first proposition of the company was that the men should accept a reduction of Is per week. When this proposal was met by a threat to strike, the company intimated that if work was not resumed within a certain period the reduction would be increased from one to two shillings These terms after a fortnight's idleness the men have been com- pelled to accept, and it should be a lesson to them that labour cannot hope successsfully to compete with capital without a good organisation and a large fund. Owing to the want of unity the strike was only a partial one. The Company employ about 600 men in the fiats, and of these only about 350. half of whom belonged to Runcorn, left their work. It will thus be seen that with the extra hands the Company engaged, and those that still retained their places' the traffic would not be hindered to a very great ex- tent. It is an unfortunate fact that the places of a number of the 11;.ttnen have during the strike been filled up by fresh hands, and these will have to seek other labour to support their families. It is only fair to state that during the struggle the men have conducted themselves in a way which deserves commendation. Beyond occasionally walk- ing through the streets in processional order, they-have made no hostile demonstrations ofdany description, and their behaviour has been orderly throughout.
LEFT TO DIE ON RUNCORN DOCKS.

HEARTLESS CONDUCE OF A SON. On Tuesday afternoon Mr. Coroner Ridgway held an in- quiry into the circumstances surrounding the death of Anthony Doogan, 67 years of age, which took place at his leon's house, 10, Fryer-street, on Saturday evening last. The E deceased was a labourer for the Bridgewater Navigation Company at the docks, and on Saturday morning was em- ployed at the Welsh low basin. His son was working a short distance away, and about half-past eleven he noticed that something was the matter with his father. He went to his assistance and wished to take him home, but the old man said he had only knocked his toe against his ankle whilst wheeling a barrow and said he should be all right in a few minutes. He could not stand, however, and the son with the aid of James Welsh, another labourer, carried him to a heap of china clay and placed a coat under him and' one over him. Although the clay was wet, and it was raining at the time, the son never went near his father again, ' and the poor old man was found about half-past one lying on the wet clay in an unconscious state. He was carried away by James Mannion, James Welsh, and several other men. On the way to Dr. Marrity's surgery Mr. Linnett administered some brandy, and the doctor also applied remedies, after which he was carried to his soles house. He died the same evening. Dr. Mouritz stated to the jury that the deceased died of a fit of serious apoplexy superin- duced by cold, wet,and exposure.—The Coroner: Supposing the man had been taken home at half-past eleven and had bad proper attention, should you have expected him to die from your knowledge of the case.—The Doctor: If proper steps had been taken to get him to a warmer place it would have been much better for him.—The son, Bartley Doogan, was called, and. said as his father deserted him when he was three years of age, and left his mother and his sisters to get along as best they could, he did not feel called upon to look after his father. He thought, however, he had gone away from the place.—Tne Coroner said in cases where the death seemed to have been a natural one, it was not his rule to hold an inquiry, but when there were any circumstances brought before him which showed that proper care had not been taken he thought it was his duty to have the fullest inquiry, although the death might be natural. It was evident that in this case there had been a great amount of carelessness and thoughtlessness in leaving this poor man in the cold and rain. The only explanation the son could give that he didn't take any notice of his father was simply that as his father did not care for him he did not see any reason why he should care for his father. But apart from the question of filial duty, there was a cer- tain amount of duty which one man, whether a stranger or not. owed to his fellow-man, and there had been heartless neglect on the part of Bartley Doogan. If one man saw another taken ill and unable to do anything for him- self, it was not sufficient to ask him whether he would do certain things. It was Doogan's duty when he left off work to have taken steps for his father to be properly attended to. So far as the other men, Ma onion and Welsh, were con- cerned, they seemed to have done the best they could under the circumstances.—The jury retired to consider their ver- dict, and on returning the Foreman (Mr. F. Fairhurst) said: Our verdict is that the deceased died from a fit of serious apoplexy induced by cold and exposure, and that Bartley Doogan deserves the strongest censure for his unfeeling conduct in the matter.—The Coroner: I can only say that I quite agree with your verdict.—Doogan was theu called to the witness box and severely censured by the Coroner, who said he could only mark his appreciation of his conduct by nOt allowing his fee for attending as a witness.

, A SHOCKING CASE AT RUNCORN. Mr. Ridgway, the coroner for the honour and fee of Halton, on Tuesday held an inquest in Runcorn Police Court on the body of Emma Kinsey, wife of John Kinsey, a labourer living at 63, Heath-road. The circumstances of the case as given in evidence were as follows : The de- ceased, who was 50 years of age, was of drunken habits, and her conduct was the cause of constant quarrels with her husband, who had struck her whilst in an intoxicated state. Kinsey is an old soldier who has served in India, where he commenced the practice of taking opium in the form of pills. His wife also was in the practice of swallowing the insidious herb, and between the two they consumed six- pennyworth of opium and fourpennyworth of laudanum. On Friday night last the deceased complained of a pain in her left breast, and her husband wished her to take a dose of opium, but she declined, and on Saturday morning she appeared in her usual state bat about noon she was sud- denly seized with a severe illness, and died almost instantly. In consequence of the rumours that agitated the neighbour- hood in regard to the manner in which the woman had died, the coroner deemed it advisable to have a post mortein examination, and Dr. Bagnall was entrusted with the task. He described the condition of the body minutely. She was very emaciated, and every organ in the body was more or less diseased, the heart being in an especially bad state. He found no trace of poison whatever, and was of opinion that the cause of death was heart disease. Neither opium nor laudanum.—Mrs. Hannah Kinsey, living at 19, Sutherland. street, the mother of the deceased, was called, and said both husband and wife were addicted to drink. On Wednesday she met her drunk in the street. She seemed to be much cleaner than usual, and told witness that if she could net get money matters right "she would some time or other take a double dose of laudanum, and that would end all." —Maria Clare, 17 years of age, who was in the house of deceased on Saturday morning, was closely questioned as to whether the deceased took any opium or laudanum. She strongly protested that she did not.—The Coroner, in sum- ming up, laid much stress upon the importance of the medical testimony, and the jury, after a short consultation, returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased died from heart disease.

Since their last gathering the boundary wall had been erected, the church consecrated, and the trustees of the advowson p;sainted. The trustees were the Rev. George Bond, as vicar of Fern worth, Mr. Timnais, Mr. Brock, Mr. Pilkington, and their humble ser- vant. (Applause.) There was a provision in the deed by which the congregation would always have one representa- tive, who would be chosen by the churchwardens of the parish. Mr. Bond bad taken the proper steps to get St. Ambrose put upon the endowment list of the Ecclesiastical Commissioners. They did not know when the endowment would be granted, but they had every reason to believe they would have it in about the ordinary length of time—per- haps in two er three years. It all depended upon the num- ber of applicants and the need of those applicants, but he thought they could show a very good case, and they would not fail to press their case as frequently and as strongly as decency would permit. The trustees had unanimously offered the incumbency of St. Ambrose to their friend Mr. Spooner. (Applause.) Mr. Spooner had very naturally asked for a short time in which to consult his friends and to make up his mind as to whether he should take the serious step of accepting the offer. He hoped they would soon have his reply, and for himself he said that be (Mr. Carey) should be extremely sorry if Mr. Spooner did not see his way to accept the office. (Applause.)—The enter- tainment was then proceeded with, the programme including several items of great interest. rhe following ladies and gentlemen took part :—Mrs. McLennan, Misses Harrison, Cooper, Troup, Valentine, Haddock, Bond, and flibbert ; Messrs. S. Kidd, F. Mercer, H. V. Black, and Perks.
A WIDNES GROCER'S SrRATAGEM UNJUST SCALES._

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, G. N. Wharton, provision dealer, Victoria-road, whose premises are known as " The Noted Cheap Shop," was summoned for having in his possession for use of trade three pairs of counter so-des which were unjust.—The defendant's manager, who ap. neared, admitted that the scales were out of order.—Supt. Barker said he visited the defendarrVrshop on Wednesday, the TOth February. As he entered the manager was in the act of weighing some bacon, but when he saw him (the superintendent) he seemed very much confused, and en- deavoured to do something. at the -scales. He said "Let these scales alone, and I will see what's the matter." He put his hand underneath the plate on which the bacon was weighed, and found attached to it a damp piece of paper which weighed a quarter of an ounce. When that was re- moved the scales were perfectly correct. Under the plate of another pair of scales be found another piece of damp paper, and a third pair of scales were weighted in a similar manner. Without the paper the scales were all right. This was as clear a case of fraud as it was possible to brine before their worships.—Mr. Gossage : Why is not Mr. Whartoa here.— Mr. Barker said he did not know. This was the worst case 4he had had for a considerable time past. One pair of scales was used for weighing tea and the other for bacon, butter, and such like, and quantities of a quarter of a pound were weighed upon them. As he was leaving the shop Mr. Wharton entered, and was very impertinent. He might have laid an information for each pair of scales, but he pre- ferred to put them together.—The defendant was fleet' £5 and costa, 12.

The Rey. S. A. SPOONER, in moving a vote of thanks to the Chairman and to those who had in any way contributed to the success of the gathering, said he had very anxiously considered the offer made by the trustees that he should accept the incumbency of St. Ambrose. It was hard to de- cide what to do at the present moment, and his mind was not exactly made up, though the warmth and enthusiasm of that evening and the kindness with which he had always been received in the parish, and the willingness there was to work amongst them, somewhat inclined him to think favourably of the offer. In case he should accept it,let him hope that there would always be the same enthusiasm in , regard to church work as there had been in LAI Past, and he certain* hoped that the same people then would occupy the positions they did now. He felt thitife mother arhe ernainei he o should always have the sympathy e Vicaragech he should always have the friendship f the family, and he should always have the friendship of their dear brother Mr. Jackson, of Sankey. (Applause.) Of course for a young man to take a position of thfficulty and responsibility, and a very poor stipend, was a matter of anxiety, and whoever was to become the iacumbent of St. Ambrose mast look earnestiv for ), the co-operation of the people, rich and poor alike, and I e hoped in case be (Mr. Spooner) accepted the incumbency he should have that co- operation and the good feeling of all the people. (An- pl &use.)
The Rev. GEo. 800 seconded the motion, which was canied unanimously, and the ineeting terminated.

div.head: RUNCORN GROCER. HEAVILY FINED.
div.p: A RUNCORN GROCER. HEAVILY FINED.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. W. Bankes and Mr. John Brundrit, Edward Johnson, grocer, of Runcorn, Widnes, St. Helens, Jac., was summoned on a charge of being in possession, for use of trade, of a pair of scales which were unjust.—Mr. Blair, the manager of the shop, appeared, and pleaded guilty. He said the scales were examined every week, and after the superintendent's visit he had them tested. They were found to be half a drachm wrong.—Supt. Williamson said, on the 13th ultimo, he visited the defendant's shop at the end of Church-street, Runcorn. He found a pair of scales two drachtns against the purchaser. The scales, which were used for weighing bacon, were in a very dirty state. There was no doubt that the scales, if they got a good washing, would not be so much out of balante. This shop was in the name of Chas. Johnson, but it was now owned by Edward Johnson. The scales in this establishment had been found defective on a previous OCCltSiell, when the name of Charles Johnson was over the door.—Mr. Blair said he had been manager of the shop for about four months, and during that time the-shop had belonged to Mr. Edward Johnson. They were very particular shout the scales.—Mr. Bankes said it was owing to the disgraceful state in which the scales were kept that they were wrong. If they had boon kept clean they would have been all right.—Mr. Brundrit asked if the defendant was the same Johnson that was Mayor of St. Helens some time agoT—Mr. Blair: Yes, sir.—The Bench fined the de- fendant 40s. and costs 103.+6d.

div.head: UNLAWFULLY WOUNDING AT WIDNES.
div.p: UNLAWFULLY WOUNDING AT WIDNES.

Before Mr. John Brock, at Widnes Police'Court, on Mon- day, Michael Donlan, labourer, was charged with unlaw- fully wounding Martin Brennan. From a statement by Inspector Wood, it appeared that the two men were em- ployed at Messrs. Gaskell and Deacon's Chemical, Works, and were working on the night turn on Saturday. About five o'clock, on Sunday morning, Brennan went into the office of the foreman, li,obert Callaghan, and when he came out the prisoner, who was outside called him by a foul name and alleged that he had been telling the foreman some- thing. Brennan replied that he would tell the foreman of the prisoner's language, and returned into the office. When he again emerged, the prisoner, who was wait- ing for him with a shovel in his hand, struck him with that implement on the right side of the head, cutting the scalp to the bone, and knotking him senseless to the ground. When he recovered consciousness he was in his Own house. His injuries were afterwards attended to by Dr. McDonnell.— This statement ,was corroborrated by the prosecutor.—George Boardman, a labourer at the works, deposed that he saw the prisoner and prosecutor, fighting. Brennan had a shovel over his shoulder, and held it as if he were going to strike the prisoner, who etruck him with hiafist and knocked him down. He be- lieved Brennan cat his head by falling on some iron platee on the floor.—Wm. Smart, also a labourer, was of opinion Brennan cut his head by falling on the shovel.—Dr. McDonnell described Brennan's injury as a star-shaped, contused lacerated wound from 1 inches to 2 inches in -length, extending to the bone, on the right side of the head, about an inch above the ear. Tile wound might have been produced by nhe shovel produced.—Evidence was given that the prisoner when apprehended and charged with the offence said, "I had no spade."—He was committed ,to the sessions for trial, but was admitted to bail, himself in 120 and two sureties.of £lO.

EXPROPRIATING A HITSBAND.—Pattick Murphy, a res- pectable-looking young man, was on Friday charged at the St. Helens Police Court with having done wilful damage to a door and window of the house 18, Hamer-street, the resi- dence of his father-in-law. Mr. J. O. Swift defended. It seemed that defendant and his wife had not lived happily together. She in consequence, left him and went to her father's house. On the Saturday night previous, about eleven o'clock, defendant went to the house with the object of seeing his wife, but as be was refused admittance he did the damage for which be was now summoned. Mrs.. Gal- Ligher estimated the damage at 225., but Mr. Swift slid he had caused the window and door to be examined by Mr. Leather, foreman to Mr. Harris, builder, and he stated th it ss. would cover all the damage done. It vras also urged that defendant's wife had left him without just cause. A fine of le. and 7s. costs was imposed, and defendant was ordered to pay ss. damages.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

THE NEW SPEAKER—DOUBT AND TRIUMPH—THE LATE SPEAKER—A PLEASANT TOWN HOUSE— ASH WEDNESDAY AND THE THEATRES—A NEW SENSATION FOR LONDON OSCAR AND HIS BRIDE—MR. BRIGHT ON THE POLITICAL SITU- ATION—DRAWING PICTURES OUT OF SMOKE— LORD GARMOYLE AND MISS FORTESCUE. LOYDON, Thursday.

"I listened with profound satisfaction," Mr. Gladstone said when, after the election of the Speaker, on Tuesday, someone asked him what he thought of Mr. Peel's speech. For this satisfaction the Premier had doable grounds. In the first place it is no small satisfaction to a Minister to know that the business of the House for an indefinite period will be presided over by a capable man. Nothing could be worse for a Government than that the chair should be oc- cupied by one not big enough to fill it. With the present dexterous and unscrupulous Opposition progress of business would in such circumstances be more than ever hopeless. Another ground for satisfaction with Mr. Gladstone was the knowledge that his choice had been worthily sustained by the object of it, and confirmed after five minutes hesitation by the House. There is no doubt that there was much raising of the eyebrows and shrugging of the shoul- ders when Mr. Peel was nominated to the chair. It speaks a great deal for the good taste and sense of public duty existing in the Press, and as far as I know no journal said a word in disparagement of the proposal. If it had been thrown down as a matter for discussion, if the public had been given to understand that Mr. Gladstone was consider- ing the suitability of Mr. Peel balancing him against other candidates, a good deal would have been said. But the an- nouncement reached the public ear in the first instance as of an accomplished fact. Mr. Peel had been selected and would beyond doubt be elected. It was therefore emi- nently undesirable l 2 weaken his authority by discussing his capability. NTr. ne has been formally elected, and within a space that certainly did not exceed six minutes he completely transformed opinion in the House, and revealed himself in a new and surprising light. The difference between Mr. Gladstone who chose him and the House of Commons which doubted, appeare to be that one knew him thOrtrd/Voly and the other very slightly. To the House Mr. Peel was a tall dark man, inclined to be gaunt in figure and gloomy in countenance. ,As a subordinate minister he has sometimes had occasion to speak from either the Treasury Bench or the Front Bench opposite. After listening for a few minutes to his hesitating voice and observing his uncomfortable demeanour members have generally cleared out, leaving him to talk to empty benches. In rising on Tuesday to return thanks for the honour done him, the whole bearing and individuality of the man were changed. He stood erect and face the crowded House, not presump- tiously, bat without fear. For the first time it was dis- covered he had a pleasant voice, something, old members say, like his father's. His delivery was excellent, and above all the high tone of his speech won over the assembly which amid all its indiscipline and occasional indecorum is proud of the traditions of the House of Commons. The Conservatives who had received him with chilling silence when he rose joined heartily in the cheer amid which he at down. It was, I think, the most complete and most agreeable personal surprise ever ex;ierienced by the House.

Sir Henry Brand has left his pleasant town house with its river front and many privileges befitting the position of the first Commoner in the land. There can be no question that as between a peerage and the Speaketship the latter is in , finitely preferable. There are peers and peers. There is the Duke of Marlborough for example, and Lord Aylesfo7d is a peer, and so of quite another order is Lord Brabourne. But there is only one Speaker. "I am very:sorry to leace you all,"Sir Henry Brand said, w.hen at one o'clock on Tuesday morning he left the chair for the last time and passed'out through a throng of members, who boisterously cheered him. One of them, by the way, tells me that'll was witiothe greatest difficulty he could refrain from starting the early morning hymn, "For he's a jolly good follow." Dochtless if the temptation had not been resisted the next thing, would have been to have raised the Speaker shoulder high and so carried him home, a spectacle the very con- templation of which sends a shudder through the well- regulated mind. Sir Henry Brand's regret is easily conceivable. The Speakership has its cares, but itc•pleasures ar outweigh them. To-clay Mr. Arthur Peel goes into the Speaker's house, Sir Henry Brand having moved his private thattela a week ago. The Speaker's house is furnished at ,the expense of the State, handsomely furnished, too, and is, take it all in all, the pleasantest to en house in London. In Ithe matter of emolument the late Speaker does not greatly suffer. His salary wee £5,003 a year. To-day the House of Commons voted him an annuity of £4,000 with con- tiauance to his eon and heir. What English people will stand in the way of absurdity is testified to in the fact that last night being Lsh Wednes- day all the theatres in London were closed. Of all the narrow-minded things done in the name of the broadest religion in the world this surely is the least defensible. Its absurdity is shown in the well-known fact that the edict extends to only one ride of the river, and that whilst on the north a night's wages is peremptorily cut oE from thou- sands of men and women who do not earn too much in a week, on the other no,such capricious tyranny is rampant Mr. Woodall, the member for Stoke, took this matter up a session or two ago. trust he does not mean to drop it. To obtain the abolition of this stupid relic of the predominance of priestcraft would .be a more useful and honourable achievement even than to hamper the passage of the Fran- chise Bill with attempts to tack on to it the principle of female suffrage. One would have thought, by the way. that actors having a holiday thrust upon them would have been inclined to enjoy it quietly at home. That, however, does not seem to be their ambition. In one drawing room last night I counted five of the planets of the Loudon -stage, liveliest amid a throng of painters, poets, literary men, professional beauties, and members of Parliament.

One of the latest notions to amuse London is to present OR some suitable stage a counterfeit presentment of a Sapanese village. A big place is to be hired, such as the Agricultural Hall or the Albert Hall. Real Japanese men and women with real houses, shops, and all the material details of daily life are to be imported. A street is to be built in exact imitation of one of the narrow,busy thoroughfares of Japan, and then the people are to be bidden to go about their daily business whilst two or three thousand English people stare at them from outside the barricad es. The idea is a very pretty one. There are few spectacles more attrac.

tiva than a street in Japan with its bustling life, its many colours, its quaint houses, and its ever chattering popula- tion. But the cost would be considerable, and the prac- ticability is at least doubtful.

It would be interesting to ascertain how many among the thousands who pass over our city bridges daily see any- thit.g but the " toil " and "grime "in the busy traffic, the going to and fro of laden barges, the smoking factories, and the general turmoil that prevails from morn till eye. Some 'few of our poets have discovered beauty in all these things. ,and Sh,kespeare knew a man who found" sermons in stones 4nd good in everything," Perhaps Mr. W. L. Wyllie is a

The monthly meeting was held at the Boar!-room, Vic. toria-road, on Thursday. Mr. T. S. Tirnmis presided, and there were present the *Rev. Fathers Clarke and Finegan, Messrs. IL W. Deacon, R. H. Davies, Dr. O'Keeffe, R. Shiva, J. B. Imison, P. Glover, and G. El. Danbv (clerk). SCHoOL EDUCATION COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee, which were passed on the motion of Mr. H. W. Deacon, stated that 47 persons had been prosecuted during the past month. Of these 45 had been convicted, and two children had been committed to an industrial school.

A RESIGNATION. The School Management Committee recommended that the resignation of Mr. a. S. Heacock, caretaker of West Bank School, be accepted, and that another person be ap- pointed at a salary of £1 1, with house, gas, and coal. The minutes were passad, on the motion of the Rey. Father FINEGAN.

FINANCE. The Finance Committee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £997 4s 3d. The following SEEM had been paid into bank :—School fees for January: Simms Cross School £l5 24s 61, Warringtcm-road School £2O 163 2d, West Bank School £3B us 4d, Public Works Loan Board £3,000. Science and Art Department: Simma Cross School £22 17s 2d, West Bank School £7 17s sd, managers Farnworth National School £2; total, £3,137 16J 7d. • The minutes wero pasaed on the motion of Mr. BRAD*

SUDAN CLOSING. A communication was read from Colonel Blackburne stating that he had presented to the House of Commons the petition of Widnes School Board with r,fc-ence to the sale of intoxicating liquors on Sunday.

_ _ A lIEADNIASTEFeS C3MPLAINT. A letter was read from Mr. D. W. Hooter, headmaster at the Warrington-road Boys' School, in which the writer com- plained that after six years' service he had been rattier severely treated, lie pointed out that one class—standard 3—was treated in a manner hardly just by the inspector's assistant at the last examination. The boys were at school from 9 a.m. until 11-25, and then when their energies were dissipated by inaction, and several boys were asking to go home to take their fathers' dinners as usual, the examiner commenced, and did not cud till the bell was ringing for afternoon school at 1-25. The result was that the per- centage of the school had been reduced to 77 per cent., and for this the writer had lest £7 bonus, and owing to the com- mittee having drawn the line at 80 per cent, he was de- prived of a rise of salary. He thought it was rather hard that he should be punished twice for the same offence. Trio committee had never announced that a favourable repert could be gained only by passing 80 per czut., and the teachers in the Board Schools worked all the year, never dreaming that their salaries were to be decided by so un- certain and fluctuating a basis. Mr. Hunter respectfully in- quired whether the whole circumstances would not warrant the Board in asking the committee to reconsider their de- cision.

The CHAIRMAN said although the Board were not respon- sible for the action of the inspector, he thought it might be desirable that an arrangement should be made so that none of the boys would have to leave school to take dinners. Father FINEGAN believNl there was some real truth in Mr. Hunter's complaint, and he could mention half a dozen other such cases. The committee had it under considera- tion to make a representation to the inspector that no schools in the Widnes School Board district should be es- amined during the dinner hour. The CHAIRMAN thought the inspector would be glad to meet their wishes. The next point in Mr. Hunter's letter was that he was not aware that it v,-as necessary to pass 80 per cent. Father CLA.REE : That is not in Mr. Hant.'..t'f favour at all. It is against him. Father FINEGAN remarked that the Committee had been influenced by several reasons, the chief one being that the school had earned Is 4d less per head this year than last. Mr. SHAW pointed out that the Board had suffered as well as Mr. Hunter, and he did not see what action they could take in the matter. It was ultimately decided that a reply should be sent to Mr. Hunter stating that the Board would take steps with the object of preventing the po,,s"...ility of such a thing complained of by him recurring. THE NEW SALARY SCHEME. The CLERK read the following letter from Mr. T. Showan, held master of West Bank senior boys' school:— Allow me to drew your attention to the following effects' of the proposed salary scheme, now awaiting the confirmation of the Board. 1. It will lessen my present ealary 25s per month, in the place of which it offers a very great uncertainty —payment for pupil teachers. 2. It deprives me of the pro- gression offered to other teachers. 3. It makes no provision for a school over 200 in average attendance, such as mine. 4. It proposes a smaller remuneration for working a school of 300 than 140, as will be proved by c mtrasting the maximum salary under the two schemes. When the Board consider my school has been enlarged to seat 320 boys, I hope they will grant me the favour shown by the London a-id Bradford BJards to their old masters, viz., that I remain under the present scheme. The school managers have expressed that they do not wish me to be reduced, which I most be £lO dur- ing the next two years, if I come under the new scheme. I sincerely hope the Board will consider my request, and thereby encourage me to make my large and growing school still more efficient and creditable to the town." —The letter was referred to the School Management Com- mittee; and the proceedings terminated.

div.head: YOUNG SHOPBREAKERS AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: YOUNG SHOPBREAKERS AT WAR- RINGTON.

On Monday, at the Warrington- Police Court, three boys, averaging from 12 to 14 years of age, named Arthur Scott, Charles William Howell, and Alfred Melling, all of Bat- tersby-lane, were charged with having stolen from a drawer in the shop of Elizabeth Hoey, provision d3aler, 1, Apple- ton's Bnildings, off Battersby-lane, 6s 61 in silver, 4s 9d ID. copper, and two earthen bowls.—About half-past ten o'clock on Saturday night the prosecutrix was in the back part of her house, and on hearing a noise she went tewards the shop, when she noticed two or three boys running away. On going to the till ske found the drawer open, and that the two bowls containing the money in question were missing. Information was given to the police, which resulted in the apprehension of the prisoners by P.C. Evans on Sunday morning, when one implicated the other. In answer to What they had done with the money, they admitted having spent it in cigars, going to the theatre, &c., and one of the lads iook the policeman and showed him where they had thrown away the vessels.—The Chief Constable said that the boys were the sons of respectable parents, but the charge against the prisoners was a nerious one, and it ought not to go unpunished.— The magistrates ordered Scott and Melling to be detained until six o'clock in the evening, and that each receive 12 strokes with the birch rod—to be given in instalments of six strokes at a time. Howell was fined lOs and costs or 14 days' imprisonment. Four other scapegraces named George Harding, Sharp-street, Thomas Baldry, Helsby- street, Ernest Paple, Appleton's Buildings, and Charles William Howell (one of the prisoners in the former case), were then charged with stealing from the shop of Hugh Ebenezer Hawthorne, 52, Chorley-street, on the night of February 7th, a quantity of nuts, sweets, currants, raisins, and three jars of jam, of the value of 3s 6rl.—On the even- ing in question prosecutor was away at a tea party, but during the evening he was told that his shop had been broken into, and on returning he found that a square of glass in his shop window bad been smashed, and a quantity of raisins, sweets, arid jam abstracted. Inquiries Were set on foot, but they did not result in anything until the pre- vious day, when one of the lads (Howell), then in custody on another charge, made a statemont through which his companion pilferers were apprehended by P.C. Evans.—Mr. Percy Davies appeared for Harding, and said this case was not in any way so serious as the one they had just dealt with, and where money had been stolen. It appeared there was a hole in prosecutor's shop window, and that the pri- soners seeing the temptation made it a little bigger to get at the jam. (Laughter.)—Howell, in this case, was fined 10s and costs or 14 days, and each of the others ordered to re- ceiye 12 strokes of the birch rod.
