div.p: Mettero to the ittor.

POT-HOUSE ARRANGEMENTS. Sir,—l must confess that I feel a little nervous at writing once more under the above heading. However, I may get along with your three correspondents, Mr. Jones, Mr. Chap- man, and the anonymous " Nemo." At least I have one satisfaction. "A Ratepayer " has seen the error of his wave, 'and very likely in your next ho will confess as mach. With all possible humility, I must admit that I am no match for three such fall-grown water melons as those we have now rolling about on the pot-house plank. To give extracts from my letter, and then say these are my opinions, is only to adopt the usual methods of abstainers. To argue with them is a mere waste of time. Like the Tories, they neither forget nor yet learn. I say they are narrow- minded. In proof, I ask them to read their pledge, and see for themselves whether it would be possible for myself to sign it. I say their language is intemperate; for proof, study Sir W. Lawson's speeches. I say it is abusive; and, referring especially to one class of speakers, can only find its parallel in the theological " rot " to be heard at Salvation Army meetings. I have no desire to pose as the friend of publicans, I can assure my abstaining friends that the pot-house keepers would be as pleased to see them as anyone else. There is always a good supply of ginger ale and pop, 2d. per bottle; very moderate profit this, but offering a good op- portunity for spreading "teetotal blessings." Mr. Jones is mistaken in thinking that I referred to the political club in Bewsey-street. I know that especial efforts have been made to stop gambling at that club, even up to the point of taking extreme measures with individuals; and I also know, as a matter of fact, that Sunday School teachers have had to de- plore their young men being inveigled to the card table and billiard table, knowing well that at least atone of these tables money nearly always changes hands, and cases have arisen where workingmen have lost all their wages on the Satur- day afternoon. Itds now a fact that men of all ages attend our political billiard rooms night after night the year round, and are in the most dense ignorance respecting the anxious political life that is now hemming in the work- ingman and his surroundings. Mr. Jones asks "Do I wish to pose as the Roebuck of Warrington Liberalism P.' I scarcely know what this means; but I will say this, that whatever work my hand finds to do, I try to do it with all my might; and whoever told "Nemo ' that I tried to "force my nostrums" was untruthful, and a traitor to the Liberal party. Each political party has within the last few years been largely reinforced, thousands of workingmen have had an immense power placed within their hands, and I ask "Nemo" and his untruthful friend if it is for the benefit of these workingmen that our ward or municipal business should be left in the same hands that have so grossly abased it in the past, that have made it possible for the Wilderspool Brewery Company to buy up week after week all the best property in the town. Now these are nuts for the teetotallers to crack. Where is the workingman that at any of the Liberal Executive meetings has cared or dared to make inquiry respecting our workhouse system, to urge the party to take up the franchise question, or te take steps for giving the workingman an administrative power. Not one has dared to do it besides myself, and this is "forcing nos- trums." If so, then each Liberal measure must be a "nostrum." Fer the Conservative working- man to be led or driven seems to use quite in accordance with Nature's laws, and as he Is a monstrocity, nature will ere long rid herself of him. "Nemo " must be satisfied with this passing notice ef him; his letter carries with it such an undercurrent of ill breed- ing and want of honour, that I leave him to study the "good old book," and from its " sacred page" learn what charity really is. Mr. Chapman being a particular friend of mine, deems it necessary to don the "candid friend's" garments, thinking by this means to make the knife he so skilfully wields more incisive in its gashes. lam not at all surprised that he saould defend teetotalism, in fact were he to gather up all the " isms" now extant. I shouldn't be surprised, nor yet would anyone else. • I wonder how many pets he has at the present time. Like the bellman he is to be found at every street corner, frightening timid folks. If the Mersey should happen to get on fire, none but he could be cbarged with hav- ing sufficieat calvricity to bring about such startling pheno- mena. He knows nothing as to what goes on "midst beer and smoke." This is the case with most abstainers, yet it doesn't hinder them from jumping to conclusions. One word I will withdraw from the surroundings so skilfully placed by Mr. Chapman, that is "moderators." There is a difference , between the moderate politician and the moderate drinker. Till ' the present timel have prided myself upon belonging to both parties; this may surprise my friends. Recent events, to which I cannot now refer, make ma think the moderate I politician is like the neutral one, a compound of chalk and I water. Mr. Chapman belongs to no political party; in this he makes a mistake. The pachydermatous idiosyncrasies peculiar to him would make his position impregnable. As ills, the old Rezinante he so often bestrides is likely to be ridden to death, and all to no purpose. I think Mr. Chap- man, myself, and a few more kindred spirits, would be quite sufficient to set Warrington on fire. To achieve this I pro- pose we throw teetotalism overboard, find some back sham " pub " where, midst "beer and smoke," we could re-enact the three tailors of Tooley-street. Aro we not the people ? Carlyle was no doubt right in his opinion of the British public. Arguments are of no use. They refuse to swellovr pop bottles. This being so, my friend has but to join myself. In ten minutes we could formulate such a programme as would convince all the world that We had not only all the 1 sense but all the " fade" necessary for man's welfare. Warrington, February" 26, 1.884. H. WHITHAM.

„DISESTABLISHMENT. Sir,—Mr. John Peers in your last issue advocates die- establishment as a sllution of the tithe question. But I should like to point out to that gentleman that this vexed question might much more easily be settled in a way I will shortly name than by disestablishment. But, first of all, does Mr. Peers think disestablishment would do away with the paying of tithes? If I understand the word disestab- lishment, it means this, and this only, viz, that there shall be no State Church. True, if we add the word disendow- ment to disestablishment, the payment of tithes would be abolished. But why not be honest in advocating this ques- tion, and not substitute a mild word for a stronger one? Some people might call disestablishment robbery. Yes, sir, Mr. Peers may live to find out that disestablishment is a knife with a double edge, whiclacan be made to cut riot only against the Church of England endowments, but also against "trust funds” of Dissent. But sir, what I have to suggest to Mr. Peers is this: why not ask the member for Warrington to bring in a bill in the House of Commons to do away with these obnoxious tithes? In other words, make it compulsory to commute the tithes. I don't think such a bill would be opposed by the Conservative party in Parliament, and thus Mr. Peers would shortly have his wish gratified instead of having to wait for an indefinite period.—Yours, &c. A CHURCHMAN.

Sir,—l shall not stoop to answer Mr. Peers in the same kind of language which he adopted towards me in his last letter, though nothing would be easier. For instance, Mr. Editor, I might have told him that his first letter was both illogical and ungrammatical and his second little better. I might also have told him—part:y in word. 3 of his own— that his arguments and answers were not only" frivolous" and "quibbling," but childish and absurd. But I resisted the temptation, thereby earning, I hope, not only the ad- miration of your readers, but the gratitude of Mr. Peers himself. And may I remind Mr. Peers that difficulty does not lie in applying adjectives, the like of which he applied to me, but in proving their applicability. So much as a preface. Let me tarn to what Mr. Pears considers, I sup- pose, answers to my queries. In reply to my first question, asking him" to state by what Act or acts of Parliament the ICehurchauottErnitgyland was established," he sIYEI As a gal ho I cannot give him the specific information on this point; but, being in possession of a little common sense (very little and very common' let me say) and seeing men who I think are probably wiser than the twin vowel (? vowels) and myself in this matter who are striving to disestablisheoeted tthh,aet English Church by Act of Parliament, I n ment was a factor in the establishment thereof, splendid specimen have we here displayed of the usual Liberationist ignorance and unfounded conclusions. Fancy a man who claims to be an Englishman saying that the Church of England is established by Act of Parliament, and when pressed for proof excuses himself that he is not a " legal authority." I presume he was in the same position when he made the statement And, having made the state- ment not as a "legal authority" he should prove it, not as a "legal authority." Again, he concludes that because there are men—whom he with novel assumption assumes are wiser than myself, which, by the by, gives rise to another query as to how he knows this—striving, to disestablish the Church by Act of Parliament, Parliament is a factor in rthe establishment thereof." He might just as well conclude that, because there were men (recently) striving by Act of Parliament to suppress crime in Ireland, Parliament was a factor in the establishment of crime. But bs reaches the summit of nonsensity in the test he gives to show thia the Church of England is established by Act of Parli.ment. The test is: "Take a tithable farm, refuse to 'ay the tithes and you'll get the bums." Mr. Peers, I don't think

you mean it, so I'll give you the benefit of the doubt by withholding my criticism and Contenting myself with an observation, and with supplying you with a little informa- tion for your future guidance. The observation is—until , you know somethi.ng more about the subject under discus- sion have nothing more to say. I can assure you that the only thing which prompted me to reply to you was a recol- lection of that wise old proverb, Answer a fool according to his folly lest he be wise in his own cmceit." The in- formation I would give you is this—the Church of England was not established by Act or Acts of Parliament. The Church of England did not begin at the Reformation, nor did it begin with St. Augustine preaching at Canterbury. A branch of the Church Cathollc exTsted in Britain long before our Saxon forefathers conquered the island, and about four centuries betore St. Augustine preached the faith at Canterbury. The Gospel was preached to the inhabitants of this country by the Church of England hundreds of years before there was such a thing as an Act of Parliament. Acts of Parliament have reference to 1 the Church of England only as an ancient religions insti- tution, holding and administering property just as the Non- conformist bodies have a great many Acts of Parliament passed with reference to them in their relation to the State. I suppose our Dissenting friends would object to the term "Act of Parliament Dissent," yet they a-e just as much open to the charge as the Church of England is. Also let me say that Parliament has no more power over the Church of England and her property than it may choose, should it see fit, to exercise over any institution or property in the kingdom. And with respect to my second query which Mr. Peers failed to answer, allow me to inform him that, al- though the Irish Church has been disestablished, and wrongfully so, too, tithes are still payable there. And now, Mr. Peers, we part—you, I hope, "a sadder and a wiser man," and I still holding my brief for that glorious old church, which Dr. Adam Clarke describes as "the purest National Church in the world."—Yours, &c., • (E.

THE LA.TE MR. G. RHODES, OF RUNCORN.

--- - Preaching at the Bethesda Chapel on Sunday evening, the Rev. J. D. Thomas made special reference to the late r Mr. 0. Rhodes, taking for his text the 6th verse of the 28th Psalat, "Thou4h the Lord be high, yet He hath tha just unto the lowly." The preacher said this might mean men of humility or meekness of mind, or it might refer to men of little Intelligence and small abilities. But the Lord had respect unto both. The lowly in mind in the former sense were characterised by two things-41.st by a readiness to learn, and secondly by a humble estimate of their own worth; arid it seemed to him these two characteristics were , very conspicuous in the life of their late friend, Mr. George Rhodes. SO far as his acquaintance with the deceased enabled him to judge, he kept his mind open to receive new light from whatever quarter it might come. He was always ready to add to his store of knowledge, whoever the teacher might be. Many a man with his store of information, but without his wisdom, would have imagined that be knew all things, and that in the univsrse of intelligence there were no more worlds for him to conquer. But their friend was a diligent student to the end of his days. He delighted in the pathways of science, botany and chemistry being the branches to which be de- voted most attention. In this respect he set a noble exam- ple before young men and men of business, who often found that their leisure hours hung heavily on their bands. He was not aware that he received at any time any professional help in the study of science, yet by his own industry and application he arrived at such proficiency as might well shame tnauv who had enjoyed much higher advantages. Then he WAS a man who had a lowly estimate of his own , worth. They knew that he occupied, and that with very great credit to himself, some of the most important poitions that it was possible for any of their townsmen to occupy. Twice he was elected to the Board of Commissioners, and at the time of his decease he was the chairman of the Burial Board. For siveral years he ales acted as treasurer of their Sunday school. Yet he ventured to say that he consented to be nominated for such positions only at the earnest solicitation of friends. Ho had not the least hankering after such honours; but whoa they were conferred upon him he did his utmost to deserve the confidence which had been , paced in him. Now he ventured to think that God had respect unto one 80 lOWIV in mind. He gave His light where there was a readiness and an eagerness to receive light. God did not despise a man because he was ignorant. "He lath compassion on the ignorant, and on them that are out of the way." This was characteristic of their friend. He did his best to promote the educational interests of their town. He had, he believed, a considerable share in the establishment of the Mechanics Institute, and after- awtt phhairettdastaahl neanbasttrthoiroeeanndi strength iarios introduction weak aat ikno knowledgenai of the Free Library, and in various other ways by lectures more partieulary, he did his beat to ntand opnr enlightenment.wpoatiin n i tass it enlightenmentw as ignorant He believed a nandd 4ark. THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 1, 1884.

Ixotigsr.—An inquest was held at the Rose and Crown lon, on Thursday, by Mr. Brighouse, the county coroner, on the bodies of male twins, the illegitimate children of a woman, named Jane Ann Webster, residing in Blue Bell- lane, Huyton.—Dr. E. F. Hall (medical officer of the Union) depesed that in his opinion one of the children must have been born alive, and to have lived for a short time. He did not see anything to lead him to suppose it died from other than natural causes. The other child's lungs were not expanded at all, and there was nothing to show mcdic illy that it had been born alive.—The verdict found was that one of the children was born alive, but there was no evidence to show the cause of its death, and the second child was stillborn.

CONCERT.-A high class concert was given in the Huyton Park schoolroom, on Monday evening, in aid of the Huyton Temperance Association. There was a very full and fashionable audience, which thoroughly appreciated the well rendered programme, by the following artistes :—Miss Kate Nono, Mr 8 Kirkham, Mr E Edwards, Mr T Phillips (ac- companist), Mr Henry Broadley, Mr Williamson Chambers (humourous vocalist). Programme :—Part song, 'The banks of Allan water,' arranged by J Cantor; song, "Tis when to sleep,' Bishop, Mr Henry Broadley; song, 'The kerry dance,' Molloy, Miss Kate Nono; (encore) Rory 0' More;' part song, 'Of a' the airts,' arranged by W Shore; song, • When lovers say good night,' Burch, Mr E Edwards; (encore) lam waiting;' duet, 'A little farm,' Magginghi, I Miss Nono and Mr Chambers (encored) ; song, Gipsy John,' Clay, Mr Henry Eroatiley ; part song, 'The image of the rose,' Reichardt, Messrs Kirkham, Phillips, Broadley, I Queen, and (solo) E Edwards; scena, 'The history of Blue ' Beard' (from a new point of view), Mr W Chambers, ac- companied by Miss NOHO ; (encore) 'The whistling thief;' song, Sing! sweet bird,' Gans, Miss Kate Nono; trio, , Johnny Smoker,' Rix, Messrs. Kirkham, Edwards, and ! Broadley (encored); part song (a), 'Absence," (b), ' Even- ( ing's twilight. Hatton ; (encore, by desire), Hush thee, my I baby' (on the troubles of matrimony), Mr W Chambers; concluded with the National Anthem (solo), Mr E Edwards. The Bev J W Walker, 8.A., moved, and Mr Terby seconded a vote of thanks to the glee party for the excellent enter- tainufent given, coupling the name of Mr Queen, to whom the association were indebted for the presence of the talent which they had so thoroughly enjoyed.

APPLETON. QUARRELSOME NEIGHBOURS AT APPLETON: AFTER THE WARRINGTON LiustEs.--At the Daresbnry Petty Sessions on Tuesday, Elizabeth Hewitt, married woman, of Appleton, appeared to a summons for assaulting Mary Bate a neigh- bour.—Mr. A. Brown, of Warrington, appeared defen- dant.—According to the statement ef complainant it seemed that on the day in question, Saturday, February 16th, de- fendant commenced a quarrel by calling her a thief, and stating that she had stolen her sticks. Repudiating this statement, defendant seized and pushed her against the wall, 1 she having a baby in her arms at the time. he called for her sister-ia-law, who came on the scene, but defendant continued the assault by knocking her down and kicking her, whilst Mr. Hewitt, the husband, stood by and en- couraged his wife.—ln reply to Mr. Brown, complainant i denied having used abusive language towards defendant, or having annoyed the latter by asking her how long it was since she was with three gipsies and following them into the back streets of Warrington. (Laughter.) Neither did she accuse her of having slept with her husband before they were married.—Mr. Brown, in defence, contended that it was owing to complainant's abuse that his client gave Bate what ha thought she richly deserved—a good tlyashing.— A cross-summons was then heard, in which Elizabeth Hewitt summoned Mary Bate for having used abusive lan- guage towards her.—Her evidence was corroborated by Geo. Hewitt, her husband, who is in the employ of Mr. Charlton Parr.—. Eventually the magistrates treated the whole affair as'a neighbours' dispute, and bound over each party in a l• surety of £5 to keep the peace for six months. CADISHEAD.

BRUTAL ASSATILT.—At the Manchester County Police Court, on Monday, before Sir John lles Mantel', a farmer of Cadishead, named John Taylor, and his wife, Margaret Tay- lor, were charged on remand with unlawfully wounding Matthew Kirkham, farm labourer, in the employ of Mr. Robert Billington, farmer, of Cadishead. Mr. A. T. H. Evans appeared for Kirkham, and Mr. Cobbett defended both prisoners —The prosecutor stated that on the 13th inst. he was ordered by his master to go to the defendants' farm for the laurpose of borrowing a plough. Prosecutor took a horse and cart to convey the plough, and when he entered the defendants' yard, Taylor stood at the gate of the yard with a thick stick in his hand. Without any provocation whatever, Taylor dealt prosecutor a severe blow on the left side of his head which knocked him down insensible. On regaining consciousness Kirkham stated that the defendant Taylor was oa the top of him (witness) striking him about the face and bead. Prosecutor struggled with the male prisoner for some time, and when he appeared to be getting the best of him, Taylor's wife, who had in the meantime coma upon the scene, began to Ruse the prose- cutor by kicking him abaut the body, and finally dealt him a most violent kick in the right eye, which caused it to be greatly disfigured and bruised. Several witnesses who were passing on the highway at the time of the assault corro- borated the evidence of Kirkham.—Bath defendants were committed for trial at the sessions, bail being accepted for their appearance.

div.head: FRODS RAM.
div.p: FRODS RAM.

MISCELLANEOUS ENTERTAINMENT. A miscellaneous entertainment was tiven in the Girls' Schoolroom, on Mon- day evening, in connection with the Frodsham Literary and Debating Society. The Rev. H. B. Blozg, M.A., presided, in the absence, through illnesss, of Mr. C. E. Linaker, and there was a good attendance. The programme was well re- ceived, and consisted of songs by Miss K. S. Rigby, Miss Edith E. Riley, Messrs. Robert Holland, A. Jones, and John W. Holland; readings by the Chairman, Mr. Samuel Davies, and Mr. S. Ormrod ; recitations by Mr. E. Rhodes; violin solo by Mr. John S. Rimmer, accompanied on the piano by Mrs. Heywood, who also kindly accompanied all the songs and gave a pianoforte solo. The modest sum of one penny was charged for admission to the entertainment, and the length of the programme showed the resources of the com- mittee for future entertainments of a similar character, which will no doubt be as well supported as the penny read- ings brought to a close some ten years ago, and which resulted in the handsome sum of £5O being handed over to- wards providing the present public lamps in Frodsham. GOLBORNE.

THE DROWNING OF A LAD AT GOLDORNE —On Satur- day last, Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest at the Legh Arms Hotel, Golborne, on the bedy of Albert Taylor, a lad 12 years of age, who was drowned in Golborne brook, under circumstances reported in our last issue. After evi- dence in accordance with the facts then stated had been given, the jury returned a verdict of "Accidentally drowned."

THB SHTTLEMENT OF THE &RIBS A GOLEORNB.--, After having been closed for nearly two months in conse- quence of a strike of the hands against a proposed reduction in their wages, the mills of Messrs. John Brewis and Com- pany were re-opened on Friday morning last, and w )rk was resumed upon the old terms. Since then the mills have been running full time, and it is to be hoped that a long time will elapse before a similar dispute is witnessed in the town. . .

ASSAULT ON A GOLBOHNE POLICEMAN.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Peter Cusliffe, of Golborne, was summoned for being drank and disorderly, and also for assaulting P.C. Ratcliffe on the previous Wednesday.— The evidence was to the effect that the defendant tumbled down a hole on the footpath and the constable endeavoured to get him up. The defendant, however, kicked him on the legs and also struck him with his fist, and it was with great difficulty he was conveyed to the station, the constable having to get the assistance of two men. In the police cell, while the constable was trying to take the prisoner's clogs off, the prisoner tried to kick him in the face. lie was committed to gaol for one month with hard labour. CMURCII OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY: MEETING AT GOLBORNE.—A public meeting under the auspices of the Golborne branch of the Church of England Temperance Society was held in St. Thomas's School, Gol borne, on Monday evening. Tnere was a good attendance, and the chair was occupied by the Rev. C. T. Quirk, M.A., rector, who was supported by the Rev. W. Thorpe, curate, and the Rev. EL Linton, vicar of Abram. The last-named gentle- man gave an excellent address' in which he condemned the liquor traffic, and pointed out the evils that accrued from it, contrasting therewith the benefits and advantages that were to be gained by being total abstainers. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Linton on the motion of Mr. A. Caunce, seconded by Mr. R. Yates, and supported by Mr. C. T. Rosbottom. Several new members were enrolled at the close of the meeting. _

div.head: TIAYDOCK.
div.p: TIAYDOCK.

FATAL ACCIDENT AT Havnocx.—An inquest was held at the RAM'S Head, Haydock, on Tuesday afternoon, before Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, on the body of Owen Boyle, 37 years, residing at 11 Lyme-street, who met with his death under the following circumstances. He was employed as a day wage man at the Queen Pit, and on Friday night last he was assisting a number of other men to repair one of the roads in the pit. Part of the deceased's business was to support the roof with iron bars secured to upright prop.• The props had all been fixed, but one of them did not give satisfaction to Boyle, who was in the act of replacing it, when, after giving it a smart blow with a hammer, it sud- denly fell and struck him violently on the back of the head.' The poor fellow was knocked to the ground, and died al- most instantaneously. The jury returned a verdict of "Ac- cidental death."

HAYDOCK NEIGHBOURS AT VARIANCE.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, Ann Lowe was summoned for using offensive and defamatory language to Henry Lowe and his wife, Elizabeth Lowe.—Mr. Swift, of St. Helens, appeared for the complainants, and explained that the parties were neigkibours residing in Greenall's-row, Hay- dock.—lt was alleged that the defendant, who although having the same name was no relation of the complainants, bad slandered them with regard to their position. She accused Mrs. Lowe of great immorality, and accused Henry Lowe of having stolen some articles of underclothing. Mr. Swift added that he had written to the defendant asking her to apologise and stating that nothing further woald be taken of the matter, but she refused to do so, making the matter worse by repeating the accusations.—The defendant alleged that the complainants had been in the habit of ill- using and insulting her on every possible occasion they could.—She was bound over to keep the peace for six months, herself in £lO and another surety of £5. ALLEGED DANGEROUS DOG AT HAYDOCK ; A QUESTION OF RIGHT OF WAY.—At the Newton Petty Sesaions.fon Saturday last, before R. Houghton and C. Pilkington, Esqs., Samuel Ball was summoned for using threatening language to Jane Wood; and Joseph Wood (husband of Jane Wood) was summoned by Samuel Ball for keeping a dangerous dog not under proper control.—Mr. Moore, of Warrington, ap- peared for Ball, and Mr. Brown, of Warrington, appeared for Mr. and Mrs. Wood.—lt was arranged that as the threaten- ing language arose out of the dangerous dog case, the latter should be taken first.—Mr. Moore stated that on the night of the 10th February the complainant Ball and his wife were going home to Haydock and they had to cross some fields occupied by Wood. A footpath across the field led through the defendant's farm yard, and when Ball and his wife had got there a large dog belenging to Wood sprang out and ran at them. Ball had great difficulty in keeping it off, but at last succeeded in pacifying it. The dog was a dangerous one, and the defendantought to keep it under control.—Mr. Brown : Even granting that that is a fact the footpath is no road. The defendant has no right to go along it. It is Ball's private premises.—The Clerk (to Mr. Moore): You don't even prove that .it is a dangerous dog.—Mr. Brown: No; and I could raise the question of right of road. I say that the place is a private occupation road, occupied by Joseph Ball, and that the dog is on his own premises. The man was trespassing to a certain degree—at an untimely hour of the night—between twelve and- one o'clock.—Mr. Moore: The mere assertion of the claim by Mr. Brown does not make it a private road.—The Clerk: You have not proved that the dog is a dangerous dog—barking and that sort of thing does not prose it.—Mr. Moore: Rushing at a man seems dangorous.—The Clerk: Oh, no. A farmer's dog is not worth much if it won't do that at mid- night.—The Bench dismissed the case, whereupon Mr. Brown said the case against Wood for using bad ' language would be withdrawn. HUYTON.

WORKING MEN'S Cixn.—.The adjourned general meet- ing, to consider the closing of this cinh, was held on Wed- nesday evening. Mr. C. Cooper occupied the chair, and there was s good attendance of members of the committee After a short discussion it was decided, owing to the want of appreciation from the class for whom it was intended, to cloee the club as soon as circumstances would permit The club has been in existence nearly eight years, and waa fairly prospering until the formation of the Volunteer Club a short time ago. The Rev. W. T. Southend, MA, bad been the president of the club, but now that be was remoytd from the parish his considerable influence has been taken away from the *lab.

div.head: LYHJA.
div.p: LYHJA.

UNITED BANDS OF HOPE.—The third meeting of the series of the United Bands of Hope was held in the Mission Hall, on Monday evening. The Rev. H. Davies, Baptist minister, Lymm, occupied the chair, and there was a large attendance. Addresses were delivered by the Chairman, and Messrs. J. Thomason, Dutton, Brown, Astlev, Ashton, Knowles, Bayley, and Mort. The proceedings were agree- ably diversified by part songs by the members of the Choral Society (accomparaed by a string band); songs by Mr. G. Jones, a duet by Mrs. Chorley and Miss Haziedine, and 3 reading by Mr. Bayley.

117.12. DAY RVENIgG CoNcERTS.--The usual penny con- cert was held in the Bridgewater Rooms, on Saturday even- ing, and was well attended. Mr. J. A. Swanwick presided, and a most enjoyable programme was gone through. Mrs. Chorley contriouted a song and a reading, and also took part in a duet with Miss Hazledine ; a violin and a violin- cello duet was given by Messrs. Kirk and Skilling ; a piano- forte and violincello duet by Mess. Blakemore and Skilling; a reading by Miss Fox, "Contest between the eyes and nese ;" readings in the Lancashire dialect by Mr. Clare and Mr. Joynson ; a vocal duet by Messrs. George and Edward Smith; a song by Mr. J. Warburton; three songs by Mr. Blakemore, one of which was encored; and a reading by Mr. Jos. Smith. Miss Pearson played the piano- forte accompaniments. NANTWICH.

Dr. Churton, coroner, held an inquest at Sttpeley, Nant- wicb, on Monday evening, on the body of John llollowood. The deceased had been ill and delirious, but becoming a trifle better he dressed and wandered away. Efferts to find him failed, and all night he was exposed to a keen frost and subsequent violent storms of hail and rain. Next day some boys found him lying dead against a fence frozen to death.—A verdict of death from exposure was returned.

div.head: OVER.
div.p: OVER.

ST. Jontes.—Pt parochial tea was held in connection with this church on Tuesday last, in the St. John's Schoolroom. There was a good attendance at it, as well as at the after meeting, when recitations and music, varied with speeches, occupied the evening. RA.INHILL.

HOLT CiLii,EL SUNDAt S4iflOOL.-0J Tuesday evening, a most successful miscellaneous concert was given in the above chapel by the elder scholars, assisted by friends and adult members of the congregation. The entertainment was organised in order to defray the expenses connected with the repairs of the chapel harmonium. Mr. W. Evans, of Ivy Cottage, Whiston, a warm supporter of the chapel mission, acted as chairman. There was a crowded audi- ence, whtch thoroughly appreciated the efforts of the per- formers, and expressed its approbation in rounds of ap- plause. The following programme was capitally rendered: —Glee, It is Well, Choir; recitation, Counting the Pennies, Miss C. J. Welling; recitation, Naughty Dick, Miss E. Ball ; accordeon solos, Mr. Thomas (Prescot); trios, A Little Farm Well Tilled and Dame Durden, Messrs. Welsby, Barron, and Renshall ; recitation: Old Slinger, Mr. J. Ball; duet, All's Well, Messrs. Welsby and Renshall •, recitation, Jack's Menagerie, Miss C. Critchley ; song, Every Bullet has its Billet. Mr. Welsby ; recitatton, Every Man in his Place, Miss M. Critchley ; duet, Horne Beyond the Tide, Misses C. J. and M. A. Welling; recitation, A Doctor and his Apprentice, Miss M. Parr; humorous dialogues, The Absent Man and the Three Buckleys ; negro entertainment. Considering the ages of the performers the recitations were all given in a highly creditable and expressive manner. The trios and duets, although well known, were rendered in a manner that made them as interesting as if they had been mueical novelties. Mr. Thomas, of Prescot, in his accoreleon solos showed himself an artiste of no mean order, and added greatly to the amusement of the audience. The dialogues performed by the elder scholars were certainly the most at- tractive items in the programme. The abundant humour 11 and the moral in each were well brought out, and appreci- ated by those present, who accorded the performers hearty rounds of applause. The negro entertainment, arranged by the scholars themselves, was extremely amusing. Special mention should be made of the capital style in which Mr. W. Ball acted as corner man.

div.head: SOUTHWORTH-WITH-CROFT.
div.p: SOUTHWORTH-WITH-CROFT.

SUDDEN DEATH.—About ten o'clock on Wednesday morn- ing as a man named Robert Price was engaged working in a garden behind a cottage adjoining his residence at Little Town, Croft, he suddenly fell to the ground and expired. Dr. Bridcoake, of Croft (for whom the deceased worked), had been talking to him a few minutes previous, and was quickly in attendance, but his services were of as avail ; the cause of death probably being disease of the heart. An inquest will no doubt be held in due course. CONCERT AT THE CROFT BOARD ScaooLS.—On Thurs- day evening a very successful concert was given in the above school to an appreciative, though not very large audience. The Rev. T. P. Kirkman. M.A.F.R.S., presided, and delivered a short address. Mr. George Riley, of War- rington, then opened the programme with a piano solo, executed in an able manner. Mr. Sherlock then gave "The wandering minstrel" in good style ; and was followed by Miss Parkinson, who was encored for the song "Some day." " Love's request," by Mr. Jenkins, was also encored, and heartily applauded. Mr. Macaulay then gave an amusing reading "A yarn on the half-deck. The song " Let me dream agaie " was well rendered by Miss Horton ; as was also the' Little hero," a very flue song, by Mr. Cavanagh. " Elwell on the Rhine was suag with taste by Mrs. Walsh, and deservedly encored. The first part of the pro- gramme concluded by Mr. Mercer's comic song " Going home to mother." Being loudly encored, he responded with "0 Joe, the boat is going over." After a short interval Mr. Sherlock wave the "Old brigade" in good style. "Golden love," by Miss Horton, then followed, and received well merited applause. The descriptive song, " The desert," was sung with great power and effect by Mr. Cavanagh, the difficult accompaniment being well executed by Mr. Riley. Mr. Mercer now came forward and con- vulsed the audience by his rendering of "Tidings of com- fort and joy," in character. A reading, "Notes on noses," by Mr. Macaulay, varied the proceedings, after which Mrs. Walsh sang "Sweet spirit, hear my prayer," with feeling, and was loudly applauded. The old favourite, "Tom Bowling," was next sung by Mr. Jenkins, and was followed by Miss Parkinson in "On the banks of Allan Water." The comic song," They all have a mate but me," in character, by Mr. Mercer,received a hearty encore, to which another absurdity, " Dumb, dumb, dumb," was given in response.—The Chairman then moved a vote of thanks to the performers for their excellent entertainment, and also to Mr. George Brimelow, who had been instrumental in pro- curing their services, and the proceedings closed by the singing of the National Anthem. .

div.head: WHARTON.
div.p: WHARTON.

The Wharton Church choir gave a soiree in the National Schools on Tuesday night, when a number of songs, duets, glees, and recitations were given by the members, assisted by a few friends. The object being to furnish funds for the use of the choir, many of the congregation patronised the entertainment. WINSFORD.

/traction ORDER OF FORESTRRS.—The annual report of the Vale Royal Court at Winsford shows they have 203 members and funds to the amount of £3Bl 7s lid. The income fer the year was £197 183 21, and the expenditure £176 14e 21, leaving a balance of £2l 43 to go to the general amount. The management fund also shows a balance in its favour of £lO 133 81 for the income Last year in excess of expenditure, while this year income was £63 123 lid and expenditure reached £63 17s, so that that the present balance is only £lO Os 7d. The court, however, is in a very healthy state. TEMPERA WC ENTERTAINMENT.—A temperance entertain- ment was held in the United Methodist schoolroom, on Monday night, ley members of the temperance committee, dm. The chair was taken by Mr. William Jones, ion,, who gave a characteristic speech on religion and temperance. There were music and recitations. Miss Buckley, the or- ganist, accompanied and gave an interesting pianoforte solo; Miss Atherton sang "Father will not drink any more ;" Mr. Hough gave "Our Jack's come home from sea," and one or two other temperance songs; Mr. Mason sang nicely "In the olden time," "Touch not the cup ;" the choir gave three choruses : " Before the brewer," Star of peace," " Down where the blue bells grow ;" Mr. Charles and Miss E. Stubbs gave a pianoforte duet; Mr. G. Hamlet a piccolo solo which was loudly encored; the humouroua dialogue, "Don't

marry a man if he drinks," by Misses Smith and Bennett and Messrs. Noden and Plumblv pleased much. The collec- tion and doxology brought the meeting to a close. ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS. CHESHIRE, SHROPSHIRE, AND NORTH WALES FARMERS' SUPPLY Assoctanoti.—The half-yearly meeting of this association was held at Crewe on Tuesday, Mr. G. W. Latham, of Bradwall Hall, presiding The financial state- ment showed that there had been during the half-year an increase in the sales of feeding stuffs, !sc., of nearly .£3,000 more than in the corresponding half. The total net profit is equal to more than 18 per cent on the capital of the associa- tion.—The Chairman said that the report was a very satis- factory one. He congratulated farmers on the improving state of agriculture, and said he hoped that the seven lean years would now give place to seven years of prosperity.— Mr. R. Holland, of Frodsham, afterwards r.-ad a piper on "Scutch."—A discussion followed on the importation of foreign cattle, and the Chairman explained the bills now before Parliament for prohibiting the importation of five cattle from countries affected with disease.

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

The contest at Cork, on Saturday, resulted in the return of Mr. Deasey, the Nationalist candidate, by 2,150 votes, against 1,153 recorded in favour of the Conservative oppo- nent, Mr. Goulding, who received 126 votes fewer than at the general election. Mr. Deasey, on the other hand, received 227 votes more than Mr. Daly, who then headed the poll. A singular scene occurred at Ballyhaunis on Wednesday, when Mr. Robinson, the Local Government Board inspector, held an inquiry into the condition of Callybaunis grave- yard, which was alleged to be overcrowded and dangerous to health. A large number of persons assembled in the graveyard and defied any attempt at interference with their ancestors' gravL3. Mr. Robins.aa promised that thc;r objec- tions should be considered, and thus averted the threatened disturbances. If we may trust the statements made at a meeting of the Dundalk Board of Guardians on Monday, the Labourers (Ireland) Act of last session is an entire failure as a means of providing dwellings for the peasantry. A member com- plaining that nothing had been heard for some months of schemes for cottage building on which the Board had spent much time, the Clerk said that all except one had been abandoned as the land was refused. One of the speakers, a magistrate, descrioed the law as impracticable, while the Chairman, still more emphatic, remarked, "I think the same Act is a farce."

EXTRAORDINARY ETICTION.-411 Clare Market, on Satur- day, in a house let in tenements, a Frenchwoman occupied one room. The other tenants complained repeatedly of the horrible stenches which arose from it poisoning the air throughout the building. The woman having disappeared, the agent of the property determined upon an evicticn, which was carried out on Saturday morning, her furniture being turned into the street. Among her possessions in the room were found the bodies of three dead cats in a basket, in a high state of decomposition, and a fourth cat, which was in a dying state, The stench in the court when they Were thrown out became insupportable, and it will not be at all surprising if an epidemic should follow this outrage On common sense and decency. FENIAN MURDERS DESCRIBED BY IN ACCOUPLICR.—The Pall Mall Gazette gave prominence on Wednesday to an account, by a person who is represented as "a leader of the Irish Republican Brotherhood," of several murders in which he has been an accomplice either before or after the fact. The murder of an " informer " in IMO is the first in the list of crimes, and the Government are accused of tyranny be- cause they immediately afterwards found themselves com- pelled to suspend the Habeas Corpus Act. The " leader " describes with much exaltation the murder of another in- former, whose body, he says, was hacked to 'pieces and thrown into an inglorious grave. Another informer was assaulted, and one of his eyes was kicked out. We are told that an "old and patriotic lady" to whom the deed was described bitterly lamented that "the other had not been kicked out too." It would be interesting to learn whether the correspondent of the Pall Mall Gazette is at present in this country or safe in New York.

div.head: SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE GOOD TEMPLAR& ANNUAL _sEssidN.
div.p: SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE GOOD TEMPLAR& ANNUAL _sEssidN.

The annual session of the South West I.a.liashire District Lodge of Good femplars was held in the Baptist Mission Hall, Walnut-street, Liverpool, on Monday, and was opened at half-past one by Bro. M. Bebbington, DOT., of Gars- ton. There was a large attendance of representatives from Widnes, Warrington, Earlestown, Wigan, Et. Helens, South- port, tim. After the opening ceremonies the annual reports of the officers were received. The District Chief Templar, in his report, referred to the condition of the order in the district, and said it would be hailed with satisfaction that they were enabled to report progress.—The District Secre- tary reported the returns from 72 lodges in the district showed 3,424 members, an increase of between 250 and 260 en the previous report. Several lodges had not sent in their reports as yet. The District Treasurer's report on the state of the finances was considered satisfactory. The District Superintendent of Juvenile Templam reported an Increase of members, and spoke of the necessity of the adult organisations to co-operate with and help forward the juvenile societies. The report of the District Electoral Deputy (Bro. Morris Jones, of Liverpool) was an excellent one, showing that the work was progressing in the district, and pointed out the efforts for furthering the cause which were being made in various directions.—The reports were unanimously adopted, after which the election of officers for the ensuing year took place. Twenty-two members were nominated as representatives to the Grand Lodge, which meets at Leicester in . Easter week, but as only seven were required the voting wac somewhat exciting. Among the successful seven were Brother J. W. Hall, of Warrington, and Brother George Clarke, of Earles- town. Brother Sergeant J. Jackson, of Warrington, was appointed District Guard; and Brother Geo. Clarke (Earles- town) was re-elected District Marshall. The officers were afterwards installed by Brother John Harrison, DOT., of West Cheshire, assisted by Brother W. J. Wray, D. Coun- sellor, of Berkshire. Several business matters were after- wards discussed, and the session closed about 10 o'clock.

div.head: ALARMING STREET ACCIDENT AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: ALARMING STREET ACCIDENT AT WARRINGTON.

An alarming accident was witnessed in Sankey-street, Warrington, on Saturday morning last, and through which it is to be hoped a check will be put on the practice of furi- ous driving in our public and most frequented thorough- fares. It seems that Mrs. Hall, 73 years of age (a netr relative of Councillor Monks), and the wife of Mr. Thomas Hall, of 37, Liverpool-road, was crossing Sankey-street, near the Circus, when she was knocked down by a horse and cart driven by a young man named Thomas Kean, in the employ of Mr. William Lawless, fishmonger, Corporation-street. Kean is said to have been driving somewhat recklessly at the time. Mrs. Hall was picked up in an unconscious state, and was taken to the Infirmary, where she was attended by the House Surgeon, Dr. Richmond. One of the wheels is be- lieved to have passed over her arm, whilst so seriously injured was her head that it was some days before she re- gained consciousness, and she has been lying at the Infirm- ary in a critical condition. Thanks, however, to the care and skill Mrs. Hall received at this institution, we were in- formed on inquiry yesterday that she was progresing, although slowly.

„ THB DRIVER BEFORE TRH MAGISTRATES. Atthe Borough Police Court yesterday, before Captain Reynolds and Mr. John White, the young man Thomas Kean was brought up on a charge of furiously driving a hose on Saturday. last.— Mr. Percy Davies appeared for the defence, and on the case being called asked that the witnesses might be ordered out of court—After a little conversation this course was adopted.—Chief Constable Hunt briefly stated the facts of the case, observing that after the woman had been knocked down the defendant acted very properly, and ren- dered all the assistance he possibly could, offering to con- vey the injured female to the infirmary.—Captain Reynolds: What is the nature of her wound? The Chief Constable: She was quite unconscious for a day or two, but is a little better to-day.—Joseph Williams, a marble mason, employed at Messrs. Williams and Clay's works, said that on Saturday morning last he was in front of the works, and had his attention drawn to Mrs. Hall, who was lying in the roadway. He and others ran to her assis- tance and lifted her up. He could not say what speed the horse was driven at. The driver pulled up about 12 yards from where the accident occurred. In reply to Mr. Davies, witness added that in his opinion if the old woman had crossed over the roadway at the proper crossing she would have been out of the way. He did not see the horse and cart before the woman was knocked down.— Michael Mayor, employed at Williams and Clay's works said he saw Mrs. Hall knocked down at the crossing, but he could not say that the horse was going to quick. It was going rather fast. The woman who was knocked down was struck with one of the shafts when she turned round. If she had gone straight across the road and not turned back the accident would not have occurred. The defendant after the accident said it would not have taken place bad she kept straight on.— Patrick Ryan, another employe of Messrs. Williams and Clay. deposed that he was attracted with a shout of "Heigh up,” which he thought came from the defendant, who was driving a horse and cart, and on turning round he saw Mrs. Hall had been knocked to the ground. He could not say whether the boy was driving too quick or not. For the defence Mr. Davies submitted that the evidence did not support the charge of furious driving and stated that Mrs Hall left the parapet with the intention of crossing the street, and just as the defendant was driving round the corner she stopped and turned back. The defendant shouted out "Heigh up, get out of the way," but it was too late, as the poor woman was knocked down and injured. It was purely and simply an accident and he did not see that the defendant was in any way to blame.— Captain Reynolds said the Bench were of opinion there was a doubt about the matter and they would give the defendant the benefit of it. At the same time he must express his opinion that there was too much fast driving about the town and those who had to pass round corners in the streets should be very careful. He hoped that case would ant as a yarning.

LE'NTRN PASTORAL OF THE RIGHT REV. DR. O'REILLY. REFERENCES TO NON-RELIGIOUS TRAINING, THE SCHOOL BOARD SYSTEM, AND CATHOLIC EDUCATION GRIEVANCES. The usual Lenten pastoral of the Roman Catholic Bishop of Liverpool was read in all the Catholic churches of the Liverpool diocese on Sunday. The Bishop opens with a quotation from St. Paul's espistle to the Ephesians :—"See, therefore, now you walk circumspectly, not as unwise but as wise, redeeming the time because the days are evil." The Bishop, after inculcating the practice of Christian charity, refers to the perils of the present time, and, in sur- veying the state of society, says :—" Wherever we look we find an almost universal rebellion against the principles of authority, an almost universal corruption of morals. Men have comae to that pass that they call evil good and good evil. If we look abroad, we see in what was called Catholic France that the Government has endeavoured to deprive the people of their religious rights, and the Church of her possessions, and has gone further still, even to the length of excluding religious teaching from the schools, and almost of denying the very existence of God. In Italy we see things fast coming to the same pass. In that unhappy country the Government of the day has deprived our Holy Father—who is the representative of God in this world—of his property and possessions, and even of his civil rights, though especially, as if in mockery, guaranteed to him. It has robbed the churches, plundered the monasteries and re- ligious houses, turning adrift religious men and women, leaving them homeless and without the means of support. Imitating the example of France, the Italian Government would deprive the people of their faith, for the attempt is there being made to banish religion from the schools. Al- ready is beginning to appear the fruit of the evil seed. The restraint which religion imposed being removed, the principles of honour, as they are called, are found to be powerless to restrain the passions of the people. Already the moral sense of right and of wrong appears to have lost all power of restraint. There is an absence of the sense of modesty amongst the young, and the sanctity of the marriage tie is disregarded amongst those of maturer years. Even the sacredness of human life is disregarded. When men have lost all idea of a God, who directs and rules all things, who is a rewarder of the good and a punisher of the wicked, when they do not believe that the soul of man is immortal, that every- • thing is material, and, consequently, that when the body moulders in the grave nothing remains of man to be liable of punishment or capable of enjoying a reward, it is no wonder that they have no fear of the judgment to come, and of the punishments that are to follow that judgment." Alluding to the absence of religious training in the public schools of the Continent, and, as a result, the ready support secret societies meet with at the hands of men animated by revolutionary sympathies, his lordship asks :—‘'What do we see in Northern Europe? Those brought up in schools from which religion had been banished, schools in which the name of God was not mentioned except to be blaThemed ; women trained in academies in which the inculcation of Christian modesty formed no part of the teaching, appear to have banded themselves to- gether in an unholy attempt to subvert all government, to destroy all right of property, to unloose all moral retraint, and to uproot every vestige of virtue and of religion. Sometimes, at the prompting of their own pas- sions, and because they have come to fear.the punishments of a future life, they will attempt and carry into execution the most fearful crimes. Generally, however, they are driven to the commission of their crimes by the tyranny of secret societies. They receive the order to commit the crime, to destroy property and life ; and they prefer to obey the command, even though they sacrifice their own lives in the attempt, rather than to await death amidst tortures at the hands of those under whose command they were act- ing." Contrasting the condition of the masses in this country with those of the Continent—a comparison much . to the advantage of the former—his lordship warns his flock against all secret societies, remarking that:—" It is true that horrors such as these are not to be found in this country ; or, if at all, only in a very modified form. Yet there have been warnings that should make us fear. We have seen that to which we ought not attempt to shut our eyes, and rumours have reached us to which ;73 ought not shut our ears, We have reason 1 to fear that secret societies ate being formed, or have been formed amongst us. Some of these eocieties may ap- pear to many to be harmless, and to have no element of mischief in them; and some may have been induced to join them under the impression that they were doing no harm in becoming members, and that, on the contrary, they were doing what was praiseworthy in trying to strengthen brotherhoods who professed to aim at securing ends which appeared to be innoent. Others of these societies cannot but be known to be dangerous and sinful. They have for their cads objects that are unlawful, and they aim at secur- ing those ends by unlawful means. The members are bound by secret oaths—imposed frequently by those who hardly believe in the existence of God—to obey commands given by persons whom they do not know, and to execute orders given without knowing what these orders may be—whether these orders may be lawful or unlawfal, whether injurious or otherwise to their neighbours' pro- perty or life, or the interests of religion or the glory of God. Dearly beloved children in Jesus Christ, be not deceived by the guileful works of deceitful, wicked men, who would entrap you, and lead you into the meshes of crime, and involve you in that punishment from which they are cunning enough to save themselves. We repeat it —suffer not yourselves to be deceived. You know that all such societies are condemned by the Church, and that as long as a person remains a member of any such society he cannot approach the sacraments. You will have seen how many of them, whom you know as active memoere of such societies, never approach the holy sacraments of Penance or the Holy Communion. You will also have seen that young and innocent men who have been entrapped into such societies soon fall away from the frequentation of the sacra- ments; you will, in addition, know that many of the crimes which have disgraced society bare been proved to have been committed by men who Would never have stained their hands in their neighbours' blood were they not driven to the commission of crime by those who enrolled them as members of the secret societies, Do not join any such society; and if, unfor- tunately, you have been induced to do so, quit it without delay.' Coming to the question of non-religious education, the Bishop gives illustrations of its work on the Coetinent, saying :—" The schools taught by religious men and women have been closed, the parochial and other schools provided by the people for the Christian education of their children have been diverted from that object. Where children were once taught to know and to honour God,to re- vere and to love the holy name of Jesus, they are now schooled in secular learning, but it is forbidden to teach them the principles of the Christian religion, or even to mention the holy name of God. They are not instructed ha their duties to society, they are not taught to love their neighbour for the love of God, nor to obey lawful authority for God's sake. They are not taught to put any restraint upon the cravings of their corrupt desires and passions, they are not encouraged to strive after virtue by the promise of eternal rewards, nor to avoid sin by the fear of everlasting punishments. Hence virtue is not encouraged, and, but too frequently, those who strive after it become objects of derision. Hence property is gradually becoming more unsafe, and human life less sacred What wonder, then, if the thrones of kings are overturned, and if, when this is accom- plished, the government of those who subverted them is also overturned, and this by people who were never instruc- ted to reverence the king, because that his power is from God. What wonder that they do not reverence God, when they were never taught to know Him. What wonder that they do not fear the damnation which the Apostle threatens, when they were taught to disbelieve in the existence of a future state." Addressing a note of warning to his flock, the Bishop, drawing deductions from the state of things abroad, as described by him, says :—Have we not, .dearly beloved children in Jesus Christ, room to fear that something similar may come upon us? The leaders of public opinion who are loud in their condemnation of the state of society, such as it is seen in many parts of the Continent, are either blind as to the • cause which has led to it, or are perverse in advocating that system of education of which it is the outcome. Godless education on the Continent has produced the frightful dis- orders which all right-minded men deplore, and our Go- vernment here would force upon us an education almost as irreligious. No one will condemn them for helping on the work of education by which the mind is harmonised, but by a strange contradiction, in this land, where it is our boasted privilege that every man is free to follow his con- scientious convictions, the right is denied to a Catholic parent to bring up his children in that faith in which alone he believes they can be saved. It may be that a school board which has unlimited funds at its disposal, funds to which a Catholic contributes hi full proportion has pre- occupied the ground by building schools far in advance of present need. To these schools a Catholic parent has con- scientious objection M send his children, because in them religion, to which education is but the hand- maid, is not taught, or if any be taught, it is such as he cannot accept; for the distinctive teaching of those dogmatic truths, which he holds as vital, is pro- hibited. Indeed the religions teaching in them seems devised to meet the wishes of those who are content to live without any distinctive dogmatic teaching. If this Catho- lic parent wishes to provide a school in which his children may be taught the doctrines of the Holy Church, it may be that liberty to build will be denied him, because it is con- tended that no additional school is required. If this permis- sion to build be granted to him he must build it at his own csost, and, further, he is to be much more heavily taxed for its support. Whereas, to obtain any aid from the public funds for its support, he must secure that the teaching be efficient, he is placed at a disadvantage in his competition with the neighbouring costly board school in this—that the latter receives from those rates to which he has contributed a special help which is denied to him. This, dearly be- loved chsldren in Jesus Christ, is a manifest injustice. We are equal before the law, and we ought not to be satisfied till this injustice be rectified. We hope that you will never willingly consent to leave matters in their present pesition. By petitions addressed to the Houses of Parlia- ment, draw attention to this grievance, and urge upon your representatives that if they expect your suffrages you in return will count upon their 'Lippert. In language that does not admit of two interpretations the Bishop expresses his view of the duty of Catholic clergy and laity towards non-Catholic schools. He says: "There is one point upon which we would insist that you should never, under any circumstances, or for any consideration, allow your children to frequent any school other than a Catholic

I school ; and you, dearly beloved brethren, never be remiss .- lin admonishing your flecks upon the absolute necessity of attending to this admonition. In all humility and lowliness we address you in the words of St. Paul to Timothy charge you, before God and Jesus Christ, who st.all judge the living and the dead, by His coming, and His kingdom: preach the Word ; be instant in season, out of season ; re- prove, entreat, rebuke, in all patience and doctrine, otherwise there shall be a time when these children will not endure sound doctrine; but according to their own desires they will heap to themselves teachers having itching ears." And as, dear Children in Jesus Christ, your pastor speak to you in God's name, attend to their admonitions, and faith- fully put them in practice. Towards the end of the pastoral, he adverts to the question of religious education :—" Again, we say a parting word on the subject of our Catholic schools. Let it be one of your good resolutions taken in Lent that you will energetically strive to obtain from the Legislature justice to our schools, that you will help in every way to provide schools were required, and that Yon , will never suffer our poor children to risk the loss of their faith or the weakening of their morals by sending or allow- , ing them to be sent to any save Catholic schools."

IRLAM AND THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. A public meeting in support of the Manchester ShiP Canal scheme was held on Thursday night in the Assembly Room of the Ship Inn, Irlam. The chair was occupied bY Mr. John Pearson, who, in opening the proceedings, said the canal if gone on with would bring a vast amount of work into the district; the deemning of the river would prevent the floods to which the neighbourhood was subjects and would greatly improve the land near the river, so that wheat and the like might be grown upon it, and not merely grass. The pelsons who owned this land ought to costri- bute very liberally to this great undert 4ting, which vfse., certain to come about. The present industry of Irlam an' Cadishead, fustian cutting, only yielded a moderate living to the working people when they put in all the hours they could, but if the canal was made other trades would be brought into the district, and, more' over, large sums of money would be spent in the locality. Mr. J. C. Mather submitted a resotutioa heartily approving of the intended application to Parliament in the ensuing session for powers to construct the canal, and pledging the meeting to support by every means in its power the Provi- sional CornmWee in its renewed efforts to secure the passing of the bill. He remarked that no other argument Was needed to convince the Barton township to put its shoulder to the wheel in this matter than the fact that a million and a quarter sterling would be spent in the construction of the canal within the township. Farther than that, labour would be brought into the township, industries of all des' criptions would spring up, and new markets would be opened to the produce of the township. Mr. John Howarth se' conded the motion, which was supporten by Mr. B. T. Leech who urged that Irlam was deeply interested in 13avi,eg put to its proper use the river which passed by them, y.,e showed how this had come about, and said that Main bad been robbed of all communication by river with Manchester, and the river instead of being a blessing had by silting OP and fouling become a curse. If the river was made navig• able Irlam of all places would receive great bsnetit, because there they were to have docks, the wide places in the river,. and it was expected that the coal traffic from South York shire would come there. If trade was brought to it the prosperity of the place must increase. (Applause.) He he' lieved that the prosperity of Irl,tm depended upon the canal. (Apnlause.)—Tne resolution was carried 11W3T. ' mously. Mr. James Andery having taken the chair, thaws' were voted to Mr. Pearson for his services, on the motion of Mr. Hooley, seconded by Mr. Wadsworth.

DROWNED IN THE CANAL AT EARLESTOWN, BRAVE AT lEMPT AT ReSCUE. The circumstances attending the death of 'a travelling pedlar named Silyester Lawler, who 1949 drowned in the, London and North-Western Railway Company'S canal eL Earlestown, on Friday night last, were investigated before Mr. Samuel Brighouse, county coroner, at the Ship 10' Newton Common, on Tuesday afternoon. The folloviing evidence was given :—P.C. Samuel Lloyd, stationed at Earlestown, deposed that on the previous Friday eveeing from information he received he went to the canal belong' ing to the London aed North-Western Railway canal. B,e. tween the Ship Inn and the bridge crossing the canal, leen" ing to St. Helens, he "dragged ' the water, with the assist' ance of P.C. Hunt. They commenced to drag at tweet,' minutes past nine, and at 10-40 found the deceased at spot seven or eight yards from the side. His body Was, conveyed to the Ship lan. The man was not known to tue police. They had no suspicion of foul play. In the pockot? they found a pedlar's certificate, number 194, granted; Rochdale on 17th September, 1883, to a person named S, vester Lawler' of Cburch-lane, Rochdale. The decease,' answered to the description on the certificate. He had els° in his possession a pair at spectacles, small bundle of We, a racing calendar, and small slips of paper which he irls, selling as "tips." The papers contained the word "Sae lite."—The Coroner (to the jury): Now, gentlemen, if Ye" want some straight tips, you can have one. (Laughter.)-- P.C. Lloyd (continuing) said he found no marks of violence upon the body.—Mr. Joseph Lythgoe (foreman of the jur)') said he knew the deceased by sight, and had frequently him seen before selling " tips."—Albert Henshaw, collier)? surveyor, residing at 70, Market street, Earlestown, deposed that on the night in question, about five minutes to eight, he was coming along the canal bank. He met the deceased, who asktd him the way to St. Helens, and he replied, " Get on the road, and follow that." He had passed the deceaeed about 80 yards when he turned round and saw him fall in the water. He then ran back, and, throwing off hie the overcoat, jumped in after him. He seized deceased by the shoulder and turned t ) pull him towards the bank. Deceased then caught hold of his (witness's) aro', but he fortunately shook him off. He then sank. sea witness came out of the water. He rose again, and witness thereupon took off his other coat and entered the water again. He seized the deceased by the head, but his (de; ceased's) bat came off and he sank. Witness again cangll' him as he was sinking, but he slipped eut of his gresP" The deceased was positively drunk. Witness then gave it.l: formation to the police.—John Edwards, collier, residing"' Viaduct-street, stated that as he was walking to his work ,at Collins Green Colliery, he saw the deceased at the ShiP Inn. He was then very "heavy" in drink, and witness to went to his work, leaving him in the Inn.—ln ren'Y P.S. Cornmins, witness added that the deceased wanted to sell him some "tips" for the "Grand. National. The de` ceased had no drink in the Inn while he (witness) was Pre; sent.—P.S. Thomas Commins, stationed at Newton, said that. in consequence of finding the certificate produced in posses' Mon of the prisoner he communicated with the Rochdale, police, who replied that the only information they noul" gather about the man was that he once stopped at a lodging' house at Rochdale and whilst there had his license renewed in the name of Lawler. He told one of the -constables that he came from Manchester. Upon the re' ceipt of that letter witness communicated with the Men; chester City Police, but they did not know the deceased anything about him.—The Coroner said they might fajEr assume that the deceased was Silvester Lawler from tuee fact that he had the certificate in his possession.—The PO, returned a verdict of "Accidentally drowned."

VULCAN (A TEAM) V. SUTTON (IST).—These teams met for the second time this season, on Saturday last. at Sutton, and a pleasant and closely contested game resulted in a win for the visitors, wi,o turned up at Sutton with only 11 men, but two substitutes donned jerseys for them, thus making the total two short of the full team. button set the ball in motion, but it was quickly returned by the Vulcan back, and the first scrim- mage was formed in Sutton territory: Vulcan soon began to Press the Buttonites, who were forced to act on the defensive in the first five minutes' play. Button again set the leather rolling, and the forwards going with a rush took the Lail along the field at a good pace, but when they were beginning to look dangerous J Harrison relieved with. a long punt, and a scrim- mage was formed at Sutton 25 flag. On the leather coming loose J Appleton obtained possession, and with a dodgy run round mar aged to get over the line and scored a t, y fur Vul- can. The place kick was not improved upon. Sutton again drepped out from the 25 flag and made another desperate aia tack, their career not being stopped until almost on the goal line. Vulcan gradually forced them back, but the ball came loose on the Sutton side. and A Preseott got possession and falling over the line ob'alned a try for Sutton, who, however, failed at goal. Play was again resumed by a long drrp out by J Harrison, the ball going in touch about Sutton 25 flag. Nrom a line out Vulcan forwards made a grand dribble, Gooch, Wright, Oatherall, and Garside being very conspicuous, and took the bail .over the line, Wright scoring another try for Fulcsn. The kick at goal again failed. -Half-time was called shortly afterwards. No time was lost in changing ends, and the Sattonites made strenuous efforts to again cross the line, but their efforts proved fruitless. Vulcan played a grand da- fensive game, and nothing beyond minor points were scored in the second half. At the call of time victory rested with the Valcanites by two tries, one minor point, to one try, six minor points. Vulcan played a good game all round, notably Joseph Harrison, J Appleton, Wright, and Blair. For Sutton, It McCully, Maitland, A Prescott, and Hunt played best.

HELENS.—Notwitbstanding the unfavourable weather on Saturday, there was an unusu- ally large attendance at these gronnds, when Samuel Delooze, of Downall Green, and It. Hart, of Lodge-lane, Ashton, ran 120 yards level for £l5 aside. Hart was made favourite. The men were despatched to a perfectly even start, but Delooze from some cause or other stumbled and nearly fell, but quickly recovering his feet he made up the lost ground in a surprising manner. div.head: WARRINGTON SCHOOL ATT ENDANCE
div.p: WARRINGTON SCHOOL ATT ENDANCE
COMMITTEES ANNUAL REPORT..
The following is the report of the School Attenclince Committee of the Warrington Town Council for the year ended 31st October, 1883: . .

"In presenting to the Council the report for 1883, your committee would first call attention to the very satisfactory increase in the average attendance of children at the various Public Elementary Schools, as will be seen on examination ' of the accompanying tabulated returns. In 1882 the average attendance at the Public Elementary Schools was 5,884, being an increase on the preceding year of 462. This year the attendance i 6,361, showing a further increase of 477. To these figures must be added the number attending private adventure and other uncertified schools, including the Grammar School, the Blue Coat School. and the Work- house Industrial School at Padgate, namely 791. The total attendance then, for the yeir both at public and private schools may be taken at 7,152. In 1877, at the close of the first year of the work of your committee, the attendance was 5,047, or lin every 7 543 of the population. At the close of 1833 the attendance was 7,152, or 1 in 6.067 of the population, thus showing a very satisfactory increase. The second return deals with the number of children presented for examination at the Public Elementary Schools. The number this year is 7,100, being an increase of 1,250 over the preceding year. The increase in 1852 was 560; and the exceptionally large increase this year may seem to require some explanation. Since the last report of your committee the new Educational Code has come into operation, which requires every child to be pre- sented for examination who has been on the school register for a period of 22 weeks previous to the examination. Under the old code a child before teing eligible for examination must have made 250 attendances I luring the year; now 220 attendances suffice, hence the great increase in the number presented. For each child that may be successful at the examina- tion there is a Government grant allowed, ranging from 17 to 21 shillings per head, according to the number of passes obtained. This system of payment by results neces- sarily acts as an incentive to the teachers; but it may be reasonably doubted whether such a system will prove in the long run altogether satisfactory. Considerable controversy has taken place of late, both in the public press and else- where, with reference to the position of dull children, over- pressure, and over-work, in schools under the new code; but your committee do not desire at present, without further experience, to enter into the discutsion of these matters, inasmuch as they only come in- directly under thei,r notice, and are mole properly subjects for the serious consideration of school managers. Many parents are now beginning to see and appreciate more and more the advantages which regular at- tendance at school provides for their children; but there are also some who are utterly regardless of it, and resort to all sorts of devices and excuses to keep their children at home. Your Committee are now pretty well accustomed to one very trite excuse, viz, that of the alleged severe treat- ment administered to children by the teachers, but they are glad to state that, after investigating these statements, they find that in most cases they are made purely as an excuse, and that complaints of corporal punishment in schools are now much less frequent than they formerly were. Your Committee are bound to deal rigidly with all cases of irregular attendance reported to them, and are compelled in a great number of them to order proceedings to be taken before the magistrates, who willingly support their efforts on all occasions. During the year 391 cases were thus dealt with, and fines ranging from 2s 64 to 5s infi,cted in 374 cases. The amount of fines paid realised £9l 9s 64; last year (1882) the number summoned was 418. The committee, While anxious to deal tenderly with this class of defaulters, find that the only way to enforce regular attendance is to take these proceedings. There have been only six cases committed to the industrial schools during the year, but eight boys in addition have been sent to the training ship Clio. Your committee are dis- inclined to press many cases for committal to industrial schools, lest they should afford encouragement to improvi- dent parents, who would be only too glad to be relieved from the burden of providing for their children at the expense of the town, and who evince every disp mition to let their children drift into the hands of the inspectors in order to get rid pt them. But there are some cases which, in the I interests of the children themselves, most be st dealt with. The total number of children now being maintained in in- dustrial schools is 29, for whom the Council contribute a sum not exceeding in each case 2s 6d per week. No charge is at present made for the maintenance of boys in the training ship Clio, but she is now full, and until vacancies arise, no more can be received.
