div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 1, 1884.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 1, 1884.

-LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD INQUIRY AT WARRINGTON. TUE PROPOSED WIDENING OF BRIDGE-STREET : A WAIL FROM THE TENANTS. Yesterday morning Mr. Thomas Codrington, M. Inst., 0.E., one of the inspectors of the Local Government Board, attended at the Town Hall, Warrington, to hold an inquiry with reference to the proposed wilening, opening, and other- wise improving the west side of Bridge-street, from Bridge Foot to Friars' Gate. The inquiry was held in the Council Chamber, and there were present, in addition to the inspec- tor, the Mayor (Alderman J. Harrison), Aldermen Burgess L and C. J. Holmes, Councillors Wright and Sutton, the Town Clerk (Mr. W. H. Brook), the Borough Surveyor (Mr. T. Longdin), the Borough Treasurer (Mr. G. Chorley), thel Medical Officer of Health (Dr. J. H. Gornall), Mr. William Owen (valuer), and Mr. J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), besides several ratepayers. The plans of the proposed , alterations were laid on the table. The INSPECTOR having read the notice of the Inquiry, called upon the Town Clerk to give a few particulars con- cerning the nature of the improvements contemplated. - The Tower CLI.RE said the subject of the improvement of Bridge-street had teen ender the consideration of the Corporation for a considerable number of years. As late as 1673 a provisional order was obtained enabling the Corpora- tion to widen Bridge-street at the part it was now proposed to widen, and also enabling them to make another improve- ment in a street called Scotland-road. The improvement in Scotland-roadiwas carried out but not in Bridge-st., and the great reason why it was not done was that the estimate which had been originally prepared for the improvement of the two streets was found to be very much less than the al- terations would require. In fact, within a trifle the whole of the estimate was absorbed in the improvement of Scotland- road. That was one and the great reason why the Bridge' street improvement was not carried out. Another reason was that an official of that date ran up in competition with the Corporation in the sale of a valuable piece of property by auction to such an extent that it frightened the Corpora- tion against proceeding any further. A short time ago certain property in Bridge-street came into the matket, and the Street Improvement Committee considered the advisa- bility of acquiring that property for the widening of the street. The property was acquired, and the committee thereupon decided to recommend the Council to carry out the improvement On exactly the same lines as proposed in 1873, and the Council had passed a resolution unani- mously agreeing to proceed with the matter. The inspector might be aware from an examination of the plans and from having seen the property that morning that the street which it was proposed to improve was exceedingly narrow, but he would probably not be aware that that street was the main highway from Lancashire to Cheshire. Then the density of the traffic, particularly on market days, was so great as , to cause a perpetual block. He would point out that the width of the footpath in the:narrowest part was 2ft. llin.,and the width of the carriage way 13f1. llin. The property on the site they proposed to improve consisted of very old shops at the back, and a great number of old cottages. There were 52 cottages in number, and they were cottages which the town had every reason to object to the existence of, but unfortunately the authorities could not deal with them as they existed before the passing of the Public Health Act in 1845. The chairman of the Sanitary Committee was pre- sent, and he would speak independent of the importance of widening the street, of getting rid of this property, which was really such as they could not allow to be built at the present time. The inspector would probably inquire that presuming these cottages were to be pulled down that there was accommodation elsewhere for the tenants who would be turned out, but he was sorry to state that at tha present time there were a great number of houses in Warrington which were empty, and there would be ample accommodation for those who would ba disturbed by the carrying out of the impravement. On the question of the estimate the Town Clerk said the total cost of the property and the making of the street would be Z 31,107, and they estimated the net cost of the improvement 411972. Alderman BURGESS, Chairman of the Sanitary Committee, spoke of the advisability of demolishing the buildings at the back of the street to which the Town Clerk had referred, from a sanitary point of view. There were 58 cottages inhabited by 242 people and the situation was as bad as they could be, and were the centres of disease as a rule. It would be most beneficial that the places should be got rid of and the inhabitants placed in better localities.—The INSPECTOR: You think there are other places for them ? Alderman BURGESS had no doubt that from what the Town Clerk had stated that there were uninhabited houses which would afford the people the accommodation requisite.—The INSPECTOR: And a suitable style of house ?—Alderman BrimEss : Yes. The BOROUGH SURVEYOR (Mr. Longdin), in his evi- dence, stated that the Corporation would acquire 6,145 yards for resale. The Town Clerk had spoken of the density of the traffic in that thoroughfare and its consequent blocking, and as regarded the estimate he thought it might be taken as perfectly correct. Really, there were 72 inhabited cot- tages with a population of 314. The figures given by Alder- man Burgess referred to the courts. The Meeron said be did not think the question of the re- moval of the property in question admitted of controversy, as there was no doubt it was extremely desirable to remove it altogether on the grounds the chairman of the Committee Lad stated, but there was a diversity of opinions amongst the members of the Council as to the desirability of doing it at present, and the principal question was the cost. He had in his hand a letter from one of their aldermen, which ran thus :—" Bowseer Chambers, Warrington, 28th Feb- ruary, 1881.—Dear Mr. Meyoe,—l cannot attend, the inquiry to-morrow as I hrve to go to Manchester, but through you I give my objection to proceeding with the scheme, and prophecy if carried out it will over-charge our ratepayers very heavily. I fear it will cost more than treble the estimate stated by the ex-Mayor. —Yours, JOSEPH Dams." Continuing, the Mayor remarked that it was the opinion of some that the Town Clerk and the Borough Surveyor were over sanguine as to the amount likely to be realised by the re-sale of land. The objections were based upon the supposition that if one por- tion of Bridge-street was widened it would beget the neces- sity ef opening and widening quite up to the top of it. That had operated on some of the minds of the members of the Council and the ratepayere, and raised doubts as to the desirability of proceeding with the matter at present. He need scarcely point out that in almost every part of Eng- land trade was in a paralysed condition, and Warrington was no exception to the general rule, and there were people who thought it would be better to defer the proposed work until they had become more prosperous. Personally he had no objection to this great improvement being carried out if it could be done for anything like the estimate presented to them. Of course he was not in a position to state whether that would be so. The Tower CLERK thought it was necessary he should make a remark on what the Mayor bad said. He was anxious that the Mayor should offer some observations he- nnas he knew his Worship held a letter from Alderman Davies. With reference to the doubt as to whether the improvements could be effected within the es- mate, he would say that the whole of the property had been valued according to the prices for which they knew it could be acquired. With the exception of four properties provi- sional contracts were actually entered into. Those four were put down at prices which the owners were willing to take, and therefore as to the cost there could be no doubt. In respect to the re-sale of land they had put it down at the low sum of £3 per yard. There were present at that inquiry one of the leading valuers in Warrington, and another who was a member of the Town Council, and he would ask those gentlemen to express their views as to whether or not £3 per yard was reasonable. Mr. War. OWEN, valuer, said he was of opinion that £3 per yard was a moderate and fair value of the vacant land back and front. Councillor J. E. WRIGHT, late builder and surveyor, said he had had considerable experience in the valuing of property, and with respect to this matter he thought they ought to get £3 at least for every yard that was to be re- sold. He had an opinion that portions of it wsuld realise more than £3 per yard, and on one occasion when he was in business as a builder he had intimated he was prepared to give more than that himself. Alderman C. J. HOLIIES stated that he had been in busi- ness in Bridge-street many years. He was of opinion that the widening of the street should take place because, inde- pendent of the ques'ion of the cottages, it was one of traffic. In reply to the Mayor, Alderman Holmes expressed himself In favour of commencing the work at once. Alderman Boneless said he was one of those who thought that the widening of the street only 50 feet was not a wise arrangement. If they widened Bridge-street they widened the street with a view to the future of Warrington as well as the present. Bridge-street might, he said, be nearly or quite two miles in length, and he thought it would be an unwise arrangement to limit the widening of the street to 50 feet, He thought it should be at least 60 feet. It would not increase the estimate very much if he was rightly in- formed. It would increase it, he believed, by about -f-2.000. He could not help thinking that if it Ives within the province of the Inspector to alter the width it would be a very desirable thing indeed. If they were to spend money the work Should be done efficiently. If Warrington was not going to increase or extend itself they need not carry out the work, but if Warrington was to grow, as he believed it was sure to do, it would be an unwise arrangement which he to limit the width to 50 feet. Another subject o like to say a word or two was the representation not would on otw will. fotulae ilayor as to the condition of their town. ue w lag to agree with his Worship that the town was °in the condition it was supposed to be. He did not know of a large number of people being out of employment, althooea a reduction of wages was threatened, and which he dare say would take place, in an important branch of industry. It was a fact that the rates, both for le maintenance of the poor and the amount of money required by the Corporation for carrying out im- provements in the borough, were as low as they _had been for the last twenty years. The whole of the rates akt not amount to more than 5s 83 at the present time, which was as low as they had been for the last twenty years. Consequently he did not think the argument of the Mayor had the weight which his Worship deemed it had. He regretted to say that, bat he took it that on such an oc- casion they should speak their mind and say whatever they had to say nn all those subjects. The question had always two sides, and perbape it would be cheaper for them to buy this property now than to wait until they became more prosperous when they would have to pay a bigger ptice for It. (Laughter.) The MAYOR wished to say he was not opposed to the pro- -posal in any way. lie was only a little bit apprehensive

that there was too much truth in what he said, viz., that the condition of Warrington at the present time, commercially speaking, was really very much depressed. He was sure of that. Alderman Burgess, he believed, was an optimist—Ca laugh.)—but he did not t.lame him for that, as they all had their little peculiarities, but he thought the majority weuld agree with him (the Mayor) that the coedition of things in Warrington was much depressed. (Hear, bear.) The TOWN CLERIC pointed out that the works in the town were continually inceeasing. Messrs. Rylands Brothers and White Cross Works had enormously increased of late. The MAYOR remarked that nobody had felt more incon- venience from the state of the traffic in Bridge-street than himself, because he had to drive up and down two or three times a day, and so frequently did he find it in that con- gested state that he did not know what he should have done if he had not exercised that virtue which he possessed to a large extent—patience. (Laughter.) There was no doubt about the remark of Alderman Burgess, when he said that the present was the time to get the property cheap, and he might say that the Town Clerk had been exceedingly for- tunate as far as he had gone. Councillor Surroee, speaking of the value of the land, ob- served that whenever the Corporation had endeavoured to purchase land in that neighbourhood they had, been asked something like £lO per yard. so as regarded the estimate for the re-sale of land he should say was a reasonable esti- mate put down for what they might expect to get for the vacant land He agreed with the Mayor that there could not be two opinions as to the desirability and necessity of widening the street, and, as Alderman Bargess pointed out, it would be a beneficial improvement from a saisitary point of view in getting rid of those tumble-down and filthy cot- tages which existed behind the property. There were a great many empty zottages in Warrington, and it would be better that these should be occupied rather than those behind the Bridge-street proTenty. He did not think the objection was on the ground of removal, but, rather as the Mayor had said, on the ground that the present was not the time for making the improvements. Mr. DoLmeer, a ratepayer, said he represented a certain number of inhabitants in the district where property was to ba condemned, and they thought that inasmuch as trade was so bad It was not the time to effect the alterations proposed. Trade was so bad in that part of the town that they were scarcely doing anything. There had not been a block in Bridge-street for some time—there had net been trade enough. only 50 per cent. of the trading inhabitants were making anything like a living, and that was a great argument be thought in favour of incurring expenses at the present time. They did not argue that the improvement was not needed, as it was quite requisite from a sanitary point of view, but the present they considered was inopportune. He had no doubt many of his neigh- bours would bear him out in what he had stated. He should I like to know whether in view of the proposed imorovement new shops would be erected so that work would not be driven completely out of the street. The Tower CLERIC said those were questions for the Cor- poration. He had no doubt, however, that they would find plenty of people willing to build shops as soon as the land was vacant. They must bear in mind that the Corporation had three years during which to make these improvements, a and it was for the tenants and those interested to make a re- presentatioa to the Corporation as to how long the work should be deferred, or whether they should be effected at

once. Mr. Donal.; said he felt sorry for many of his fellows. Personally, be had shops, one being at Latchford, where he could conduct his business without loss, but there were others who would be removed from the neighbourhood, and perhaps go into a street where they would be doing no trade at all. The Tows CLERK thought that Mr. Dolman misappre- hended the nature of the inquiry that morning. The in- quiry was to know whether or not the property should be acquired within the next three years. If the Corporation did that they could take any time they wished to carry out the improvements. Any representation from tenants must be made to the Corporation through their representatives, mil then tf the Council thought from the arguments which were put before them that it was necessary to deter the work they would no doubt do so. Dr. J. H. GORNALL, Medical Officer of Health, endorsed the views of the Chairman of the Sanitary Committee not only with regard to the back cottages, but to the front houses and shops. The majority of the cottages, he said, were unfit for human habitation, and they had no through ventilation. If the Council had not had the present subject in view he should have been compelled to have brought all the cottages under the notice of the Sanitary Committee with the object of dealing with them under Torrens' Act. Many of the cottages never saw sun-light at • all, and this district is not only a Centre for the development of zy motic disease, but the habitation of diseases of debility and pulmonary consumption. In fact they were a disgrace to civilisation if the places were allowed to exist for a minute. The inquiry then terminated, the INSPECTOR intimating that he would present his report to the Local Government Board with the object of obtaining the provisional order re- quired.

£139,082, is considerably under one penny in the Z. Du- ' ring the past year your coumittee have caused to be made a house-to-house visitation among the working classes throughout the borough, the result of which showed that there were 7,103 cl,ildren attending school. Ia our report for last year we pointed out that there was accommodation at the public elementary schools for 2,728 children over the then requirements, and for 3,221 over the average attendance for that year. Since then a new wing has been added to the St. Ann's School capable of seating 200 more children, and in a short time a new school in connection with floly Trinity Church will be opened, which will accommodate 350 children. There will then be accommodation for 10,156, or for 3,785 more than are now attending school. In addition, there is accommodation at the private schools for 791 children besides.—S. M. WARRINGTON WIREDRAWERS.

PRES gNTATION TO A LATE MANAGER. An event which afforded a pleasant interlude to the momen- tous wages questien now confronting the Warrington wire- drawers took place on Wednesday evening, when the repre- sentatives of the workpeople of Messrs. Rylands Brothers, Limited, waited upon the late manager, Mr. John Chappell, at his residence, Manchester-road, and presented him with a beautiful and substantial souveeir on the occasion of his leaving the employ of the firm. Mr. Chappell has been in the service of Messrs. Rylands Brothers for a period of 38 years, and during the last 14 years he has occupied the position of manager, the arduous duties of which post he lhas discharged no less to the satisfaction of the masters than to the men, as the latter testified on Wednesday evening by their gratifying presentation. The deputation, consisting of Messrs. William Willett, Henry Whitham, Bmjamin Farrar, Thomas Sykes, Alfred Gibson, Thomas Wadsworth, Wm. Woods, Wm. Bullock, Isaac Hicks, and John Little. wood, ware entertained by Mr. Chaperll, and afterwards Mr. Willett was elected to preside. The CHAIRMAN remarked that th 3 event which bad called them together that night was one perhaps each one of them would to a certain extent be delighted with, though it might bring back to their minds things that had happened years ago. Some of them had had the pleasure of working with Mr. Chappell for a long time. He himself had worked at Messrs. Rylands Bros. something like 20 years, during which period Mr. Chappell had also been emplOyed there, and for the last 14 years as manager. In acknowledgment of the manner in which he had discharged his duties they were met as the representatives of the workpeople of Messrs. Rylands Bros. to present to him a testimonial. He did not know that it was necessary for him to say much regarding the testimonial, as they had all had a lengthened acquaint- ance with Mr. Chappell; but he trusted .when Mr. Chap- pell looked upon their testimonial it would awaken within him pleasant memories of the past, and that when it be- came tube handed down to his children as an heirloom they might derive pleasure from the remembrance that it WAS presented to their father by the workp:ople of Messrs. Ry- lands Bros. as a token of the respect and esteem in which he was held by them during the years he was manager to the firm. (Applause.) Mr. WHITHAM then rose at the request of the chairman to make the presentation. He said their business that night was, as the chairman had said, of a somewhat melancholy character. It was to present a testimonial to one who had been with them for a number of years, who had taken an active part in the conduct of Messrs. Rylands Brothers' Works, and who had, as they might say, stood between them and their employers for so many years—he referred to Mr. Chappell. Althaugh he might not have pleased theta often —and at times he had grieved some of tham—he dared say they were quite satisfied of this, if Mr. Chappell had pleased them very much he would have grieved other people—his employers and tbeira. It was a most difficult poeition as they all knew to stand between two opposing forces (as it seemed to him) employers and workmen. That was the position they had got to, and it wee impossible for a man to stand between those forces and satisfy everyone. When they looked back upon the time Mr. Chappell had been connected with the works they mast be surprised at the magnitude to which the trade had attained. When he first went to Messrs.Rylatids Prothers' Mr. Longshaw was the man ager, and he remembered Mr. John Rylands saying at that time that they hardly needed a manager, for if the men would only etielt t 9 their work the place would manage itself. That was in the days when the word with which they were now so familiar—competition—Wa9 seardely thought of. When Mr. Longsbaw left Mr. Chappell succeeded him, and the two gentlemen represented two periods in the history of the wire trade. Mr. Longshaw represented wire drawing in its infancy, so to speak, and Mr. Chappell represented wire drawing in its maturity. What, however, wire drawing was going to still further develops into none of them could say. It was certainly now in a state of transformation ; but whether it would be for its weal or its woe they could not say. Certainly the outlook at present was rather dark. Al- most every other trade had passed through a similar stage, ' during which they had embraced the teachings of science, and used them for the general welfare; and he was satisfied the wire trade would be no exception. Coming to the ob- ject for which they were met, he said it had a melancholy side. The manager who was leaving them was one who well knew his trade, who understood what every man's work was, and how it ought to be done. (Hear, hear.) That he considered was a very important feature in the management of the place. Their manager had now, from various circumstances—ill-health generally, he thought—seen fit to sever his connection with the works. They were all sorry for him. They nearly all of them re- cognised this, that although he had a temper, which made itself known at times, he had a good heart. (Hear, hear.) He was sure, speaking personally, although Mr. dttappell had snubbed him many times, he had always believed Mr. . Chappell was his friend. He had been his friend ever since he came into the town, aad, mere than that, ha had been the friend of his family. He thought Mr. Chappell had been the same friend to many other- men at the works, and had done what he could to help them on. He for one was sorry the time had come for Mr. Chappell to leave the works, and more especially just now. He could say nothing about the trade just now, but be fancied they were all in the same predicament. They were passing through a most important crisis. Whether they should be at work next week or not none of them knew. Appearances seemed to say they should not be at work but on strike. That would be a most unfortunate thing, and no one would deplore it more than he, and he was sure he expressed the feelings of the men when he said they all deplored such an event. On this oc- casion they would not have Mr. Chappell's counsel, and if 1 it was any advantage to them they could say the firm would not have the benefit of his counsel. That possibly might be of benefit to them. When the suggestion of a testi- monial was broached it was heartily responded to by the men according to their means, and all of them would have I liked, under better circumstances, to have met Mr. Chappell and seen the testimonial presented. (Hear, hear.) How- I ever, Mr. Chappell was not, unfortunately, in a robust state of health, and perhaps the excitement of meeting all his old workmen would have still further upset him. They had, therefore, consulted Mr. Chappell's feelings on the matter. They had not invited Mr. Chappell to a banquet, but by a sort of side wind had got Mr. Chappell to invite them to ode. That was a very unusual thing, but it had its advantages for them on the score of economy. (Laughter.) Besides the presentation to Mr Chappell they had also thought fit to make Mrs. Chappell a little present. It was a smell present, but he hoped she might live many years to use it, and that both Mr. and Mrs. Chappell would live many years, not only to enjoy I one another's company, but to look upon the testimonials which he had great pleasure in presenting to them. He trusted Mr. Chappell would see the fingers of the timepiece move round the dial for many years yet, and that when he left them, his sons would take it as a token of the respect in which their father was held by the workpeople of Messrs. Rylands Brothers. (Applause.) The testimonial consisted of a massive marble clock of a rich and chaste design, with handsome real bronze moun- tings, togetner with a very floe pair of bronze statuettes. The clock strikes the hours and half-hours on a tine-toned gong, and goes for 21 days, the whole being fine specimens of workmanship. The present to Mrs. Chappell was a beautiful silver cruet frame, the whole of the articles being supplied by Messrs. G. Blackhurst and Son, Sankey-street. Mr. CHAPPELL, in acknowledging the presentation, told them that he had not left Messrs. Rylands Brothers, nor bad they asked him to leave, as some people said. His re- tirement arose from necessity through illhealth. As some of them had seen, he had stood at the work until he could stand no longer. He could assure them that he was truly sorry to leave the men, as he intended to have had a few more years with them. There was no one at the works be had greater respect for than the two he had left to do his duties. He had nothing against them, and he might tell those present he said to them "If you will follow my example—treat every man according to his abilities and have ne friends, you will find your work easy." He had no Mende, and he found those who had been his best and most attentive workmen had made their work very much more conifertab'e than those who had gone away at times and neglected their duties. That was the great difficulty he had had to contend with, but he could say that the morality and attention of the men at Rylands Bros. was considerably better than it was 14 years ago. He was very sorry indeed that he had to come I away, and he could tell them it was the hardest day's work he had in his life. He still felt the separation, but he hoped he would improve and ultimately recover from its ' effectsals to the dark cloud that was now hanging over the men, some people said be had left on account of that diffi- culty, but be could assure them he never heard a word about It until one hf the men asked him if he had heard anything about the matter. He was truly sorry to leave them all, and truly sorry to leave the old firm. They knew 38 years from the centre of a man's life was a great deal. Messrs. Rylends Bros. had had that out Of him, and he had don. something for them that would stand looking upon both in the yard and in the books when they came to balance up. As Mr. Whitham very truly said it was a difficult matter to be the fulcrum between capital and labour. Still he could not say that he had had much trouble with the office as a rule, though sometimes he bad been somewhat captious when men had neglected their work and thrown others behind in getting goods off. On the whole be thought they had worked together very comfortably: He assured them that he was truly thankful to those pr-teat and those absent who had contributed to the testimonial, and expressed the hope that they would amicably settle their dispute if they possibly could. He urged them to try and avoid a strike for hls sake, because strikes never did any good, and never would. In conclusion he again thanked them from the bottom of his heart for their handsome present. (Ap- plause.) Mr. WILLIAIf CHAPPELL, as the eldest son, acknowledged on behalf of his mother the memento they had presented to

her, assuring them that their gifts would never be forgotten, and that when they looked upon them the presents would remind them of the confidence the workmen had in his father, and that the men felt almost as much regret at part-. in as his father did himself. (Applause.) Mr. B. FARRAR bore his testimony to the good feeling that existed between the workpeople and Mr. Chappell, and hoped when Mr. Chappell's children looked upon the time. piece it would encourage them to try to follow in their father's steps. (Applause.) The remainder of the evening was devoted to a varied entertainment of recitations by members of the depatation, and selections of music by Mr. Ohappell and members of his family, Mr. Chappell contributing three flute solos. 1 The evening concluded with votes of thanks to Mr. and Mrs. Chappell for their hospitality.

Carleton, Anglican Priest, of the parish of Holy Trinity in this town, which contained various statements respecting the Reformed Episcopal Church which were grossly incor- rect. I had not heard of its publication, but at once endeavoured to obtain a copy. The only response I could meet with for some time was that it was printed for '"private circulation," and it was suggested by more than one that the said "priest" Carleton was so ashamed of his own production that he thought it the more expedient course to give it to only a few of his parishioners who may be like-minded with himself. I will allow the intelligent reader to pass his own judgment upon an action of that kind. I have at last succeeded in obtaining a copy, and am pot surprised to find that priestly assumption and incorrect statements are its only characteristics. Mr. Carleton chooses to be "explanatory rather than controversial" for reasons probably best known to himself, though others may perhaps have an idea when they remember that propositions based upon fact and ability to argue are two great essentials in successful argument. 'The sore point with the aggrieved Mr. Carleton evidently is the validity of Bishop Gregg's orders, but he seems to forget that if he succeeds in disprov- ing Bishop Gregg's Episcopate he also shows by the same process of reasoning that Dr. Rvle has no claim to be called a Bishop, nor has Dr. Benson any claim to be called an Arch- bishop. The Reformcd Episcopal Church stands in pre- cisely the same relation to the Establishment as that in which the Establishment stands to the Church of Rome, and any arguments used to establish or to invalidate the claims of the one apply with equal force to the other. The parish priest of Eloly Trinity speaks with bitter sorrow of the departure of those days when the act of the Reformed Church of England in framing "Canons, Constitution, &c." (which by the way may be had of Messrs. Marlborough and Co., Old Bailey) would have been considered as an offence against the authority of the Sovereign, and evidently mourns the fact that liberty if conscience is the inalienable right of every Englishman to-day. "The doctrine that the end justifies the means has usually been considered a Romisk one," says Priest Carleton. Does that explain the reason why he adopted such a Jesuitical method of circulating his libellous tract? Did he adopt that method simply because it WO a Romish one ? Taking Rome as his pattern in other things, it need not be surprising that he also copies her in that. The best exposure of Mr. Carleton's real character and his priestly teaching would be the wide circulation of his oacc tract, which, if it prove anything, fully proves the need alit justifies the existence of Emmanuel Reformed Church in his own parish. For the value to be placed on Mr. Carle- ton's assertions, I would refer your readers to the Reformed Church Record for March, wherein Mr. Carleton is dealt with as he richly deserves for his priestly interference, and which may be had of any respectable bookseller. Hoping that I have not trespassed too much upon your valuable space, and expressing my conviction that the ninth commandment as well as the second is as binding upon " priests " as upon people, I am, sir, yours, dm., WILLIAM MULES,

div.head: WARRINGTON MUSEUM AND
div.p: THE WARRINGTON MUSEUM AND
LIBRARY. CONTEMPLATED ALTERATIONS.

The Museum, Library, and Arts Committee of the Cor- poration have prepared the following report respecting the appropriation of the rooms lately used by the School of Art, and the necessary alterations of the Museum building: —"ln considering the matter of the use of the rooms liberated by the removal of the School of Art, so many points have presented tharneelyete that we have felt it our duty to somewhat enlarge upon Our instructions, and open up several questions, offering to you such a report upon them as shall be full and complete, and, though probably not requiring immediate action under all the heads, give you our opinion, that each portion engaged in shall form part of a whole or complete scheme. The order in which we ask your conlideration to Out tepott is as follows: Ist, repairs that are necessary; 2nd, tentllatifer., and floors strengthening; 3rd, concentration of ' Museum on upper floors, and ground floor left avail- able for extension of Library; 4th, the dividing of the reading-room from the lending department of the Library; sth, general items; and 6th, cost. Ist. We would point out the defective slating, skylights, and lead gutters over the Museum generally, as exhibited by the many places through which the water new finds its way; also the defective state of the brickwork of the chim- ney shafts on the roofs. These matters require immediate attention, and the whole of the woodwork on the roofs and to the whole building outside requires scraping, cleansing, and painting—some three good coats, as it has net bed attention for seven years. We find that since our attention was first called to this, the General Purposes Committee has taken up the question, and men are at work. The gutters should be provided with snow boards to pre- ' vent overflow, and to protect the lead from the boots of workmen. 2nd. We would call your attention to the ventilation of the reading room, which remains anything but good; and we recom- mend the adoption of four divided tubes in the angles of the old School of Art, running from the ceiling of reading room directly through the roof, creating a syphon of draught, and so supplying fresh while extracting the foul air. The com fort of the reading room would also be increased by cover- ing the pipes under the floor with some non-conducting material. The floor of the late School of Art is weak in the extreme, and the eimple walling of one or two visitors, while inspecting cases in the centre of the room, would be sufficient to throw out of position any small objects, and render any collection liable to disarrangement. The joists and beams require examination, and a scheme devised for rendering them sufficiently strong for the purpose, without more than a very slight deflection. 3rd: We propose for your consideration the removal of the entire collection of fishes, birds, and shells from their two present moms to the new room (late School of Art); the fishes and birds being arranged in new wall-cases all round the room, and the shells in their posent cases in the centre. For these purposes the centre lefttern light will be admirable and ample, and the skylight and window may be darkened to render the room symmetrical. By the removal of these collections we shall have two rooms into which can be taken the antiquities now occupying two rooms down stairs, and thus we shall have available for library extension the whole of the ground floor. In the event of this being carried out, we should recommend a wrought-iron wicket gate be- ing hung at the foot of the stairs, that, on closed days for the museum, visitors will be prevented passing up. 4th: The growth of the reading department, and its usefulness, demands that we should give attention to the comfort and convenience of the readers, and this cannot be better done in the first instance than by the removal of the lending depart- ment into a separate room, where the bustle, movements, and noise necessary in the obtaining of books shall not in- terfere with the readers. How to separate these departments, and yet maintain due oversight of both, without increase of staff, has entailed some thought; but we are of opinion that a plan has been arrived at by which the departments can be separ4ted entirely, larger space given to the readers, better access to the bookshelves provided for, whilst proper super- vision of each department is maintained, and without an increase of the stiff. The reference library can also be brought into use if required; and the objectionable crossing of the reading room to the lecture room can also in a great measure be avoided. A glance at the plan with this report will better explain this. We propose to use the local antiquity room (or Warrington room) for the lending department, and through the door opening of this room all would enter who wanted the library department, those to borrow books pass- ing through a pair of glazed doors to the left, and the readers through similar doors to the right. The present entrance to reading room would be blocked up, and the counter removed to the opposite end of the room. The Librarian and Attendant will have access to either counter of reading room or lending library, and through the glass screen will see everyone approach. In the lending department as much book apace can be obtained by an arrangement and shelving as in the present reading room. The antiquity room on the north side of the hall might be of use for comMitte room or spare room. sth : General Items.—Amongst the general items of work (some of which we suggest and others that are necessary), upon which it is needless we should enter into detail, are the following :—The alteration of hot water piping where inter- fered with ; the plastering of the walls in reading room; the painting throughout the building inside; new bookcases for the lending library and counters there ; and in the reading room the covering of certain floors with kamptuli- curn, or other soft material; and the re-arrangement of the gasfittings and service pipes in several rooms. We would recommend that the town over the Curator's house should be thrown into it, and a small stair fixed to communicate with it; that the sufferance light be blocked tap, and a light opened on our own ground ; with etudded partitions, a bedroom and bath-room can be formed, and as there is already a water supply a bath would render the place complete at little cost. 6th: cost.—We recommend that the General Purposes Committee be requested to undertake the structural altera- tions, and all partitions, and then the Museum, Library, and Arts Committee will be in a position to pay for the remainder out of ordinary revenue by spreading over two years. We have not prepared any approximate estimate of the total cost, as in the present report we are deatince only with general schemes, and do not propose to enter into de- tail until we have the intructions of the committee to pro- ceed further.—We are, gentlemen, Yours faithfully, William Beamont, S. M. Webster, Wm. Fell, Wm. Owen. With respect to the foregoing, the General Purposes Committee who considered the matter, hare passed the following resolution :—" That this committee apsrove the structural alterations suggested in the report, and request the Museum Library, and Arts Committee to submit a detailed estimate of the probable cost."

ALLEGED WIFE DESURTIO/C—On Wednesday, at Prescot Police Court, Edward Id‘Tague, a labourer at Sutton Lodge Chemical Works, St. Helens, and formerly a saltcake worker at Widnes, was charged on warrant with deserting his wife and seven children.—Mr. Hartley, clerk to the Pretest Union, stated that for the last three years the prisoner had scarcely done anything at all towards maintaining his wife and children. In August, 1883, he was committed for two months for neglecting them, and when he came out of Prison the Guardians milted him to make some arrangement, especially as his wife was suffering from puerpural fever, but he refused to do an, and left the district, and it was only on Saturday last that it was ascertained whet* he was. The family bad cost the Guardians £llO through, the pri. sonar's neglect,—The prisoner was remanded,

div.head: TEE REV. E. C. E CARLETON
div.p: TEE REV. E. C. E CARLETON
AND THE REFORMED CHURCII, WARRINGTON.

"Are Dr. Gregg's followers really members of the Church of England ?" is the question discussed in a tract issued for parochial circulation by the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, 8.A., vicar of Holy Trinity, Warrington. In the preface Mr. Carleton states:—

My attention has been drawn to the inconvenience likely to arise from the new Dissenting body in my parish which uses the name of the Church of England, and in other ways contrives to give the impression to many unthinking people that it is in some way connected with the Established Church. There is a possibility that some who attended the " Confirmation " lately held by Dr. Gregg in the chapel to which I refer may think that they were receiving a rite which would admit them to Holy Communion in the Church of England. As this is a matter upon which there ought to be no mistake, I take the opportunity of the approaching Confirmation to be held by the Bishop of Liverpool in this town to write in the form of a tract a few words which may possibly remove any such misconception. Under the heading, "Dr. Gregg's Followers," Mr. Carleton then proceeds to say that his object in writing is to remove a wrong impression. " I shall, therefore," he observes, " strive to be explana• tory rather than controversial, and endeavour also to keep in view the unlearned reader.. It may seem strange that it . . . .

should be necessary to explain that Dr. Gregg is not a Churchman, and that his followers are not Churchmen ; but nevertheless the necessity exists. There are some who are led astray by the adoption of the Church's names, the use of her titles, the wearing of vestments,. the ringing of . .

, bells, Lo., and have unthinkingly allowed themselves to believe that, in some way or other, this body is connected with the Church of England. This, however, is so entirely incorrect that I think it a duty to du what I can to clear away the misconception. Dr. Gregg is really as much out- side the Church as is the most dissident Dissenter. If he presented himself for Holy Communion in any of her places of worship he would be rejected. Ile has no authority to perform any rite or ceremony within the Chat ch of England, and those who went to him to be ' con- firmed ' should understand that what he did upon that . . .

occasion cannot be recognized in the Church; it has DO real validity; and before any of those individuals could be permitted to receive Holy Communion in the Church of England it would be necessary for them to be confirmed again." Having pointed out that the body to which Dr. •Gregg belongs is really of American origin, also that "there is only one Reformed Church of England' in this country, and Dr. Gregg does not belong to it," Mr. Carleton asserts that Dr. Gregg's " use of the name, therefore, is unwar- ranted." Mr. Carleton next shows that what authority Dr. Gregg professes to have he obtained from a certain Dr. Cummins, who was for a time an assistant bishop in America, but was deprived of his position. The writer then continues,-4 Dr. Gregg himself publicly renounced his membership of the Church of England in the year 1872, ostensibly on account of what is called 'the Bennett Judgment.' Now, a man cannot renounce membership of a body and at the same time be entitled to it. Therefore, neither he nor the body he has formed have any connection with the Church of England." After quoting the 12th canon of the Church of England in order to show that it is unlawful for any sort of ministers or lay persons to make canons, &c., Mr Carleton points out that Dr. Gregg has done just what the canon condemns.-IThe body to which be belongs has Its canons, constitutions, &c. His conduct in setting forth these instruments is not only an offence against the Church, but was also regarded in past days as an offence against the authority of the sovereign, and a violation of the constitution. Orangemen especially, who regard that constitution with loyalty, should bear this in mind. Dr. Gregg, nevertheless, calls the body to which be belongs by the name of the Church of England. He designates him- self Bishop on the strength cf what Dr. Cummins could confer upon him' m who was himself deposed from his episcopal office; and sow he (Dr. Gregg) professes to lame letters of orders, licenses, and other instruments, none of which are worth the paper they are written tipotl, as anyone who relief) on them will find to his cost." Mr. Carleton concludes as follows It is not enough to have good ends in view, we must likewise use honest means for their attainment. The doctrine that the end justifies the means has usually been considered a Romish one. There is, indeed, nothing that so effectually gives a handle to unbelievers as want of moral principle amongst men professing religion. As this body his chosen to locate itself in my parish, I necessarily feel some responsibility lest there should be any misunderstand- ing. I therefore desire to have its character plainly repre- sented. It is Dissent without the consistency which en- titles it to respect. It is Dissent passing under the guise of conformity. . . . . I have said quite sufficient to make the least intelligent reader understand that this new body is not, and has no connection with the Church of England, and that those who have joined it have joined the ranks of Dissent in its most un- desirable and least reasonable form." Bishop Gregg replies to the pamphlet in the March number of the Reformed Church Record, the organ of the "Reformed Church of England," as follows : " Most people agree with the Earl of Shaftesbury in thinking that the day is very near when we shall see the total extinction of the Church of England as the Estab- lished Church of the country.' Feeling that her end is near, many ecclesiastical undertakers have been and are busy in preparing her shroud and her coffin. The latter is being studded with nails so that she may be decently buried, and , that the minds of the onlookers may be diverted from the I body to its surroundings. All kindsof ecclesiastical car- penters are at work that at least she may have a respectable interment. Her glory is departed through the introduction of the mummeries of Rome, and the hour of her sepulture as the establishment of this land is very very near. We fully believe the words of one of our correspondents that 'The final struggle will come on very soon after the suffrage and redistribution questions are settled' and the rallying cry, spoken of by Bishop Gregg in 1875 in his pamphlet on The Church.' will very soon be ' The Disestablishment and Disendowment of the Church of England.' Now one person who has recently endeavoured to drive another nail in the coffin of the Establishment is a certain Mr. Carleton, of Warrington, who has written a libellous tract on what he Is pleased to .call a New Schism,' by which he seems to mein The Reformed Church of England The fact is Mr. Carleton is, we believe, a priest' in the Establishment, and, like Demetrius of old, he evidently writes as one whose craft is in danger.' We feel sorry for poor Mr. Carleton. Doubtless his parish ' feels the effect of Emmanuel (Reformed) Church situated therein, and pos- sibly some of his flock have wandered thither to find better pasture in an Evangelical and Protestant Church than is to be gathered from the Sacerdotalism of the Establishment. Mr. Carleton has written his tract for the unlearned' and for 'the least intelligent' people in Warrington, England, or elsewhere. How kind! and he actually asks them ('the unlearned' and the least intelligent') to believe, what, if Mr. Carleton were not 'a priest' we should be inclined to call by a name which might real, Mr. Carleton's temper; and in the guileless simplicity of his least intelligent' readers this 'priest' appeals to orangemen. We have learnt for the first time from Priest Carleton that orange- men ' are the unlearned ' and 'least intelligent' of the community. But just to know what the statements of this priest, in his tract, are worth, let us take one as a sample of many; and we con assure our readers that in four pages of leaded type, of which this tract consists, we have counted more than twenty statements just as reliable as the following, which this priest' asks the unlearned' and least in- telligent' people of Warrington and elsewhere to believe. The statement by which we test the others is this : Mr. Carleton alleges that Bishop Gregg Gregg (whose episcopate perhaps Mr. Carleton does not know, is from the Bishops of the primitive church through the See of Canterbury), pub- licly renounced his membership of the Church of England in the year 1872, ostensibly on account of what is called the Bennett judgment.' Truly Mr. Carleton's readers must indeed be the unlearned' and the least intelligent' (does he refer to his own congregation?) if they accept such a statement as true. Let us see what it is worth. (1) Bishop Gregg has never 'publicly renounced his membership of the Church of England at all; neither, so long as there is an Established Church, of which everyone in the State is a mem- ber, can he legally do so. He is still a 'priest' by his letters of orders as even Priest Carleton. (2) It was not in the year 1872 that Bishop Gregg resigned his benefice of East Harborne. (3) Bishop Gregg did not resign his Vicarage owing to the Bennett judgment.' (4) The Bennett judgment' was not pronounced in the year 1872. (5) Bishop Gregg never publicly renounced' anything owing to the Bennett judgment: So that we have here in less than three lines, no less than five priestly dicta which 'the unlearned' and the least intelligent' are asked to believe on the authority of the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton. But what will not a priest ask the ignorant to believe, when the figments of Auricular Con- fession, Baptismal Regeneration, Priestly Absolution, and the Real Presence are taught by the ecclesiestical sect of which Mr. Carleton announces himself as a Vicar? If such be the weapons of Mr. Carleton, we pity the cause which he endeavours to support. He has succeeded simply in adding another nail to the coffin of the Establishment. In refer- ence to the above bold assertion of this Warrington priest Iwe say to all intelligent readers ex uno disce omnes (i.e., from one of his statements learn the value of them all). [6ince the above was written, we have observed that Mr. Carleton's tract is 'for parochial circulation.' Can it be that all the intelligent members of his congregation have gone to Emmanuel (Reformed) Church, leaving with Mr. ICarleton what he is pleased to call the unlearned' and the least intelligent? R G.R.]
We have receivel the following letter on the same eubject : Sir,—Some time ago I was asked by a friend if I were 'aware of the publication of a tract by the Rev. E. C. E.

div.head: LATEST NE WS.
div.p: LATEST NE WS.

THE SOUDAN REVOLT. REPORTED BATTLE NEAR TRINKITAT. A Cairo telegram, dated yesterday afternoon, says : Rumours are current that a battle has been proceeding between Major General Graham's forces and the enemy since seven o'clock this morning. No authentic intelligence has, however, yet reached headquarters here. The Central News learns that the battle between the British expeditionary force and the rebels under Osman Digna opened shortly before seven o'clock yesterday morn- ing, at about six miles from Fort Baker. The enemy, num- bering from 10,000 to 12,009, advanced to attack with de- termination. The result of the engagement is not known yet, but firing was still going on when this message was despatched.

div.head: DYNAMITE OUTRAGES.
div.p: THE DYNAMITE OUTRAGES.

The Central News says the most elaborate arrangements have been made at the Great Northern, Midland, and North- Western stations to guard against dynamite attempts on their property. Each parcel left at the cloak room at any of the terminus is carefully inspected before being taken in, and in the case of the Great Northern instruotions have been given to the clerk in charge to insist upon inspecting the contents of any trunk or other parcel which from its weight or other circumstances he may consider suspicious. In addition to these precautions the Great Northern Company have engaged a large staff of private detectives, who keep a most careful watch on the platform and the various waiting and other rooms and offices at each of the London stations of the three companies men- tioned. The left luggage is frequently inspnted, but up to the present nothing of a suspicious character has been brought to light. The incoming and outgoing Irish mail trains and expresses at Easton Station are carefully watched by a special staff of Scotland Yard detectives. The police are still pursuing active enquiries both in this country and in America and in France, but so far their efforts have not been rewarded with any measure of success. It is under- stood that the authorities are convinced that the large quantity of dynamite—nearly 19 pounds in all—used in the I three attempts already dikcovered could not have come from

_ America by way of Liverpool, or any of the ports connected with the American trade. It is in fact considered certain that it was conveyed from New York to Havre by one of the French steamship lines, and thence brought to Dover or Folkestone, where the Customs' Inspector is much less strict. This is the more probable because it is known there are at present in Paris unusually large numbers of Irish revolutionists, including, it is believed, the famous Captain Maccafferty, who would, of course, find Havre a safe and most convenient trysting place with their friends arriving from America. It was announced some few months ago that a number of English detectives had been stationed permanently in New York, charged with the work of watching the leaders of the American Irish dynamite faction, but their vigilance has evidently been at fault. They have, however, been instructed by cable to make enquiries into the character and prece- dents of every person who left New York and Boston since the beginning of February.

Six hundred Bury cotton weavers have struck work against a proposed reduction of 5 per cent. in wages. At Northampton yesterday morning, the Mayor presented Police-constable Hickman with a certificate and medal of the Royal Humane Society for gallantly rescuing a man ' Who jumped IMO riTor Ilene to c1f9,91 MBI!c!f; A uriasgow newspaper states it is reported dial accept-, ances of a large and well-known East Indian firm in Glas- gow were returned yesterday. The liabilities are said te be very large, and are due to serious depreciation in value of foreign and colonial produce. This failure is said to be one of the most serious that has occurred in Glasgow since the collapse of the city of Glasgow Bank in '7B. ANOTHER STRIKE AT DARWEN.—The weavers at Mr. W. T. Ashton's, Hope Mill, Darwen, again strack work yester- day morning, when they complained of being underpaid. Mr. Ashton allowed four of them, with the weaver's secre- tary, to reckon up his sorts, and the result shows that they were overpaid, and will have to come down to standard list. They now strike against this, alleging that their selretary has blundered in his reckoning. The mill contains over 600 looms.

EXTRAORDINARY SCENE AT A WRECE. Yesterday morning about ;a dozen labourers, who had been engaged salving the cargo of the wrecked steamer Geofredo, were brought to the Liverpool receiving-house in a helpless state I of drunkenness through broaching the salved cargo of epirite, Mod Of the Men had fallen in the water, and it was reported that one was drowned. Some of them had to be conveyed to the police-station in a handcart. RENAREABLE RESTITUTION OF STOLEN JEWELLERY.— A couple of months ago the shop and warehouse of Messrs. M'Clelland, at Sheffield, Birmingham and Sheffield mer- chants, was broken into and a number of watches and other articles of jewellery stolen. The thieves were never traced. On Wednesday a boy came to the shop, bringing with him a large parcel, and saying he had boeu told to leave it. On I its being opened the whole of the stoles goods and others which had not been missed were found. ALLEGED EXTRAORDINARY OUTRAGE IN IRELAND.—The Freeman's Journal says that while a commercial traveller named White was driving near Ballaghadereen, County Mayo, he was met by five men armed with guns, and one fired at him. Mr. White was unhurt, and asked the min what he did that for. The man replied, again pointing the gun at him, "I will put the contents through you." At the same instant some of the other men fell upon Mr. Whi e, knocked him down, inflicting injuries on the nose and finger of the left hand. After some time begot on the car again and followed the whole party, who kept together till they came to the entrance of the military barracks at Billagha- dereen. He came up to them as they were in the act of shutting the gate and demanded their names. The response was a kick and a jeer. He turned away and proceeded straight to the police barrack where he reported the affair. The constable to whom be made his complaint ordered him Out on the spot ander pain of arrest. Mr. White departed, and on the next day, the 22nd, deposed upon oath the circumstances before the resident magistrate at Ballagha- dereen. Subsequently several arrests were made.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.

On the convention relative to the slave in Central Africa, Earl CARNARVON criticised General Gordon's pro- clamation.—Earl DERBY replied that lOCLI Circumstances warranted it.—The Marq-uis of SALISBURY complained that the proclamation tore up the treaty of Paris.—Earl GRAN- VILLE stated no information had been received of fighting at El Teb.—The Matrimonial Causes Bill was read a third time.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.

_ MEETINGS OF THE NATIONAL LEAGOE.—TIiti SOLICITOR- GENERAL for IRELAND, replying to Mr. Macartney, said the Government were advised that no sufficient reason existed for instituting prosecutions against persons who held meet- ings of the National League in spite of the proclamation of the Lord Lieutenant, and proclaiming the same in the county of Derry. The matter had been much exaggerated. MILITARY OPERATIONS IN EGYPT.-Sir S. NOWT/COTE asked if the Government.could give the House any further information as to military operations in Egypt.—Lord HART- INGTON said up to the present time he had received no tele- grams. He had had no telegrams at all direct from General Graham.

INHABITED HOUSE DUTY —On the motion for going into Committee of Supply, Alderman Lay:mimes moved a reso- lution in favour of the repeal of the Inhabited Rouse Duty Acts in order to facilitate the erection of dwellings for the working classes. He pointed out the ineqaalities that at Present existed, and said If his motion were agreed to practical steps would be taken towards improving the dwellings of the poor.—Mr. COURTENAY promised full con- sideration to the Points raised, and hoped, in short, such alterations might be made that would render the tax one that should be conserved rather than abolished.—A discus- sion ensued, in which Messrs. Grantham, Hubbard, and Peddie took part.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCEMITTER admitted inequalities existed. He could not consent to abo- lish the tax, but he hoped the time was not distant when it could be placed on a more satisfactory footiug.—The motion of Alderman LAWRENCE was negatived without a divi- sion.

THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD —Lord G. HAMILTON called attention to the conduct of the Local Government Baard in erecting a fever hospital on Winchnaore C. RUSSELL defended the action of the Board and denied it was such as to bring the principle of local self-government into disrepute.—The subject then droppped. SUPPLY.—The House then went into Committee of Supply on the Supplementary Civil Service Estimates.—On the vote for the supplementary sum of ten thousand pounds for secret service, Mr. SEXTON objected to the vote, and desired that it should be postponed until there was a fuller attend- ance of members.—Mr. GLADSTONE defended the vote. He said the Government could only ask for this vote as confi- dence, and expose themselves to whatever might be said as to their not giving details as regarded the expenditure of the money.—Mr. ARTHUR O'CONNOR s4d as there was an ob- jection to give details he would simply ask for the amount of the secret money spent in Ireland.—On a divis'on 40 members voted for and 60 against. The vote was agreed to.

ASSAULT ON A TRAM-CALL CONDUCTOR.—Warrants were issued at the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, in de- fault of appearance, for the arrest of two men,. named Dennis McCue and John Woods, who were charged with having assaulted Henry Dutton, a tram-car conductor, and also with having damaged a tram-car.—Mr. Swift appeared I on behalf of the St. Helens and Districts Tramways Co. te prosecute.—The facts of the case were that on Saturday night. the 16th Otinao, Dutton was in charge of the ten o'clock tram-car from St. Helens to Haydock. Whilst the car was standing at a crossing in Parr-street the two defen- dants got on to, the vehicle, and although they were told ny the conductor that the inside of the car was full, and that they most not go in, they pushed a way up the midele of the car flinging their arms aboat and knocking one woman down. Afterwards one of them struck the con- ductor, pulled him off the c.ar by his mufller, and knocked I him down, when both of them kicked him. As the car was moving off one of the men picked up a stone and threw it at Dutton, whom it, however, missed, and broke the tram-oar window, the splinters of glass also cutting this head of a child in the (AL—Warrants were issued,
